title: Soutien à Gino et aux antifas incarcéré·es : rassemblement place Mazagran mercredi à 18h30
content:
Le 19 août, la cour d'appel de Paris a rendu un avis favorable à l'extradition vers l'Allemagne de Gino, militant antifasciste interpellé

pour s'être opposé aux néo-nazis hongrois à Budapest en février 2023

. Il y risque jusqu'à 10 ans de détention et surtout une extradition vers la Hongrie où la peine sera plus lourde encore. Suite à cette décision, un pourvoi en cassation a été déposé par les avocats de Gino, laissant un délai de 40 jours pour statuer définitivement.


Le 30 septembre, la justice française doit se prononcer sur la possible remise de Gino à l'Allemagne.


Zaid A. se trouve lui aussi en France et risque une extradition vers la Hongrie. C'est pourquoi le Comité Solidarité Budapest appelle à une mobilisation le 30, et notamment à un meeting antifasciste contre l'extradition de Gino à la Bourse du Travail de Paris.


À Lyon, l'attente de cette décision de justice résonne avec la repression des antifascistes dans le cadre de

la mort du néo-nazi Deranque

, survenue en février dernier. le 24 septembre,

8 nouvelles interpellations ont eu lieu

.


Le contexte, est partout le même : celui d'une criminalisation croissante de l'antifascisme, alors même qu'on assiste à une résurgence des forces fascistes et réactionnaires à travers l'Europe. Partout, les antifascistes sont poursuivis, réprimé·es, emprisonné·es parce qu'iels s'opposent de manière conséquente à cette situation.


En écho à la mobilisation à Paris contre l'extradition de Gino, et en soutien à tous·tes les antifas incarcéré·es, on se rassemble à Lyon


 Mercredi 30 septembre

 Place Mazagran

 À partir de 18h30


Retrouvons-nous pour échanger autour de la criminalisation de l'antifascisme. On vous propose de

ramener de quoi boire un coup et grignoter

, mais aussi des feuilles et stylos, pour participer si vous le souhaitez à

 un atelier d'écriture

. On tentera aussi de

créer ensemble une banderole

 en soutien à Gino et à tous·tes antifas incarcéré·es (n'hésitez pas à ramener peinture et bâches si vous en avez

 

!).

author: Husam Mahjoub
title: The war Abu Dhabi didn’t need to fight
content:
Several outside actors have stoked the flames of war in Sudan, but none has had as great an impact as the United Arab Emirates. The evidence of its destructive role is overwhelming, but the Gulf kingdom’s Western allies have turned a blind eye to it.

At one time or another, Sudanese governments have hosted, armed, or tolerated rebels and opposition groups from all of the country’s neighbors, from Egypt and Libya to Uganda and Ethiopia. Sudan’s neighbors have repaid the favor, and a range of outside actors are now involved in the Sudanese civil war.

Key supporters of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) include Chad, Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, and South Sudan. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Eritrea support the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the de facto government. Among all the external actors, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) is the most consequential, even though it has the least reason to be involved.

Every other external actor has a stake in Sudan that derives from geography, security exposure, or the influx of Sudanese refugees. Even Saudi Arabia, while not a land neighbor, shares the Red Sea coastline with Sudan and has a direct interest in stabilizing its western maritime frontier.

The UAE has no security interest, no shared border or river, and no reason to be concerned about refugees reaching Emirati territory. We can only understand its role in Sudan as part of a broader subimperial project that rests on four connected strategic pillars.

The first pillar is economic hegemony. RSF-controlled mines in Darfur feed gold smuggled to Dubai, often routed through South Sudan, Egypt, Chad, or the Central African Republic. This gold can be monetized into hard currency that sustains the war while giving the UAE leverage over Sudan’s economic and political trajectory.

Beyond gold, Sudan is also a critical node in the UAE’s continent-wide strategy of port and logistics dominance, part of an investment program now worth more than $110 billion across the continent, with dozens of port concessions, dry ports, and logistics hubs. Controlling Sudan’s ports, land, and mineral wealth is one of the reasons the war serves Abu Dhabi’s interests.

The second pillar is political expansion. Sudan is a strategic frontier in the UAE’s broader effort to project political influence across Africa without incurring the costs of formal empire. A subimperial power is not a global imperial force; rather, it acts as an imperial actor within its own regional sphere while aligning its actions with the overarching interests of a global power like the United States. Sudan’s gold, its fertile agricultural land, its Red Sea coastline, and its sheer size make it a central testing ground for that project.

The third pillar is the UAE’s desire to counter Islamist political movements and the influence of Iran. Abu Dhabi has been willing to cooperate with Islamist governments, including Omar al-Bashir’s regime in Sudan, whenever doing so served its interests, just as it has long functioned as a conduit for Iran to evade international sanctions. What its leaders actually oppose is not political Islam or Iran as such, but any political force, whether Islamist, secular, socialist, or democratic, that threatens their preferred regional order.

The final pillar is a concern with regime survival and fear of democratic contagion. The roots of this concern go back to 2011, when the Arab uprisings confronted the UAE with an existential threat to its own model of governance. It responded by becoming an organized counterrevolutionary force across the region, intervening by different means in different countries.

Such interventions included bankrolling the coup that brought Abdel Fattah El-Sisi to power in Egypt and backing the militia of Khalifa Haftar in Libya. In each case, a popular or revolutionary movement threatened a regional order Abu Dhabi wanted to preserve, and Abu Dhabi acted to reverse it.

Sudan’s December 2018 revolution set off the same reflex. This was not because Sudan threatened the UAE materially, but rather because a successful democratic transition next door to the Gulf, achieved by ordinary people rather than by elites, might offer a dangerous model to its own population and to the wider region it is working to shape.

Those four pillars don’t operate through the UAE alone. Most of the states that serve as the RSF’s enablers are not acting solely out of an independent interest in what happens to Sudan. They are acting, to varying degrees, on the …

author: Moataz Hagag, Mada Masr
title: Italian court sentences 3 Egyptian officers to jail in Regeni murder case
content:
An Italian court

sentenced

 on Monday three Egyptian security officers to 10 years imprisonment in absentia for the 2016 kidnapping of Giulio Regeni.

 


The convicted officers are Major Magdy Sherif of the National Security Agency and police officers Colonel Ather Kamal and Colonel Hesham Helmy. 


The court dismissed the charge of

conspiracy to commit aggravated murder

 that was leveled against Sherif, while another security official implicated in the case,

Major General Tarek Saber, was acquitted of all charges.

 


The Italian prosecution had requested in its closing arguments a life sentence for Sherif and 17 years and six months for the three other defendants.


“A ruling issued in the name of the Italian people, a ruling that stands as a safeguard for all the Giulios and Giulias of the world,” said Alessandra Ballerini, the family’s lawyer. Ballerini added that the verdict proves that the body of evidence presented before the court withstood its scrutiny.


“From this evening on, all regimes, along with their apparatuses and agents, will be forced to remember that human dignity is inviolable, as are human bodies; that impunity can be defeated; and that democracies can put a stop to arbitrary abuse,” she added.


Riccardo Noury, Amnesty International Italy’s spokesperson, believes the verdict played an important role in “scratching the wall of impunity built by the Egyptian authorities, since it found three security service officials guilty of a serious crime of international law. It is a victory for human rights and for accountability.”


But Noury added that a full read out of the verdict needs to take place. “There was not sufficient evidence to corroborate the charge of murder. As for the crime of torture, no one of the accused was found guilty, because in 2016 torture was not recognized as a crime in the Italian law. Otherwise, the sentences could have been harder.”


Yet, “the Italian judiciary was our best ally,” Noury concluded, adding that the Italian authorities might not welcome the verdict.


In his

statements

 following the verdict, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said that “Egypt has not been convicted, three people have been convicted,” in a nod to how the verdict would not affect bilateral relations.

  


Tajani was

in Cairo

 earlier in September to sign off some bilateral agreements concerning human trafficking and irregular migration.

Meanwhile, Italian Prime Minister Georgia Meloni made a

major visit to Egypt in March 2024

, alongside other European leaders, to sign off the “comprehensive strategic agreement” between Egypt and the European Union, which elevated relations, including with a 7.4 billion euro in financial support.

 


On the Egyptian front, a government source told Mada Masr that a high-level call between the Egyptian and Italian leaderships took place ahead of the verdict to find a legal way out that takes into consideration the nature of bilateral relations. 


According to Italian law, there are levels of appeal before a final ruling is reached, and it is not believed at this time that there will be any

requests

 for the accused’s extradition to Italy.

 


***


A PhD student at the University of Cambridge, 28-year old Regeni had been in Egypt studying independent trade unions when he disappeared from a downtown Cairo metro station while on his way to meet a friend on January 25, 2016, the fifth anniversary of the 2011 revolution. His body was found just over a week later on February 3 by a highway on the outskirts of Cairo.


Upon hearing that a body had been discovered, then-Italian ambassador to Egypt Maurizio Massari promptly

visited


Zeinhom morgue.


He and his entourage were at first refused entry but after their insisting were allowed in, where they found Regeni’s body disfigured, showing marks of heavy torture.

 


A joint Italian-Egyptian investigation was launched.

Egyptian investigators

initially

 denied that Regeni’s body bore marks of torture and gave a number of narratives behind his murder, including that he died in a car accident, before announcing in March 2016 that they had

killed

 five members of a criminal gang specialized in robbing foreigners and impersonating police officers, as well as the discovery of Regeni’s passport and personal belongings in a flat owned by one of the gang members’ sister.

 


Italian investigators

rejected

 this account, with information subsequently showing that the gang’s alleged leader …

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: Akoko Akech
title: Homa Bay: The Road to Afgoonistan and the Van-goons of Democracy
content:
The political violence that characterized Linda Mwananchi’s forceful entry into Homa Bay and earned the county online mimetic mockery and nicknames such as Afgoonistan or Yemen didn’t begin in either the dust bowls of its lakeside town of Nyandiwa or the dusty roads of the county’s Ruma National Park, the route that the Linda Mwananchi entourage took to the heart of Homa Bay County, Asego ka DC, the administrative headquarters. 


It began in India with the intestate death of Raila Odinga. For over two decades, Raila’s charismatic leadership and competitive presidential ambition singularly disciplined both leaders and voters in Nyanza. Although it was the magnet that attracted disciplined ideologues, crass opportunists, and fellow travellers in Nyanza’s politics, it held competing egos and political ambitions in check. It also maintained a delicate balance within ODM: the contradictory or opposed politics of protest against the powers that be and the politics of protecting the powers that be, as the case may be, as well as the Luo elite politics of righting the wrongs of Kenya’s postcolonial state primarily as a national common good and only secondarily as a particular Luo ethnic good.    


Raila is dead. It is the end of an epoch. A new leadership struggles to be born in his Nyanza strongholds. Now it is time for monsters: castration angst, misogyny, sexism, mythical histories of Luo origins and migration, the bitter historical memories of postcolonial betrayals, elite and ethnic tribulations. Violence. 


Homa Bay’s road to “AfGoonistan” on 16

th

 August began when James Orengo, Siaya governor and a Linda Mwananchi advocate who is also popularly known by nicknames such as Nyatieng’, wuod nya Mayanga, or “the walking constitution”, took to the sun roof of his car and made an incendiary, vulgar, and sexist speech in May.  


In a speech “full of sound and fury, dignifying nothing” in Kadongo, the far-flung fecund highlands of Homa Bay County where peasants grow some of Kenya’s sweetest pineapple and sweet potatoes, Orengo fired the first sexist and vulgar salvo against Homa Bay governor Gladys Wanga, in Dholuo. True to his Nyatieng’ moniker, Orengo hit Governor Wanga below the belt. He said: 


“Dhi nyis nya Wangaya, ni an ja siasa ma ok onego otug godo. Ase neno siasa ma opogore gi siasa ma oseneno. An ok alony siruaru ni ngato. An ok alony siruaru ni ngato. Ma saa duto oloso mana e nyinga, an ma enana ni, an ok nindo koda, an ema anindo gi ngato. Koso awacho ma rach? Koso awacho ma rach? Moko wacho ni Orengo otii, sani e koro ka aroch, sani abith. To ka oneno ni ati, obi otem, one mach, koro e ka obiro neno. Kadongo Oyee! Kasipul, Oyee!”


“Go tell Nya Wangaya [Gladys Wanga] that I am a seasoned politician she should not joke with. The kind of politics I have experienced is different from what she has seen. I do not strip my panties for anyone. I do not strip my panties for anyone. All the time she talks about me. As you can see, no one sleeps with me, I sleep with someone. Have I said something bad? Have I said something bad? Some say Orengo is old, yet I have now rejuvenated. I am virile. But if she thinks that I’m old, let her try, she will see fire, then she will know. Kadongo Oyee! Kasipul Oyee!”


Although Orengo had addressed Governor Wanga simply as “Nya Wangaya”, ordinarily a term of endearment, there was nothing endearing or romantic about his invitation. Orengo’s speech in Dholuo rhymed with Catherine MacKinnon’s syntax of “Man fucks woman”, an expression that captures the contemptuous diminution of women to mere sex objects and women’s bodies to sites where violent men perform their patriarchal heterosexual fantasies.  


If Orengo often punctuates his political speeches with words such as

“dhako wadwa, mon wetena”

 – “fellow woman, fellow women” – to signal symbolic identification with the womenfolk, when challenged by a woman leader in the ODM leadership struggles, Orengo reached for the phallus. The walking constitution’s velvet gloves were off. He was revelling in the privilege of the phallus, to cheers from the crowd surrounding his car. He came to Homa Bay to express a strong patriarchal will to power.


Orengo’s vulgar, sexist speech in Homa Bay County – a county that not only elected the first woman governor in Nyanza and chair of the ODM party, but also boasts three elected women members of parliament out of eight constituencies – signified the end of an era: the end of civil politics of …

author: Mariam Mayet
title: Who controls the food system controls the future
content:
Walk into any major supermarket in South Africa, and the shelves seem to tell a story of abundance: aisles of bread, meat, dairy, fruit, vegetables, cereals, snacks, and processed foods wrapped in the language of choice, convenience, and modernity. This food system is often held up as a model for the rest of the continent: modern farms, sophisticated logistics, powerful processors, dominant retailers, and the capacity to produce, import, export, and distribute food at scale.


Yet behind this display of plenty lies a brutal contradiction. Millions of working-class people are hungry, food prices are punishing, and child malnutrition and diet-related disease persist. While farm and food workers labour under exploitative, insecure, and often dangerous conditions, small-scale farmers struggle to survive.


The African Centre for Biodiversity’s (ACB’s) new report, 

The architecture of control: corporate power, financialisation, and democratic food futures in South Africa

, argues that this is primarily a problem of power. It is about who owns, controls, and profits from the food system; how corporate concentration shapes production, prices, markets, labour, and consumption; and how the state has retreated from its constitutional duty to guarantee the right to food, leaving corporations and financiers to decide what food future is possible.


Across the chain, fewer companies control more.


Bayer/Monsanto, Corteva, Syngenta and BASF shape seeds and agrochemicals.


Omnia, Kynoch, Nutri Feeds, Meadow Feeds, AFGRI, Senwes, VKB, and NWK influence fertilisers, feed, grain trading, and storage.


Astral, RCL Foods, Rainbow, Tiger Brands, Premier, Pioneer Foods, Clover, Lactalis, Nestlé, and PepsiCo dominate poultry, meat, dairy, milling, baking, and processed foods.


Shoprite, Pick ‘n Pay, Woolworths, and SPAR decide what reaches shelves and on what terms.


They are not one cartel, but coordinate through contracts, procurement, standards, credit, logistics, cold chains, storage, advertising, data, and finance. Together, they create an hourglass-shaped food system: millions of producers and consumers squeezed through a narrow corporate middle.


How control works


Control no longer depends only on owning land or factories. It operates through storage silos, ports, cold chains, procurement systems, retail shelves, credit, contracts, standards, intellectual property, data systems and digital platforms – the bottlenecks farmers, workers, traders and consumers must pass through.


When corporations control these bottlenecks, they set the terms:


which seeds are available,


which inputs farmers must buy,


which standards producers must meet,


which products reach shelves, which prices are paid, and


which risks are pushed down the chain.


For workers, this architecture is lived as class discipline. Farm workers – shaped by apartheid land and labour legacies – remain tied to low wages, seasonal contracts, insecure housing, pesticide exposure, and weak protection. Workers in processing, logistics, retail, and fast-food face casualisation, labour broking, outsourcing, speed-ups, surveillance, and anti-union pressure, while corporations use procurement, pricing, and contracts to push costs and risks down the chain. The workers who grow, pack, transport, cook, and sell food are forced to buy it back at prices they can barely afford. This is not simply ‘precarious work’; it is a political economy of extraction built on cheap labour, racialised inequality, and fragmented working-class power.


Hunger in a system built for profit


The dominant story says hunger is caused by too little production, and that the answer is more technology, bigger farms, more chemicals, and more private investment. Another version blames poor people themselves – as if hunger were a private failure rather than the result of land dispossession, racialised capitalism, low wages, unemployment, debt, spatial apartheid, and the erosion of public support.


Hunger exists alongside abundance because food is organised as a commodity before it is protected as a right. This is also a political indictment of the state. By retreating from public provisioning, weakening public capacity, and outsourcing food security to markets, the state has abandoned its constitutional obligations and helped create the space for corporate rule over food.


Smangele Jansen, a social relief of distress grant recipient, shopping for her staple foods. Archive photo by Ramatamo …

author: Rosebell Kagumire
title: Who Does “Mutual Interest” Serve in an Unequal World? On EU Development Cooperation Pivot
content:
What is mutual interest in an unequal world? That’s what I was reflecting on this week in Brussels, when I joined the “Mutual interests in practice: How should Global Europe balance development, economic and geopolitical objectives?” panel at The Future of EU Development Cooperation, hosted by the European Centre for Development Policy Management (ECDPM) and Oxfam. The discussion came at a decisive moment, as the EU negotiates its next long-term budget and the Global Europe Instrument, while the Commission prepares for consultations with civil society and local authorities from 28 September to 1 October. Regional sessions include “Sub-Saharan Africa”, while global thematic sessions cover human development, the green and digital transition, democracy and human rights, and partnerships.

The EU is pivoting development cooperation towards its own economic, security and foreign policy goals through a “mutual interest” approach. But mutual interest means little unless it confronts the unequal systems that determine whose interests count, whose risks are ignored, and whose lives are rendered negotiable.

I spoke alongside H.E. Dr Naomi A. Ngwira, Ambassador of Malawi; Martin Seychell of DG INTPA; Christophe Lam of BusinessEurope; and William Roos of the EBRD, in a discussion moderated by San Bilal of ECDPM. I drew on the Afro-feminist work of the AfIP Collective, including members such as Memory Kachambwa of FEMNET, who also made a presentation, and the work of many African feminists challenging foreign policy in a time of faltering multilateralism.

For many in Africa, the EU’s pivot offers little that is new. Europe has repackaged its approach to Africa without altering the fundamentals that produce inequality. The Global Gateway has, by the EU’s own count, mobilised over €300 billion since 2021, including an Africa–Europe package of around €150 billion, and now targets €400 billion by 2027. But mutual interest is not mutual benefit: interests may overlap while benefits, risks and decision-making power remain profoundly unequal. As San Bilal writes in a new ECDPM briefing, wrapping every project “in a cosy mutual-benefit narrative is misleading.”

Africans have long critiqued, opposed and contested donor narratives and models of development financing and aid, calling for partnerships that are accountable and mindful of historical context. The pivot towards capital investment, with the private sector presented as the new magic formula, does not account for the reforms needed in relationships that remain hegemonic, rooted in a long history of colonialism and racial capitalism. Investment language alone forgoes critical responsibilities rooted in reparatory justice for the continent’s historic underdevelopment and exploitation.

The next Global Europe Instrument won’t escape imbalances. In its recommendations to the Irish Presidency, Oxfam warns that an explicit mandate to pursue EU interests “places excessive emphasis on the EU’s priorities over partner country objectives.” Development funding could build infrastructure for extracting critical raw materials, often for European firms and export, a trend “particularly visible on the African continent.” Fragile and conflict-affected states, which offer investors little, risk falling off the EU’s radar: left to their own devices, or pushed into extractive investment models that can deepen the very conflicts they need to escape.

Decolonial Afro-feminist perspectives argue that decisions and seemingly new approaches to trade, finance, security and cooperation are made within an existing unequal global order, its structures and relations, which distribute power, risk and harm unevenly. Who defines the bargain, whose trade-offs are treated as inevitable, and who is disposable before negotiations begin? In systems built to drain value from Africa, the same deal benefits Europe while Africa bears the costs. As economist Fadhel Kaboub warns, the colonial division of labour “locks you permanently at the bottom of the global value chain.”

Too often, “mutual interest” also means the interests of ruling elites: mineral agreements whose costs fall on neighbouring communities, and migration deals that serve regime survival. Amid the war in eastern DRC in 2024, the EU signed a raw materials agreement with Rwanda, which UN experts have found to back the M23 rebels. Several EU states are now in talks with Uganda and Rwanda to host “return hubs” for people deported from Europe. This is the …

author: Dr William Nii Ayitey Menson
title: A Child’s Fifth Birthday Should Not Depend on a Foreign Budget
content:
A fifth birthday should be unremarkable.


For too many African families, it is not.


An estimated

4.9 million children died before reaching the age of five in 2024

, and nearly six in ten of those deaths occurred in sub-Saharan Africa. Most were preventable with interventions we already know how to deliver. In Nigeria, the latest estimate is

116 deaths per 1,000 live births

, roughly one child in nine.


Judith Leveillee, UNICEF’s field chief in Nigeria, recently

told

The Independent

 that child survival will be one of two priorities in the agency’s next country programme. “These are the most basic of the basics,” she said. She also warned that short-term funding makes the slower work of strengthening systems harder.


The OECD projects that

health aid could fall by 29 to 46 percent between 2024 and 2026

, equivalent to $5 billion to $8 billion. Those cuts will hurt. But they also force a harder question:

how did we allow a budget decision made thousands of miles away to have this much power over whether our own children live or die?


Aid cuts are exposing weaknesses in African health systems. They did not create all of them.


I have seen this problem as a physician, hospital administrator, researcher, and now through health financing and policy. The amount of money available matters enormously. But so does what happens after it is allocated.


I encountered this directly while working on immunisation financing in Niger. Even when resources had been provided for planned activities, moving them through administrative levels could take time as approvals and signatures were completed. We began designing a mechanism to shorten that path and move some resources more directly to districts and facilities, including through digital transfers.


The work is ongoing, so I will leave the results for another day. But it changed how I think about health financing. Sometimes the question is not simply whether money has been made available, but whether it reaches the point of service quickly and predictably enough to be useful.


How money moves can matter almost as much as how much is pledged.


Years earlier, as a clinician in Ghana, I saw another part of the same problem. For people outside the National Health Insurance Scheme, almost everything could become an out-of-pocket payment. Even insured patients sometimes had to buy medicines privately because what they needed was unavailable at the facility.


At the bedside, the financing terminology mattered less than the consequence. A clinician could know what a patient needed, insurance could exist, and the medicine could be available somewhere in town, yet the family still had to find the cash before care could continue.


To the parent of a sick child, the distinction between an inadequate allocation, a delayed release and a stock-out is largely irrelevant. The child still does not get the care.


Ghana’s new Free Primary Healthcare programme is an interesting test. In an

analysis Banda Khalifa and I wrote for

The Meridian Letters

, we argued that it is best understood not as a replacement for NHIS, but as an attempt to make first contact with care earlier, easier and more reliable. It begins in 150 underserved districts and brings maternal and child health services, immunisation, screening and treatment for common conditions closer to where people live.


The difficult work starts after the announcement. Are medicines and staff available? Does screening lead to treatment and follow-up? Are resources reaching facilities and families paying less from their own pockets?


As we argued in

The Meridian Letters

, good reforms are not sustained by applause. They are sustained by design. Free primary care can make the front door of the health system easier to enter. It still has to lead somewhere.


That is also how I think about a

Fifth Birthday Guarantee

: less as a new programme than as a test of whether the financing system works.


No government can guarantee that every child will survive. But governments can identify the services most likely to keep children alive, cost them, budget for them, release the money, make sure the services reach children, and report honestly on what happened.


Cost it. Budget it. Release it. Deliver it. Report it.


The package will differ by country, but would typically include immunisation, maternal and newborn care, nutrition, malaria services where relevant, treatment for pneumonia and diarrhoea, and functioning primary care …

author: WoMin
title: Women on the frontlines: Organise, Educate, Liberate, Celebrate!
content:
Across social justice movements, both in the Present and in the Past, education has been a central piece binding theory and praxis. It is from this understanding that, from the 17

th

 to the 18

th

 of September, the

Afro-International Feminist Organising School (AFRO-IFOS),

 a movement building space that uses popular education to strengthen our collective knowledge, share our experiences, and grow our international movement, hosted a School of Facilitators in Nairobi, Kenya, to support the deepening of a Decolonial Feminist Popular Education praxis across the more than 30 countries and territories represented, from Africa and the Americas.


There is power in naming the inequalities and wounds we carry as peoples who have been dispossessed of land, livelihoods, cultures and Knowledge. However, our greatest challenge is creating spaces that encourage us to dream of a world beyond the limits of colonial imagination.


Popular education has been a powerful practice for creating such spaces. Rooted in the knowledge and lived experiences of the people, it invites us to learn not only from books and institutions, but from one another.


Education is a political commitment


In the 1971 BBC film “

Behind the lines

”, Maria, a Mozambican guerrilla fighter explains that education was at the heart of why she decided to join the liberation struggle. In her experience

“If a girl reached a certain class [The colonialists] said that is enough for us, Africans.”


(Literacy Campaign, Guerrilla warfare in Angola, 1968. Photo: Augusta Conchiglia)


Our feminist

herstories

 across Africa and beyond have been deeply shaped by anti-colonial struggles. It was within the liberation movements that many women and men encountered education as a practice of freedom, in learning to question colonial power, reclaiming their histories and wisdom, fighting to protect their sovereignty and imagining forms of collective life beyond the impositions of heteropatriarchal, capitalist, colonial systems.


As feminist ancestor Nawal El Saadawi reminds us

“good education means creating dissatisfaction and disobedience.”

 Her wordsspeak to the transformative power of education to nurture the critical consciousness needed to both understand the conditions that constrain us and to connect them to our personal experiences, which is fundamental to organise collectively towards liberation.


But liberation cannot be achieved by a few, full liberation requires all of us. Our political project must be sustained by an intentional educational project that deepens our proposals and equips us to build the worlds we envision.


The educator is a pollinator


Through processes of learning, unlearning, relearning and imagining together, we become both teachers and students in our movements. This is one of the many ways in which decolonial feminist popular education inspires us to cultivate relational ways of working together that are grounded in mutual learning, listening, solidarity and care.


Instead of positioning the educator as the one who holds all the answers, popular educators create spaces where all can collectively formulate the questions that emerge from our struggles and where all can develop the knowledge needed to respond.


“Vou aprender a ler

 /

Para ensinar minhas camaradas

 /

I will learn how to read

 /

To teach my comrades”


Brazilian struggle song


The same way bees are essential for healthy environments, popular educators are an important part of feminist movements infrastructure. Popular educators nurture the power that already exists within movements.


Like the flower, each individual carries something that can nourish the collective. Learning is never only for ourselves. What we learn becomes a good we carry around our movements, to share, to exchange, to teach and to transform. Knowledge moves between us, allowing new ideas, possibilities and material actions to be activated. It is through this circulation of knowledge that we can produce the sweet taste of hope needed to build different futures.


Organising and liberating as we educate


“The beast is too big, and we need a political project that inspires us to build something every day and not just to fight and destroy the world as we know it.” –


Sandra, Guatemala


A decolonial feminist popular education praxis can build bridges across our different struggles, experiences, beliefs and movements, creating the conditions to move beyond simply resisting what exists …

author: Abahlali_3
title: March Against the Separation Wall in Cape Town
content:
4 September 2024 Abahlali baseMjondolo press statement

March Against the Separation Wall in Cape Town

Today thousands of people are marching in the street of Cape Town against the building of a separation wall that repeats the logic of apartheid spatial segregation.

The City of Cape Town continues to entrench neo-apartheid laws in post apartheid South Africa by building a wall that segregates and hides the poor from the rich along the N2.

This wall is sign that the City of Cape Town under the Democratic Alliance does not recognise the poor, who are black in particular. The DA has always introduced and favoured laws that are anti-poor and anti-black.

Abahlali baseMjondolo supports the struggles of the people of Cape Town who continue to face segregation and racism under the DA led municipality. We support the march that is taking place today against this act of hatred and undermining of the poor in Khayeltsha, Langa, Dunoon and Gugulethu and Mitchels Plain. We will not support neo-apartheid segregation.

author: Yatta Zoker
title: We are oil to you
content:
I’m exhausted. As are many of my peers.

When I was in my 20s and more spiritually adventurous, I would obsess over the 27 club.

During this time, I was opening for Sun Ra Arkestra and floating in the tradition of Black spiritual music. Mostly by accident.

I had a theory at the time that the story of Robert Johnson meeting a man at the crossroads and receiving the knowledge of how to play the guitar was actually about Elegba.

And that at 27, musicians had to decide whether to be in collaboration with the devil or choose another way.

A crossroads. A coming of age. A portal.

No wonder we are exhausted.

As musicians, we are in the business of energy.

Performances can be athletic, like a windmill. Poems, singing, and playing an instrument can generate energy as we receive inspiration like solar panels hearing instructions from the sun.

On the other side of things, there is the audience.

Depending on the context, the relationship between performer and audience can be life-giving or extractive. I’ve played festivals in Europe that have made me feel like my soul material is being mined.

I think of singers who have sedated themselves to stay alive but end up dead.

*

As artists who are children of immigrants, some of us have chosen a path different from our parents.

We’ve chosen a path of ideas, sounds, images, and expression. We are in the business of exchanging thought, extrapolating, and expanding worlds. We have the time to express ourselves. I will never take that privilege for granted.

A father in Patricia Engel’s

It’s Not Love, It’s Just Paris

 tells his daughter that every immigrant conjures an entire future out of nothing more than a dream, that “the immigrant’s life is art in its purest form.”

Survival on foreign land demands immense creativity.

And there are places of collective expression: parties with exuberant decoration,

lappas

 that glint in the spinning lights of a wedding reception, and then on the phone, WhatsApp.

WhatsApp is a curatorial space; a place of collective ingenuity. These phones tie together the diaspora and are where expression and collective culture consumption take place.

YATTA, Bu waa, 2025. Silver bluetooth earphone with suspended pendants of engravings of krio lyrics. Exhibited in FATHAGOD.EXE.

Last year, I had my first solo exhibition,

FATHAGOD.EXE

, at Blade Study in the Lower East Side. I was thinking about those phone stores on Fulton Street. I imagined that the vitrines in the show, if turned on their side, just might resemble the glass cases that hold SIM cards, prepaid phones, and calling cards.

I made a grill out of a SIM card. The dental mold became geological and the black line holding it became

Ngloei

 (or “oil” in Mende).

YATTA,Ngloei, 2025. Sim card, white brass. Exhibited in FATHAGOD.EXE.

For the show, I was thinking about West African immigrants using Bluetooth wearables and SIM cards to stay connected to family back home. And as I said, coltan. These cell phones are built from materials that could be mined by the relatives of those who use them to stay in touch.

The exhibition asked: What does it cost to stay connected? Who is laboring so that connection is possible?

YATTATAWA (L), 2025. Silver bluetooth earphone with suspended pendants of engravings of krio lyrics. Exhibited in FATHAGOD.EXE.

YATTATAWA (L), 2025. Silver bluetooth earphone with suspended pendants of engravings of krio lyrics. Exhibited in FATHAGOD.EXE.

The pendant says, “me body gef fo brok done.” A lyric from my song “

Cyborg

,” on the album

Spirit Said Yes

 (2016).

Then I think of children in Congo dredging up coltan. Backs bent. iPhones pending.

Bodies of Black people breaking down. Children bent over digging in Congo. Adults bent over picking cotton along the Mississippi.

We Are Oil to You II

At the gas station down the street, the earth tells me that oil is evil alchemy. Extraction, like black goo, drips and compresses to form records that tell me why I was afraid to play them backwards

.

Heavy to hear the songs of forlorn laborers

from Motown

to men bent over along the Mississippi

Installation view of YATTA’s

Iron + Palm Wine

 at Art Omi, 2025

The music industry has long been extractive. And then we do it to each other. Motown music executives owning masters.

My great uncle, a palm wine musician, S. E. Rogie, started his own label called Rogiephone. He protected his legacy.

*

I’m upstairs on the veranda in Freetown, overlooking the yard where cars …

author: Shams Eddin Essam
title: Supply Ministry postpones bread price review amid ongoing push from bakeries, mills
content:
Supply Minister Sherif Farouk has asked for a week’s review period before the ministry responds to a request to raise its guideline consumer prices for two categories of non-subsidized bread, according to a source who was present at a Sunday

meeting

 where representatives from bakeries and mills put forward their request.


The request is their second in just a few months, following a dispute over the extent of the ministry’s role in setting and enforcing non-subsidized bread prices.


Their push for higher guideline prices comes as the industry’s production costs rise steadily, with wheat prices spiralling again amid an escalation in the intensity of Russia’s war on Ukraine, and as domestic fuel prices continue to rise against the backdrop of the regional war.


Farouk said the ministry would review price movements over the coming week, and, if prices did not fall over that period, the ministry would revise guideline prices for the tourist and fino bread categories, the source said. The ministry did not commit to a specific percentage increase.


Senior representatives of the General Bakeries Division raised the issue of production costs at the meeting and called for a review of tourist and fino bread prices, proposing a 15 percent increase.


Milling sector representatives also presented an update on the wheat and flour markets and recent pressures on production costs, particularly higher maritime shipping and logistics costs and rising global wheat prices amid the shipping disruptions in the Black Sea.


Imported wheat reached record prices at the beginning of this week, rising to between LE16,600 and LE16,800 for Ukrainian wheat and LE17,000 for Russian wheat, compared with a maximum of LE12,200 to LE12,500 per ton in June.


Bakeries selling tourist bread rely on the free market for their flour supplies, which account for more than 50 percent of production costs, the source said. Transport and other operating costs have also risen, leaving bakeries facing significant losses. 


The meeting is the latest in a series of calls bakeries have made to the ministry regarding tourist and fino bread prices, which intensified in August as flour and other production costs increased. 


The Supply Ministry did not respond to the demands, issuing a

directive

 instead on August 4 to maintain the prices and weights for tourist and fino bread

set

 in

March

.


As bakeries continued to call for price increases, sources in the sector questioned the legal basis for the imposition of mandatory pricing on tourist bread, whose production inputs are not subsidized. 


Lawyer Khaled Ali previously

told

 Mada Masr however that since wheat is a “strategic commodity,” the ministry has a role in market oversight.

 


The ministry also threatened legal action against violators of its price directives at the time, with Interior Ministry

statements

 later announcing “large scale campaigns to control supply crimes” against those violating Supply Ministry decisions on prices and weights.


The changes in wheat and flour prices come amid volatility in global wheat markets, particularly continued tensions in the Black Sea region, the main source of Egypt’s wheat imports.

Import

data

 for the first eight months of the year showed that Russia and Ukraine together accounted for more than 82 percent of Egypt’s wheat imports, despite repeated announcements by the Supply Ministry of plans to

diversify

 import origins.

The post

Supply Ministry postpones bread price review amid ongoing push from bakeries, mills

 first appeared on

Mada Masr

.

author: Xinhu
title: The Reserve
content:
Cheng Huaijin stood before the enormous floor-to-ceiling window, swirling the South African red wine in her glass and admiring Mount Kilimanjaro in the distance under the clear sky. When she had moved into this office two years ago, she heard that seeing the snowcap of the mountain was a sign of good luck. Over these two years, the number of times she had received this “good luck” increased day by day, which made her firmly believe that she and Moshi city at the foot of the mountain were becoming luckier and luckier.


The city of Moshi, historically, was a trading center for the nearby farmers, herders, and merchants. Later, it became the gateway for foreign conquerors and climbers in the name of conquest to enter the Kilimanjaro region. Its long-standing agriculture, modestly successful light industry, and tourism had earned it a reputation for prosperity and tranquility in Tanzania. On the world stage, it remained an obscure city, until 2045, five years after enhanced robots spread across the globe. It was then that East Africa’s first Human Art Protection Reserve was established in Moshi. 


In an instant, this small city slumbering in the cradle of the highest mountain on the equator became a byword for fashion, modernity, and human dignity. Countless human tourists flocked here, just to leave a trace of their existence as humans in a dramatically altered world.


Cheng Huaijin’s office was located in the tallest building in downtown Moshi, where the Reserve Committee had its headquarters. She served as its Resource Coordination Director and had personally witnessed the small city below her transform from its drab appearance two years ago into today’s colorful art center.


When describing how Moshi had changed, she would, like many Chinese merchants of the past, make familiar comparisons: “Two years ago, Moshi couldn’t even compare with a county town in China—at best it was just a slightly larger town,” and then turn to enthusiastic praise, “Now this place is the Jingdezhen of East Africa. We’re following the Jingdezhen model, and we’re going to do it even better.”


Jingdezhen, of course, was China’s first Human Art Protection Reserve. Officials in that city drafted and signed the world’s first universal standards regulating the autonomy of human artistic creation and the limits of technological assistance.


Some critics believed this regulatory document came too late, as the enhanced robots had already penetrated every aspect of artistic creation; but many others said the Jingdezhen proclamations could only have been born in an era where artificial intelligence and its application in the enhanced robots were fully widespread. In other words, it happened because people panicked. Silicon-based creations had become stronger, smarter, and longer-lived than humans. If they also monopolized art, that jealously guarded human expression, what would then make a human a human?


When humans panic, they turn to nostalgia. European countries had expressed this tendency by not only initiating human art protection projects on their own territories, but also singling out proposals from several developing countries and supporting them in establishing Human Art Protection Reserves in those lands—perhaps stemming from some post-industrial fantasy that in these less developed places, the human artistic spirit was less tainted. Cheng Huaijin was a supporter of this argument. She always told her compatriots and audiences from other parts of the world in interviews, “Africans are so good at singing and dancing, and their appreciation of art is undoubtedly superb. Everyone must come and see it in person.”


As a manager of an art protection reserve, Cheng Huaijin needed to understand not art, but marketing. This was also why her resume stood out among numerous candidates. She had been a core member of the overseas strategic planning department of a renowned robotics company, bringing large numbers of medical robots into the East African market. Therefore, her new employers expected that she would sell artworks the way she sold robots, harnessing the commercial success of artificial intelligence for the cause of the Human Art Protection Reserve. 


She did not disappoint them. After taking the role, she established product standards, introduced an agent system, and invested heavily in all-platform marketing, quickly turning the Reserve from deficit to profitability.


Yet her interventions could not be described merely as good …

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Public Safety minister appoints full time correctional investigator
content:
The federal government has appointed the new head at the Office of the Correctional Investigator, it announced Tuesday.


This will be the permanent successor to Ivan Zinger, who took his early retirement in February 2026, two years before his position expired.


The position was left vacant for four months until Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree appointed an interim commissioner.


David Paradiso, the deputy Ombudsman in B.C. will take the seat on Oct. 13.


Canada’s correctional investigator works as an independent watchdog for the federal corrections system, investigating submitted complaints and concerns that have to do with living conditions, overpopulation, and several other issues faced by incarcerated people in federal prisons.


Paradiso has been the deputy

British Columbia Ombudsperson

 since 2014, and, according to Canada, has “35 years of experience in public sector oversight, legal analysis, and independent investigations.”


According to the

Forum of Canadian Ombudsman

, he helped establish the national Ombudsman for Canada Post and then spent time at the RCMP Public Complaint Commission.


He served as director of investigations with the Office of the Correctional Investigator [OCI] for six years and handled complaints and allegations from or concerning those in incarceration.


“He has advanced fairness, accountability and organisational performance across multiple Canadian jurisdictions and is well-positioned to lead the OCI on a permanent basis,” stated Anandasangaree in the announcement.


Each year, the OCI publishes a report which outlines these concerns, as well as trends and results from investigations in prisons across the country.


For example, the

2024-2025 report

 covered “

The Discontinuity of Post-Release Mental Health Services

;” “

An Update on Therapeutic Ranges and Intermediate Mental Health Care

;” and “

Assessing and Addressing Trauma in Federally Sentenced Women

,” among other topics.


Zinger often shared his concerns around the overrepresentation of Indigenous Peoples in federal prisons.


When he announced that he’d be leaving in November 2025, he said it was out of frustration with

Correctional Service of Canada

.


“Our recommendations for systemic reform have too often been disregarded or dismissed by the CSC,” he had said at the time. “Over the years, the Department of Public Safety and successive ministers have also shown a reluctance to compel CSC to act on OCI recommendations, despite acknowledgement of the soundness of our findings.


“Canadians are not well-served by a correctional system that is exceptionally costly and well-resourced, yet persistently fails to deliver on key correctional outcomes.”


Anandasangaree stated that he was looking forward to working with Paradiso and his team, “to support a correctional system that is safe, humane and focused on rehabilitation and successful reintegration.”


The post

Public Safety minister appoints full time correctional investigator

 appeared first on

APTN News

.

author: Daron Letts
title: Modular home factory begins production in Arviat
content:
With a ribbon-cutting ceremony, the modular home factory officially opened Tuesday.


The

$75-million, 64,500-square-foot facility started production at 60 per cent capacity Sept. 23, said operations director Jason Gibbons in an interview.

Within 18 months, the factory will achieve peak capacity, producing up to 40 single- and multi-family houses a year.


The Inuit-owned modular home factory in Arviat is operated under Sakku Innovative Building Solutions, a joint venture between Sakku Investments and Quebec-based modular manufacturer R.G. Solution. (Photo courtesy of Denise Kusugak/Sakku Investments Corporation)


The factory employs 15 staff, including 14 Inuit, said Caroline Nault, CEO of Sakku Innovative Building Solutions, a joint venture between Sakku Investments, the business arm of the Kivalliq Inuit Association, and Quebec-based modular manufacturer R.G. Solution, which operates the Inuit-owned facility. Of those workers, 10 work on the factory floor in non-administrative roles.


“There is only one non-Inuit employee, and it’s me,” Nault said in an interview.


By early 2028 the workforce will swell to 40 full-time staff, including journeypersons, carpenters, plumbers and electricians, Gibbons added.


To certify carpenters and other specialists, the company will provide in-house training and work with Nunavut Arctic College to certify its workers, Nault said.


Sakku estimates an additional 100 indirect jobs will be created in transportation, installation and finishing.


About one-third of the factory, which underwent construction in 2023 with an initial budget of $50 million, is occupied by a heated warehouse. A cold storage warehouse beside the factory is expected to be completed by November. It will have space to shelter a full-year’s production of raw materials.


This sixplex in Rankin Inlet was built as a pilot project by Sakku Innovative Building Solutions, a joint venture between Sakku and Quebec-based modular manufacturer R.G. Solutiona. (Photo courtesy of Denise Kusugak/Sakku Investments Corporation)


Sakku Investments Corp. funded the factory using Inuit equity and partnerships with Inuit organizations, the Northern Economic Development Agency, Next Generation Manufacturing Canada, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp., National Research Council of Canada and the Government of Nunavut.


This month, the factory is producing components for nine three-bedroom houses, scheduled to be installed in the community next spring, Nault said.

The company is also preparing to build two 12-plexes in Rankin Inlet.


Prior to factory completion, and with materials from Quebec, the company erected pilot projects that included two five-plexes in Arviat; a duplex in Coral Harbour; and four two-storey houses, a six-plex, and a duplex in Rankin Inlet.


The buildings are designed to incorporate aspects of Arctic living, with separate entrances for the multi-unit dwellings and cold porches on the front and back of single units, Nault said.


They ward off condensation and mould using ventilation and other preventative materials and systems, she said.


Tuesday’s ribbon-cutting ceremony was attended by Kivalliq Inuit Association president Kono Tattuinee, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. president Gloria Uluqsi, Premier John Main and MP Lori Idlout.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Chuck Grassley, 93, Laments a Democrat Could Replace Him If He Dies in Office
content:
The remarks come as Sen. Mitch McConnell, 84, faces calls to step down over health- and age-related concerns.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), the oldest member of the Senate, has said that he worries Iowa may elect a Democratic governor because that person would pick his replacement if he dies while in office, amid renewed attention on fitness-related concerns due to Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Kentucky) prolonged absence from the Senate.

“At 93 years of age, I don’t know how many more groups of Republicans like this I’m going to have a chance to talk to. I want to take advantage of it,” Grassley said in remarks at Iowa Republicans’ annual Reagan Dinner last week.

“One of the reasons I’m worried about who’s going to be elected governor — I don’t plan on dying in office, but if I did, I don’t want a Democratic governor choosing my successor,” he went on.

Grassley, the Senate’s president pro tempore, was born on September 17, 1933, and will be 95 when his term expires in January 2029. He has declined to rule out running for reelection again; if he won another term, he would be 101 when his next term would end.

Grassley has held his seat in the Senate since 1981; before that, he was a member of the House starting in 1975. In all, Grassley has been a member of Congress for over half a century.

When a U.S. senator dies, the governor in their state chooses a temporary replacement until a special election can be held, meaning that a Democrat could potentially pick Grassley’s successor if he dies next year or in 2028.

There is a chance of this happening. Polls show that the Democratic candidate, Rob Sand, is leading in the Iowa gubernatorial election over his opponent, Zach Lahn. They are fighting to replace current Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds, who announced last year that she is stepping down to spend more time with her family.

Grassley’s comments come amid renewed scrutiny over age- and health-related concerns for members of Congress. During his three-month absence this summer after he suffered a fall at his residence, McConnell faced numerous calls to resign. McConnell, who is 84 years old, and his office gave very few updates or even proof of life during his absence, fueling further concerns about his health after other recent incidents raised concerns about his fitness.

This episode came after public scrutiny in 2023 over now-deceased Sen. Dianne Feinstein, of California, when reports found that the 90-year-old was potentially facing elder abuse and was refusing to leave office despite appearing extremely frail after a prolonged absence due to shingles. Feinstein died while in office three years ago on Monday.

author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: New book aims to ‘push back and defend survivors’ against denialism
content:
Pre-signed copies of ‘Truth Before Reconciliation’ were made available for audience goers of the September 17 launch in Winnipeg. Photo by Crystal Greene


Outside a Winnipeg bookstore, about 25 volunteers in orange shirts formed a welcoming line as sage smoke rose from an abalone shell. 


Inside McNally Robinson Booksellers, more than 300 people gathered for the launch of

Truth Before Reconciliation: Confronting Residential School Denialism

. Outside, the volunteers helped provide security as organizers anticipated denialists might try to disrupt the event on September 17. 


“We want to make sure that it’s safe for the survivors,” said Emma Tardiff, one of the volunteers. “I really care about my community.”


Published by University of Manitoba Press ahead of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, the collection grew from an effort by scholars and authors to confront the denial and downplaying of what survivors experienced. 


The book consists of 13 chapters that include survivor interviews, expert analysis and examination of the denialism movement. Contributors include historians, educators, survivors, archivists and archaeologists, alongside the book’s two co-editors, Sean Carlton and Niigaan Sinclair. 


Drawing on survivors’ lived experiences, historical evidence, and peer-reviewed scholarship, it examines the origins, methods, and consequences of denialism, challenges its claims, and highlights sources denialists ignore or misrepresent.


“We felt like we needed to collectively pool our expertise to push back and defend survivors, defend truth, and help us not get distracted in this hard work of Truth and Reconciliation,” said Carleton, a settler historian and associate professor of history and Indigenous studies at the University of Manitoba.


“Through the peer-reviewing process, everybody pulled together; it was a true, collective team effort.”


Carleton noted that academic publishing takes time, particularly for an edited collection. People had repeatedly asked him to do the book, he told the audience.


“Someone needed to do it, and we figured, ‘why not us?’” he said.


“This book is a collective statement in defence of survivors and survivor truth.”


Pictured from left to right: Host Shelagh Rogers, contributor Michelle Good, co-editors Niigaan Sinclair and Sean Carleton. Photo by Crystal Greene


Confronting 150 years of misinformation


People in “Canada” have been subjected to 150 years of misinformation about Indigenous Peoples and the residential school system, co-editor Sinclair told the audience. Indigenous Peoples, meanwhile, have lived with the institutions’ effects and hold first-hand knowledge of what happened.


Sinclair, an Anishinaabe writer from St. Peter’s/Little Peguis, is a Winnipeg Free Press columnist and a professor of Indigenous studies at the University of Manitoba. His father, the late senator Murray Sinclair, chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC).


Sinclair pointed to decades of research documenting the residential school system, including the commission’s work.


“There is a contingent of Canadians who are still full of doubt, easily — perhaps — confused or manipulated by information that would be hearsay or cherry-picked facts, or by individuals that perhaps are nefarious and trying to sow division, trying to create conflict,” he said.


“Denialism isn’t the denial of the schools themselves; it’s the denial or the downplaying of the atrocities that happened in those schools.”


Michelle Good, a member of Red Pheasant Cree Nation and a former lawyer who has represented survivors, joined the co-editors for a panel discussion during the launch. She spoke about malnutrition and conditions in the institutions that left children vulnerable to disease.


For Good, the evidence also comes from years of listening to survivors and from her own family.


“I represented survivors from many different schools across the country, and the similarity of stories that came from these folks just makes it so entirely undeniable,” she said. “Not to mention my own mom, who was locked up in one of those awful places for far too long.”


How the media lends denialism legitimacy


Carleton drew a connection between the tactics used to minimize residential “school” harms and those used by Holocaust deniers.


“They are basically copying and pasting Holocaust denialism,” he said.


He described how those arguments focus on disputing the number of deaths to downplay what …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Lili Reinhart Wants To Adapt a Lesbian Vampire Novella — Let Her!
content:
feature image photo by Emma McIntyre / Staff via Getty Images

Bisexual baddie Lili Reinhart has been on a press tour for her new film, The Love Hypothesis, and I’ve been really enjoying her interviews. The film seems to be the CLASSIC fake dating trope come to life — in fact, the book it’s based on started as Star Wars fanfic! — and despite the movie being seemingly extremely heterosexual, on this tour, she has been quick to remind interviewers and fans that she’s queer. She has also said she hopes in her next project is gay. (Fingers crossed!)

In one video interview she says, “I’m instantly way more interested in doing a movie if my character is a little gay,” she continued. “Because I’m a little gay.” She also reads a comment about being one of “the five pillars of bisexuality with preference to women” and she called it an honor.

In that same interview, she also mentioned that she’s trying to get a film adaptation of a lesbian vampire novella made but that Hollywood seems “too afraid” to make it. She also wonders aloud who WOULDN’T want to make it, a sentiment I agree with. The general assumption people have been making is that it would be an adaptation of the 1872 novella Carmilla, which the popular webseries starring Natasha Negovanlis and Elise Bauman was based on, and I think that would be fun if true. I personally think there can’t be too many adaptations of that novella. The gayer the better. In fact, I just read Hungerstone by Kat Dunn, which is one of a few retellings of that novella and offers a very different take than the webseries.

I, for one, am delighted that Lili keeps making her press tour about a heterosexual love story as queer as she can, and I’m glad she’s using it to pitch her idea. I really hope someone with the means is paying attention and can pick it up and let her run with it.

In my opinion, there’s no such thing as too many lesbian vampire adaptations in general. When is someone going to make a Bury Our Bones in the Midnight Soil miniseries? A movie version of A Long Time Dead, anyone? Let’s get all the lesbian vampires out here while we’re at it. Tis the season!
