author: rti_admin
title: From Inheritance to Inquiry: The Courage to Question
content:
A society becomes dynamic not when everyone thinks alike, but when people possess the freedom and courage to question, debate and rethink what they have inherited. Every generation receives beliefs, customs, institutions and social practices from the past. Some enrich human life; others may perpetuate inequality simply because they have acquired the authority of tradition. The true measure of a mature society, therefore, is not how faithfully it preserves its inheritance, but how intelligently it examines it. In the Indian context, this becomes particularly important when we reflect upon caste, religion and patriarchy. These are not merely abstract concepts. They influence family life, marriage, social status, personal choices and opportunities. Yet meaningful discussion of them is often displaced by sentiment, identity politics, unquestioned authority or fear of disagreement. What India needs is not less tradition or less faith, but more reasoned discourse about their social consequences.

I. Caste, Religion and Patriarchy: Examining the Inherited Order

Caste is one of the most enduring forms of social stratification in India. It historically connects social status with birth and influences occupation, marriage, social interaction, and access to resources. B. R. Ambedkar’s Annihilation of Caste remains a foundational challenge to a social order in which birth becomes the basis of hierarchy. His analysis also highlighted endogamy—the practice of marrying within the group—as a mechanism through which caste boundaries are reproduced. The fundamental question is simple: Can the circumstances of one’s birth legitimately determine one’s dignity, status or opportunities? Modern India has transformed caste through constitutional equality, education, democratic politics, social mobility and affirmative action. Yet caste continues to influence matrimonial choices, political mobilisation, social networks and community identities. The challenge, therefore, is neither to deny caste nor to reduce it to a political slogan, but to understand how an inherited hierarchy adapts to modern conditions.

Religion raises a different but equally important question. Religion has provided meaning, morality, community and spiritual consolation to millions. It cannot simply be dismissed as superstition. A democratic society must protect freedom of belief. But freedom of belief must coexist with freedom of inquiry. When religious claims influence public behaviour or decisions concerning health and human welfare, they necessarily become open to discussion. The growing influence of charismatic spiritual figures and the wider “Baba culture” makes the question of authority especially relevant. Spiritual guidance may be valuable, but spiritual status should not automatically confer unquestionable authority. Patriarchy presents a third dimension of inherited social organisation. Traditional gender roles have often assigned authority, responsibility and freedom differently to men and women. Simone de Beauvoir demonstrated how social expectations can transform biological difference into unequal social possibilities. The question is not whether men or women are superior. It is whether gender should predetermine freedom, dignity, security and opportunity. Caste, religion and patriarchy frequently intersect within the family, marriage and community, where identities and expectations are transmitted across generations.

II. India’s Own Tradition of Questioning

The call for reasoned discourse should not be presented as an imported Western idea. India possesses a long and diverse intellectual tradition of questioning, argument and dissent. The Buddha challenged unquestioned authority and encouraged inquiry into suffering, conduct and knowledge. His intellectual approach placed emphasis on understanding rather than merely accepting claims on the basis of authority or tradition. The Charvaka or Lokayata tradition represents another striking strand of Indian intellectual history. Its materialist and sceptical orientation challenged metaphysical claims and questioned religious authority. Although much of what is known about Charvaka comes through its critics, its historical presence demonstrates that Indian thought included vigorous disagreement about religion, knowledge and reality. The Upanishadic dialogues similarly reveal a culture in which fundamental questions about existence and knowledge were explored through intellectual conversation.

author: ALR Editors
title: Announcing Asian Labour School Oct-Nov 2026 Semester
content:
Dear friends,


We are back with an amazing list of new and returning courses for the Asian Labour School. If you are interested in

acquiring democratic facilitation skills, navigating conflicts and taking collective care, working cooperatively, strengthening a union core or leading your own radical walking tours

, please check out the course information below and study with Asian Labour School.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Chie Matsumoto


We all have attended meetings where decisions were made by only a few members, most outspoken ones or someone at the top. We may have once thought, “Why am I even here?” and left without saying a word. Democracy starts in the smallest conversations, dialogues and meetings by raking in most diverse opinions and ideas, piecing them together to create something new and meaningful to all participants.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Facilitators: Emi Do and Matt Noyes


Worker cooperatives are enterprises that are owned and governed by workers. When all of our working experiences have been in profit-maximizing enterprises, or in workplaces that are structured hierarchically, it is no wonder that we can encounter challenges when attempting to work together cooperatively. In this course we will explore the challenges and tensions when there are no bosses to hate!


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Facilitator: Nash Tysmans


Movements are built through relationships. Yet the pressures of organizing (urgency, conflict, exhaustion, political disagreement, and unequal power) can strain those relationships and undermine our collective capacity. How can we build movements that are both effective in challenging injustice and caring in how we work together?


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Sithar Chhim


In order to win any campaign at workplace, unions need to be strong enough to pressure the company. Building a strong and representative committee is the only way to win over the bosses who have well organized structure at workplace compare to workers.


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)


Facilitator: Kevin Lin


Have you ever thought about leading your own radical walking tour to share with friends the significance of places and histories in your city? Leading and participating in a radical walking tour is not only educational but fun and always memorable. A walking tour provides a concrete sense of places, people, and histories. This course will walk you through the conceptualisation, research and logistics of a radical walking tour, and hear ideas and experiences from other participants across Asia.


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)

author: Unknown
title: Besê Hozat: Women are the vanguard of this process and its defining force
content:
Besê Hozat, co-chair of the KCK Executive Council, said in an interview with Medya Haber that the Peace and Democratic Society Process cannot succeed in Turkey without democratization.


The first part of the interview can be read

here

.


A campaign has been launched by a number of writers, intellectuals, and politicians in this regard – taking responsibility within this process – called “1001 Signatures.” Presuming that you are aware of this campaign, how do you assess it?


This, for example, is truly a meaningful and valuable initiative. It needs to be expanded further and make it more widespread. What is Turkey’s fundamental impasse? In Turkey, many groups are waging their struggles in their own separate spheres. These struggles do not converge, do not unite, and do not transform into synergy. The women’s movement is waging a struggle on its own front, the youth on theirs, the ecological and environmental movements on theirs, workers on theirs, peasants on theirs, and the democratic forces on theirs – everyone is waging a struggle in their own neighborhood, on their own periphery, in their own lane. If we think of each of these as a river, every river flows from a different place and flows to a different destination. If these rivers were to merge, if these dynamics of struggle were to come together and transform into a common, united struggle, this would give rise to a very powerful democratic movement in Turkey – a very powerful democratic dynamic – and this process would also foster a strong sense of ownership. It would play a decisive role in the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process.


This newly launched initiative, developed primarily by intellectuals, is very valuable and meaningful. But if it remains limited to intellectuals alone – and if it is confined solely to a petition drive with a thousand or so signatures, or a stance that barely goes beyond that – it certainly has meaning and value, however, in terms of the results it will produce, its impact would remain limited.


There was also a decision by autonomous women’s organizations. They will organize a conference – involving artists, politicians, intellectuals, and academics – to discuss women’s role in the Peace and Democratic Society process and to create a common front against male and state violence.


Correct. Women have also launched a process under the name “Side by Side,” a process of struggle. I believe they will hold a meeting in late October or early November, where they will develop a joint plan for their struggle. And it will be a united and collective struggle. This is very important. So, this struggle led by women unites all workers, environmental and ecological movements, and all democratic forces in Turkey into a single pot if it transforms into a common struggle, and if the central demand of all those at the heart of this struggle is, after all, democracy, freedom, equality, justice, and a shared, democratic life – then this will give serious rise to a very powerful democratic movement in Turkey. It will also play a decisive role in the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, and I am convinced that it will accelerate this process.


It will also create serious pressure on the government. It will compel both the government and the state to take democratic, political, and legal steps more quickly, without dragging their feet. This can only happen through struggle. Sitting back and watching, waiting, or having everyone continue this limited struggle only in their own neighborhoods will not lead this process to success in the short term. I reiterate that these struggles do have meaning, but we need to bring them together in a joint effort, transforming them into a common struggle and a shared synergy. This will bring to the fore a very strong democratic will, power, and movement and will compel the state and the government to take democratic steps. It will facilitate the swift advancement of this process. We need to develop this further.


The same applies to women. Women are the pioneers of this process. They are its vanguard and its defining force. They are the driving force behind the construction of a democratic society – its fundamental building block. This process will develop under women’s leadership, with their significant and active participation and struggle. Women must be able to bring their struggle together with other democratic dynamics in society and unite them. They must succeed in …

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: ‘Trump not welcome’
content:
Trump is no ordinary foreign guest.

Should Filipinos welcome guests and express concerns another day?

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro thinks so in relation to the possible visit of United States President Donald Trump to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit in November.

Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) told Malacañang, “Trump is not welcome in the Philippines.”

“Trump is no ordinary foreign guest,” the group said in a statement. “His waterloo in Iran and West Asia, his continuing support for Israel’s genocide in Palestine, the proxy war in Ukraine, and his unprovoked interventions in Venezuela and Cuba, have made the entire world suffer.”

Castro made the request when asked by a reporter during a Palace press briefing on September 23 if there were additional security measures in place for the 49th ASEAN Summit in Metro Manila, considering what happened to the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) Investment Forum held at the Grand Hyatt Manila on September 10 where protesters barged to the venue. In this incident, five paralegals who responded to the protest were arrested but were eventually released.

The 1,600-hectare industrial hub under the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative is planned to be built in New Clark City in Tarlac which is within the LEC.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Does China Intend to Target Taiwan With New National Security Legislation?
content:
TAIWANESE GOVERNMENT officials, speaking under conditions of anonymity to the media, have warned that China may roll out national security legislation directed at Taiwan in the coming months. Such national security legislation would follow up on China’s recently passed ethnic unity law.

The law criminalizes actions aimed at disrupting a vaguely defined “national unity”. Although initial warnings were that the law was mainly aimed at Tibetans and Uyghurs, the Lai administration has framed such national security legislation as potentially a threat to Taiwan. Under such laws, after all, support for Taiwanese independence–or even just maintaining Taiwan’s current democratic freedoms and its de facto independence–could be construed as illegal and criminal under the law.

Such Taiwanese government officials have pointed to a number of laws, some of which are still in the review process, as potentially impacting Taiwan. This includes the Regulations of the State Council on Exit and Entry Administration, Measures for the Supervision and Inspection of Cyberspace Security, and National Defense Mobilization Law.

In particular, the Regulations of the State Council on Exit and Entry Administration could be used to prevent Taiwanese who have traveled to China from leaving. This already occurred in the past, however, most prominently in the case of activist Lee Ming-che, who spent over five years in Chinese jails on charges of seeking to subvert the state. Lee is thought to have been detained over exchanges with Chinese friends on Taiwan’s experiences regarding democratization. Others imprisoned, however, have been noted to include pan-Blue academics, who seem to have fallen afoul of espionage charges in spite of pro-unification viewpoints.

Measures on cybersecurity take place at a time when the Chinese government has attempted to depict Taiwan as engaged in cyberattacks against critical infrastructure. Such allegations seem to be an attempt to depict Taiwan as engaged in the same activity it routinely accuses China of being engaged in, seeing as China consistently conducts cyberattacks on Taiwan and probes key infrastructure. Importantly, such allegations could also be used to cement a casus belli to justify war.

Indeed, to this extent, the National Defense Mobilization Law has been warned as potentially intended to provide the legal grounds for wartime mobilization. Indeed, such a law might be necessary ahead of a Chinese invasion, particularly if the Chinese government intends to move Chinese society as a whole toward war footing, and mobilize all of society to conduct an invasion.

Still, at a time of highly polarized politics between the KMT and DPP, it can be expected that the KMT will probably deny that China has intentions for future national security legislation. KMT chair Cheng Li-wun has, of course, attempted to depict China as only having goodwill toward Taiwan, while depicting the DPP as, in fact, the ones who have sought to provoke China. As such claims to the media are made ahead of elections in November, they will be depicted as simply intended to drum up public fear for the sake of electioneering.

author: Cas Smith
title: Anti-war activists prepare to protest Land Forces weapons expo
content:
As the third anniversary of Israel’s assault on Gaza nears, a coalition of anti-war activists is preparing to protest against the Land Forces International Land Defence Exposition, from October 6–8.

The expo, at the Perth Convention Centre, is being advertised as “Australia’s largest land defence industry event”. It will include Lockheed Martin, Elbit Systems, BAE Systems, Honeywell, Boeing and Thales. Elbit is Israel’s largest weapons manufacturer, supplying drones and surveillance technology used by the Israel Defense Forces to target Palestinians. Lockheed Martin supplies the F-35 jets that have been used to bomb and destroy Gaza.

The expo underscores WA Labor’s recently unveiled plan to turn the state into a hub for weapons manufacturing, guided, in part, by the controversial AUKUS war pact.

Premier Roger Cook told the Indian Ocean Defence and Security Conference in May about plans to establish a weapons manufacturing hub, where missiles for the Australian Defence Force could be produced.

This is in addition to WA’s intended AUKUS role — to host up to four United States and a British nuclear-powered submarine on rotation at HMAS Stirling (located on Garden Island, south of Boorloo/Perth) from next year.

Sam Wainwright, from Stop AUKUS WA and the WA Anti-War Collective, told Green Left that WA Labor’s attempts to stop the protest at Land Forces set a dangerous precedent.

“The protections lavished by the state government on this conference, which is a private event, have been staggering,” Wainwright said. “It shows how determined the Cook government is to push the expansion of the arms industry and shield it and the expo’s participants from public scrutiny.

“Labor has not only allocated $10.4 million for security; it has passed extraordinary laws to restrict civil liberties and enhance police powers around the venue. This sets a terrible precedent and may not even be constitutional.”

Wainwright said the expo shows how state and federal governments want to tie the country to military industries worldwide, setting up serious implications for Australia’s international human rights obligations.

“The expo comes in the context of a long-standing plan by Labor and the Coalition to make Australia one of the world’s top 10 weapons exporters. This has been reinforced by the Force Posture Agreement, which expands US access to Australian bases and other facilities, and the AUKUS pact, which further enmeshes Australia in the US’ war plans.

“Australia is therefore deepening bilateral military ties with highly repressive states committing gross human rights abuses and war crimes, such as Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Israel.”

Wainwright pointed out that the exhibiting arms dealers include Rafael, which manufactured the spike missile that killed Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom.

He said the push towards militarism as an economic “answer” is not only coming from Australia. “This strategic turn to weapons production has been further encouraged by the Donald Trump regime, which wants to increase US military spending next year by a massive 50%, bringing it to US$1.5 trillion.

“A section of Australia’s corporate elite is very keen to get some of the contracts, as are the state governments and the neoliberal managers of most public universities, which have joined the stampede.

“The WA government is proposing weapons manufacturing as a replacement industry for Collie’s coal mining and thermal coal power industries.

“The sobering reality shows that the Australian government is preparing to face the threat of runaway global warming and the poly crisis of capitalism through repression and war.”

[Join the protest against Land Forces on October 6 at 5pm, at Yagan Square in the Boorloo CBD.]

author: Danica Rachel
title: Protest called against October arms fair in Perth
content:
The Land Forces Exposition 2026, to be held at the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre on 6-8 October, will be a three-day extravaganza of exhibitions, talks and luncheons, where the main topic of conversation is how best to kill people. More than 20,000 weapons company executives, politicians and military personnel from around the world are expected to attend.

We have to protest against this outrageous celebration of death and destruction.

Photos from the 2024 event on the front page of the

Land Forces website

 are enough to make you ill. A smiling representative of Anduril, a company specialising in AI-powered warfare, shows off a battle drone. A live demonstration of a robot dog, presumably designed to carry autonomous weapons, takes place on the exhibition floor. A drone as big as a car hangs from the ceiling.

Lockheed Martin, the world’s biggest arms dealer—and builder of the F-35 fighter jets Israel uses to bomb Gaza—will have its latest death machines on display. As will Elbit Systems, Israel’s biggest weapons company.

Senior executives from Anduril and BAE Systems will speak on a panel discussing “the realities of Ukraine, Iran and other current conflicts”. Today’s bloodshed used as a case study to make tomorrow’s killing more efficient. What could those “other conflicts” be? Israel’s invasion of Lebanon? One assumes that there’s much these monsters have learned from Gaza, too.

Lockheed Martin and BAE will be joined by Babcock, Boeing, Honeywell, Northrop Grumman and Thales. Aside from all having had significant roles in providing Israel’s weapons for use in Gaza, they are all on the exclusive list of companies involved in creating nuclear weapons.

The list goes on, and on, and on. More than 650 companies will have exhibits on the floor, all of them dealing in weapons, military hardware or AI systems for warfare.

To say the state Labor government is rolling out the red carpet for this smorgasbord of warmongers would be an understatement. It is going above and beyond to keep conference-goers comfortable by pouring $11.5 million into security.

Special legislation gives police the power to set up checkpoints, stop and search anyone for any reason, and ban anyone they like from a significant section of Perth’s CBD, including a major train and bus station, for ten days surrounding the event.

Police Minister Reece Whitby said of the laws: “We saw the scenes that occurred when Land Forces was held in Melbourne in 2024, and we do not want to see anything like that here in Perth”. Whitby was referring to the

protest by 1,500 people

 against the last iteration of this festival of death.

None of this—the war profiteering, the authoritarian police powers, the increased drive towards a world of total war—should pass without protest.

So a coalition of anti-war and Palestine solidarity organisations has called a demonstration against Land Forces on 6 October, 5pm, at Yagan Square in the Perth CBD. We need as many people as possible to make it clear that we reject Land Forces and everything it represents.

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Balmain meeting calls for public housing in Bays West, opposes Labor’s plan
content:
Bays West includes public land at Glebe Island, White Bay and parts of Rozelle and Lilyfield. Labor’ wants to hand this to developers to build high-rise apartments; it proposes only 10% be reserved for “affordable” or “essential worker” housing.

The 150-strong meeting was organised by the Better Future Coalition (BFC), comprising resident groups which oppose NSW Labor and the Labor-dominated Inner West Council’s (IWC) pro-developer planning schemes.

Many community and housing groups supported the meeting including Leichhardt Matters, Save Dully, Action for Public Housing, Save Marrickville, Hands off Glebe, Friends of Erskineville, Doing Density Better, Mosman Matters and others.

Judy Mundey, a long-time activist and barrister set the framework for discussion by outlining the historic decline in public housing across NSW and the consequent rise in homelessness, housing insecurity and expensive rents and house prices.

“It’s not as if the government is not aware we have a housing crisis; there is no shortage of announcements and promises … but almost all proposals involve the private sector.”

Mundey said there are “almost daily” reports on dodgy developers, to whom Minns is handing over public land.

“If we’re going to address the housing crisis, we need less privatisation of public land and more well designed public housing,” Mundey said.

“In opposition, Labor said any surplus land would be subject to a mandatory requirement for 30% of social, affordable and universal housing. But now in government, at Bays West, it has reduced that to 10% for affordable and essential worker housing.

“There is no commitment for public housing to be any part of the plan. This is a failure to utilise public assets to address the social injustice inflicted on so many, a failure to ensure a decent, safe, secure home, essential for health and wellbeing.”

Architect and urban designer Eddie Ma gave details about what is known about the Bays West plan. He said Minns had commissioned international architecture firms to make proposals.

Ma emphasised that the plans could be changed — for better or for worse. “It should be the community that decides what we do with Bays West, not the government and certainly not architects.”

Former independent Inner West councillor John Stamolis said that the inner west was one of the country’s highest density areas and that it was ridiculous for Labor to accuse people who want better planning of opposing any development. He said there needed to be more public housing now because of the security it brings.

Greens MP for Balmain Kobi Shetty said it was hard to know a lot about Labor’s plan as it has been vague. She said the Greens welcome Labor’s commitment to delivering the Glebe Island Bridge as an essential walking and cycling link.

Ben Radford, a town planner and Green Left journalist, MCed the meeting, which voted overwhelmingly to adopt a resolution opposing Labor’s plan, calling for community consultation and to add a sixth point calling for any housing at Bays West to be public.

BFC had invited Philippa Scott, Labor’s candidate for Balmain and deputy mayor of IWC, to come and listen to the concerns. She did not reply.

[Isaac Nellist is a member of the Better Future Coalition and is the Socialist Alliance candidate for Balmain in the NSW elections.]

author: James Plested
title: Victorian Socialists’ election campaign in full swing
content:
The Victorian state election will take place in just over two months, on Saturday 28 November. The Victorian Socialists’ campaign is now in full swing, with local campaign activity taking place daily across Melbourne and regional Victoria.

The scale of the campaign—with VS candidates set to run in all 88 lower house seats and all eight upper house regions across Victoria—is beyond anything the socialist left in Australia has attempted for generations (if ever). Even just a few years ago, a statewide campaign like this would have been unthinkable. That it’s happening at all is something of a breakthrough.

Between 1 June and 19 September, VS volunteers knocked on more than 80,000 doors, already well on track to reach the 2022 campaign total of around 190,000. The party received around 2,000 requests for campaign signs to be put on front fences and in yards, eclipsing the 2022 total of 1,000, with hundreds of orders a week still coming in. More than 2,400 people donated to the campaign, and almost 1,800 registered for a party event. 

New branches are springing up everywhere. Wherever they do, we’re finding people who want to get involved. VS events in places like Pakenham, a suburb on the far south-eastern fringe of Melbourne—more than 50 kilometres from the CBD—are attracting many new faces. And we now have active branches in regional centres including Geelong, Warrnambool, Ballarat and Bendigo, and the beginnings of branches in Shepparton, Wodonga and Warragul. 

We’re accustomed to being almost completely overlooked by the mainstream media, but the sheer size of our campaign this time means we’re increasingly difficult to ignore.

ABC News reported

 on the VS campaign launch on 1 August, and Channel 9 reported on our “all-in” Footscray doorknock on Sunday 16 August, which was attended by more than 350 volunteers. VS candidate for the Northern Metro upper house region Omar Hassan has become something of a regular fixture on talkback radio 3AW’s morning show with Tom Elliot—most recently on the topic

“what is socialism?”

VS candidates in the regions are attracting particular attention.

Hera Sheppard,

 in the seat of

South-West Coast

 (comprising Warrnambool, Port Fairy, Portland and surrounds), has been featured in several articles in the

Warrnambool Standard

, including the front cover. An

article at ABC News

 and an appearance on ABC Radio followed—the latter

drawing the ire

 of Australia’s richest billionaire Gina Rinehart, who objected to Hera’s claim that she was pushing for Australians to work for $2 a day (in the 2012 quote Hera referenced, Rinehart worried about Australia’s competitiveness when “Africans want to work, and its workers are willing to work for less than $2 per day”). It certainly helps that, at 18, Hera is one of the youngest candidates ever to run for parliament in Australia, but regional media in general have shown a keen interest in VS candidates everywhere. 

Signs also suggest the campaign is resonating. In Footscray, where VS volunteers have already knocked on around 17,000 doors, and the campaign has put up more than 200 yard signs, a steady trickle of people have turned up to volunteer at the campaign office after receiving VS material.

There’s no escaping the fact that politics in Victoria has shifted decisively to the right, and it’s likely either a Liberal or a Liberal-One Nation Coalition government will be elected on 28 November. But there’s no shortage of people who are horrified by the rise of One Nation and who are relieved to find, when visited by a VS volunteer, that there’s a party offering a genuinely anti-establishment alternative on the left. 

Hassan tells the story of Mary, an 82-year-old he met while doorknocking in the outer northern suburb of Thomastown. A long-time Labor voter, Mary told Omar that she wouldn’t vote for the ALP this time because “they’ve completely lost their way”. He later recounted:

“Unsure where things might go, I raised Pauline Hanson and her racist attempt to blame migrants for all our problems. She shook her head. ‘It’s very sad, very wrong’, she said, before explaining that she grew up in Reefton, where her father worked building the Upper Yarra Dam alongside thousands of migrants from around the world. She described playing with all the Italian and Yugoslav kids, going to each other’s houses and having great fun. ‘It made life richer, having all the different cultures, growing up together’.

author: AWSM
title: Errico Malatesta – Vote? What For?
content:
George: This beer’s not too bad, is it?

Jack: Yes, it’s alright, but what a price!

George: Shocking – especially when you remember what things used to cost. Still, you can’t wonder with all these taxes. It costs you twice as much to live as it used to. They put up the price of some things, and say you can do without them. But you can’t do without bread, and food, and clothes – you have to pay the rent all the same, and then there are the taxes on this and the rates – on our wages too! What a life! And it’s our own fault! If we wanted to we could alter things. The working class has the remedy in its own hands.

George: Easy enough! You’ve got a vote?

Jack: What’s that got to do with it?

George: Have you, or haven’t you?

Jack: Well, I’m entitled to a vote – but I never make use of it.

George: There you are! You’ve got a vote, but you just won’t take the trouble to use it, and then you wonder why things are so bad. You deserve all you get, honestly! People like you are responsible for all the trouble in the world!

Jack: Alright, alright, keep your hair on! Just tell me what’s the good of voting?

George: It’s obvious. Who makes the laws? The M.P.’s. Elect good M.P.’s and you get good laws.

Jack: Good councillors and good M.P.’s? We’ve heard that for a long time. But you’d have to be deaf, dumb, and blind not to notice it’s the same stooges that always get in. Oh, it’s wonderful to hear them when they’re after votes at election time. They pat you on the back, ask after the wife and kids, kiss the baby, promise you railways, bridges, work, cheap bread, less taxes, higher wages, protection – absolutely everything! And once they get in, they’re no better than anyone else. Goodbye promises! The wife and kids may starve, there’s no more or less work than before, the whole town can be falling to pieces for all they care. They’ve other things to think about than your troubles! Then a few years later they start the ballyhoo again. It doesn’t matter what colour the party is: they’re all the same. As soon as they’re elected, they forget all about you. They’re in their clubs and at their select dinners, and they don’t even trouble to come and have a look at you until the next election.

George: That’s correct! But why elect the rich? Don’t you know that the rich only live on the work of the masses? So how do you expect them to worry about the masses? All they think of is getting as much out of the ordinary man as they can.

Jack: Now you’re talking! But it’s not only the rich. There’s the other type, who want to get elected so they can become rich.

George: That’s true. So don’t let’s vote for them. Let’s elect workers, experienced friends of ours, as you might say, and then we won’t be fooled.

Jack: Oh, we’ve got some of your “experienced friends” in now, and they’re no different from our acknowledged enemies! Anyhow, what do you mean, “let’s elect – let’s elect.” As if we – you and me – could do as we like!

George: But it’s not only us two. If each one of us tried to convert other people and they would do the same, labour would have a majority, and we could elect whoever we liked. And that’s when we could form a government of the workers, and then . . .

Jack: And then it would be a paradise – I mean for those who were in Parliament! You’re arranging things a bit too quickly! Those in command always have the majority. The rich are always in power. Just imagine a poor worker, perhaps with an ill wife and four hungry kids, and you tell him to risk his job and get thrown out of his house to starve; just to give his vote to a candidate his master doesn’t like. Just try and convince those poor devils who can be thrown out of work by their boss whenever he likes. They’re never free; if they want to be free, they don’t want to waste their time voting – just take what they need.

George: But if we didn’t do that, no-one would vote. We couldn’t go to the workers and ask them to vote for our party, and say at the same time that votes were useless.

Jack: That’s just it! And on top of that you have to make election promises you know you can’t keep. And then you have to stand in with the Government, and mix with the well-to-do, and all the rest of it. As soon as any of your men are elected they have to kow-tow to the people you admit are the opponents of the workers. So why the hell talk about propaganda when the first thing you do is to counteract propaganda?

George: But you must admit, it’s an advantage to have our own men with …

author: Shamikh Badra
title: Between the ocean and Palestine: Remembering Peter Manning
content:
People will remember Peter Manning’s long career in media, politics and academia. They will rightly remember his years at the ABC, from Four Corners to leading news and current affairs.

But I want to write about the Peter I knew: he was a friend, who gave solidarity a human meaning that went well beyond public statements and political positions.

I first met Peter at a seminar at the University of Sydney in 2014. We talked for a long time. He was there with his partner Carol. He was warm and easy to be around. It did not take me long to realise that his support for Palestinian rights was not just something he brought out for public occasions.

For Peter, solidarity was something you did. He wanted to know the people affected by it, to hear their stories, to understand what they were going through and to be there if someone needed advice, support or a bit of help.

Palestine, for Peter, was a question of justice, rights and human dignity; it was never abstract. He saw the people behind the headlines: families, friends, people with names, stories and ordinary lives.

That is what made Peter’s solidarity different; it meant trying to understand why injustice happens, how politics, media and power shape people’s lives and then asking what you can actually do, even if it is something small.

Peter understood international solidarity. For him national borders did not limit our moral responsibility. He knew you do not need to share someone’s experience to stand beside them, but it is enough to recognise their humanity and right to freedom and justice.

Peter also understood that some voices find their way easily into the media and public life, while others are pushed to the margins.

Maybe that is why Peter cared so much about listening to people who were not always heard, and about creating space for others to speak. He did this in all the small things; a phone call to check in, advice at a difficult time, reading a draft and giving me his thoughts.

Palestine was part of Peter’s life in many ways — in his books and writing, in his friendships, in the keffiyeh he wore, the food he enjoyed and in the people he chose to stand beside.

Our friendship also moved beyond public events and political discussions. Peter became close to me and to my family, including when I graduated from the University of Sydney and when my father died during the war in Gaza.

Peter was one of those people from whom it was difficult to hear the word “no” when someone was needed support. He was generous with his time, experience and his contacts.

Peter spent many years at the centre of Australian media institutions and later turned a critical eye on the media itself.

He cared about how Arabs, Muslims and Palestinians were represented, about who was given the chance to speak and who was left out of the frame. These were never just academic questions; they were connected to how he saw other people and how he listened to them.

I learnt a great deal from Peter’s long experience in journalism, politics and academia. His encouragement was never just polite — he would ask questions, disagree sometimes, offer advice and share what he knew.

Then came the war in Gaza and my life became consumed by grief and worry, which meant we were not in touch as much as before.

Peter also loved the ocean and the beach; we used to swim and race each other. He considered himself a great swimmer. We used to challenge each other and argue, jokingly, about who was the better swimmer.

Some of my best memories are of him laughing. The jokes usually started quickly and sometimes we would barely stop. He had a great sense of humour.

Today it is hard to put into words how sad I am to have lost a dear friend.

My deepest condolences and love go to Peter’s family, to his friends and colleagues in journalism and academia, and everyone who worked with him at the ABC and elsewhere.

Peter taught me that real solidarity is not only about declaring where you stand. It is about making that position part of the way you treat people.

Farewell, Peter. The next time I go to the ocean, I will think of you. And maybe, just this once, I will let you have the title you always liked to claim without an argument from me: “The great swimmer”.

author: Tom Bramble
title: What’s the deal with productivity?
content:
The bosses are trying to convince workers that lower corporate taxes, fewer regulations and workers’ rights, and less union power would be good for real wages. What they really want is more profits at the expense of the working class.

For years, business lobby groups have decried what they call Australia’s “productivity crisis”. They don’t say workers are producing less than they used to; they say they aren’t increasing production as quickly as before and aren’t keeping pace with overseas productivity growth.

It’s true: growth in workers’ hourly output has slowed over the past decade, and Australian workers don’t produce as much value for the bosses as American workers. But the bosses argue that this means living standards are held back, and prices rise more than they otherwise would, contributing to the cost-of-living crisis.

They say that government regulations (rules about wages, hours of work, health and safety standards, construction standards, environmental protections and professional and occupational registration requirements) and trade unions are preventing business investment. Their solution is “deregulation”, “slashing red tape”, “more competition”. These are simply code words for attacking the working class.

Let’s break this down. First, what is productivity? The simplest definition is “output per hour”. For BlueScope Steel, it could be tonnes of steel produced per hour per worker. For a childcare centre operator, it could be the number of children in care per worker per day. Lift those and productivity rises.

But who benefits? Does the steel worker or childcare worker see their wage rise automatically if they get more done? Of course not. In the first instance, all the money made from extra production by every group of workers goes to the capitalists, not the workers. Workers’ standard of living depends on how much they fight for. And that applies across the whole economy.

The bosses say some of the additional money coming in from workers’ extra effort will come back through higher wages and maybe more jobs. They argue: “a rising tide lifts all boats”. Is that true, though?

First, productivity in Australia may have slowed in the past couple of decades, but it has still risen. Yet household living standards are no higher than they were in 2012. There is no indication that workers are seeing any of the higher value they produce in the form of higher real wages.

A starker example is the United States, which bosses always point to as the high-productivity benchmark, where output per worker is higher and rising faster. In that country, workers’ share of national income is now at its lowest since World War Two—the productivity gains have gone to the capitalists, who have grown ever wealthier at workers’ expense.

Take things down another level. Even if bosses shared a cut of the higher revenue from increased productivity with workers, or unions successfully struck to extract a higher wage, bosses would still be ripping off workers.

All wealth ultimately comes either from the world’s natural resources or from human labour. You only have to see what happens when workers go on strike to see the truth of this—nothing gets produced, not a wheel turns, the childcare centres lie empty. All the machinery, all the factories, all the railway lines can only be put to good use if workers labour on them. And these in turn are the product of previous generations of workers’ labour.

What the capitalists call productivity should really be called exploitation: the extraction of value from the worker over and above the cost of their reproduction, i.e. what is necessary to get them to come to work each day in the form of wages. They call it profit; in fact, it’s theft from the worker.

This theft lies at the heart of capitalism. It explains why the workers labour their whole lives and have not much more than their home to hand on to their kids, and often not even that. While their employer has significantly expanded their operations at the workers’ expense. Some of the bosses may blow the money on a more self-indulgent lifestyle, but personal greed doesn’t get to the heart of it.

Every boss is driven to extract more from their workers, i.e. to lift productivity, because if they don’t, their rivals will, and they will be undercut and go out of business. The winner is the boss who can exploit their workers the most. That’s why every boss in every country demands that governments make it easier for them to rip off their …

author: Alex Bainbridge
title: End Australian complicity in genocide
content:
Israel’s genocide in Gaza is now approaching the three-year mark, with no sign of slowing down. Yet, the federal Labor government continues to side with the United States and Israel, refusing to support Palestinian self-determination, despite giving lip service to a “two-state” solution.

Labor teamed up with the Liberals and One Nation on September 17 to vote down an Independent Senator-initiated senate inquiry into the Red Lines Package to ensure Australia complies with international law.

Days later, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese fronted the United Nations (UN) in a bid for Australia being given a seat on the Security Council. He bemoaned the “breakdown in international rules” and said countries must “lean in … to build peace and promote economic development and sustainability”.

Israel has murdered more than 1400 Gazans since the so-called “ceasefire” began in October last year. The genocide is still happening, albeit at a slower pace, because the United States is appeasing Israel. In August, Israel’s national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for nightly killings of 30-40 Gazans including those who do not “pose a danger… at that particular moment”.

Gazans are also dying because the health care system has been destroyed, economic life has been decimated and the blockade has not been lifted.

A new report from the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) said Gaza has experienced “the world’s most severe economic crisis on record”. It found that Gross Domestic Product last year was $US0.58 per day, “equivalent to 83 per cent below the already low level in 2022”.

Israel also continues to shift the “yellow line” confining Palestinians to an ever shrinking part of Gaza. Palestinians report that they wake up to find that they can no longer access their own land because Israeli troops are occupying it. The Guardian reported on September 27 that the “area still accessible to people and aid workers is barely 30% of the whole Gaza Strip”.

Google maps satellite depictions of Gaza, updated in September, laid bare Gaza’s utter devastation. Al Jazeera reported the “number of destroyed structures across Gaza has increased by 9%” since the so-called “ceasefire” began. This takes to 82% the proportion of structures in Gaza that have been damaged. Two thirds of all buildings have been completely destroyed.

Israel is also extending its ethnic cleansing and genocide in the Palestinian West Bank. This includes the Israeli parliament allowing 200 new settlement outposts over its term, leading to the forcible displacement of more than 100 Palestinian communities.

Israel is also pushing ahead with a plan to establish the E1 “settlement scheme” — “not just another colony” — which would divide the West Bank in two. Amir Dawood, head of documentation at the Palestine Authority’s Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, said: “This plan is one of the most dangerous settler-colonial plans in the entire occupied West Bank.”

A UN Commission of Inquiry found last year that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza. Its June report found that Israel is deliberately killing children. “The evidence shows that Palestinian children have been deliberately targeted and killed by the Israeli security forces,” said commission chair Srinivasan Muralidhar.

The federal Labor government is complicit in the genocide by allowing the supply of weapons components to Israel, supplying signals intelligence from Pine Gap and by muting its criticism of Israel, among other things.

It is also seeking to isolate the movement against genocide by promoting the Zionist smear campaign that solidarity with Palestinians amounts to a hatred of Jews. Its extremely biased royal commission into antisemitism is expected to recommend more restrictions on freedom of speech, including restriction on using the word “genocide”.

Australian international law expert and UN Commissioner Chris Sidoti, a supporter of the Red Lines Package said Australia “has obligations under international law” and that “unfortunately we seem more and more to be ignoring many of those”.

The International Court of Justice made several rulings in 2024 imposing “provisional measures” to prevent genocide on all countries including Australia. Sidoti said Australia’s response has been “far less” than the minimum of “what is required of us under international law”.

author: Emma Black
title: Strangulation: How did attempted murder become normal?
content:
A 16-year-old woman from Sydney’s northern beaches died in hospital in late August after reportedly being strangled during consensual sex with her partner. The tragedy has sparked a long-overdue reckoning with the consequences for young women of the pornification of sex and the normalisation of sexual violence that has come with it.

In recent years, sexual strangulation has gone from being a relatively marginal phenomenon to an everyday sexual practice. In Australia, 61 percent of young women report having been strangled during sex, according to a

2024 survey

 of thousands of 18- to 35-year-olds. Men are most likely to be the stranglers. There is no safe way to strangle someone. According to David Corlett and Marie Crabbe, founders of anti-strangulation advocacy group Breathless:

“Potential 

consequences

 [of strangulation]

range from

 neck pain to loss of bladder and bowel control, headaches, memory loss, seizures, brain damage, stroke and, as seems to be the case with the young woman from the northern beaches, death. The risks and consequences are cumulative, so the more someone is strangled, the more likely they are to suffer harm.”

Only a tiny percentage of middle-aged and older adults have engaged in sexual strangulation, but among young people it’s become commonplace. Maree Crabbe, who is also the director of

It’s Time We Talked

, says strangulation wasn’t an issue before about 2019. But things have changed dramatically since then. “In recent years, we’ve been hearing it’s become normal for young people of all backgrounds, socioeconomic groups, cultures, sexual orientations”, she recently told the

Sydney Morning Herald

.

So how did a potentially deadly act become a normal sexual practice?

The main driver is pornography.

Recent research

 found more than 60 percent of 18- to 35-year-olds had encountered sexual strangulation depicted in pornography. One study comparing the content in the most popular pornography across the two and a half decades to 2024 found that sexual strangulation has gone from almost non-existent to featuring in 15 percent of scenes.

Pornography has become the de facto sex education system for millions of young people. And strangulation is just the latest trend in an industry that maximises profits by selling more extreme depictions of violent and degrading treatment of women.

A landmark 2010 study of best-selling pornographic videos, published in the journal

Violence Against Women

, found that 88 percent contained physical aggression, while 49 percent of scenes contained verbal aggression. Perpetrators were usually male, whereas targets were overwhelmingly female. Targets most often showed pleasure or responded neutrally to the aggression.

So the vast majority of mainstream pornography, whether it depicts strangulation or not, reinforces the idea that violence and humiliation are not only permissible, but pleasurable for women. The pornography industry has “blood on its hands” for propagating this sort of violent content, according to Chanel Contos, founder of

Teach Us Consent

.

An example of how normalised strangulation during sex has become came from this year’s Eurovision song contest.

Romania’s 2026 song entry

 “Choke Me” repeats the words “choke me” 30 times in three minutes. The song also contains the lyrics “It’s hard to breathe in” and “make my lungs explode”.

Many mainstream commentators

emphasise

 the importance of avoiding “kink-shaming” when addressing the issue of sexual strangulation with young people. This dresses up the prioritisation of men’s sexual gratification over women’s safety as sex-positive open-mindedness. And it wilfully ignores the fact that sexual desires and practices are not simply a matter of individual preference; they are shaped and constructed in a society where women are not equal to men, and enormous profit can be made from sex by companies competing for market share.

The reality is that people’s sexual inclinations have not radically changed on their own over the last 50 years, such that the majority of men now enjoy inflicting harm on women. Market forces have pushed things in this direction. In an attempt to be more sensational and attract market share, pornography companies have taken the male-dominant trope that underpins the construction of mainstream heterosexuality and pumped it up to a new extreme. This has shaped attitudes to sex and sexual desire, which in turn further reinforces the business model. And …

author: CMI Argentina
title: Exigen la prórroga de la Ley de Emergencia Pediátrica antes de que el gobierno la deje caer
content:
El próximo 21 de octubre vence la Ley de Emergencia Pediátrica (27.796), sancionada por el Congreso Nacional con la mayoría más amplia de la era democrática, que además rechazó los sucesivos vetos del Poder Ejecutivo Nacional. La FESPROSA exigió su su prórroga y cumplimiento de manera integral, violentado por el gobierno nacional de ultraderecha de Javier Milei.


“A pesar de estar vigente (el propio Poder Ejecutivo condicionó por decreto su aplicación real a que el Congreso definiera el financiamiento), su contenido nunca se cumplió: no se actualizaron los salarios de las y los residentes ni de las y los trabajadores que atienden a la niñez en todo el país, y tampoco se concretó la exención de Ganancias para las horas y guardias extra del personal de salud”, señalaron desde la Federación Sindical de Profesionales de la Salud de la República Argentina (FESPROSA), conducida por María Fernanda Boriotti.


Y agregaron: “Para que la ley se cumpla de manera integral, lo primero es que no caduque: necesitamos su prórroga”.


“Junto al colectivo de discapacidad, a las y los universitarios y a todo el pueblo que exige el fin de las políticas de ajuste del gobierno libertario, el 21 de octubre volveremos a elevar la voz en todo el país por una salud pública de calidad, universal y con trabajadores con derechos, al servicio de todas y todos los argentinos”, reclamaron desde la organización gremial.

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Pressure Mounts at Labour Conference to Kick Palantir Out of NHS
content:
The NHS’s contract with Palantir has come under pressure at Labour party conference, with 20k party members backing a motion to end the service’s reliance on the US spytech firm. 


Healthcare workers and patients protested outside the venue, calling for the government not to renew a highly controversial £330m patient data contract with Palantir.


The company provides tech to the Israeli military during its genocide in Gaza, as well as custom surveillance tools to ICE in the US.. 


A majority

 of Labour voters


(76%)

 believe Andy Burnham’s government should allow Palantir’s NHS contract to expire without renewal in February 2027.


Around 30 health workers dressed in scrubs attended the No Palantir in the NHS demo outside the conference in Liverpool on Tuesday, ahead of Burnham’s speech. 


NHS doctor Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, a campaigner at Medact, told Novara Media: “The government has the perfect opportunity to end this contract. It can do so safely and transition over to NHS-owned infrastructure. 


“Palantir’s NHS contract is a threat to the ethics we sign up to as health workers, it’s a

threat to our patient relationships

 and data privacy, and it’s a threat to the integrity and independence of NHS infrastructure.”


Patients cannot opt out of having their sensitive healthcare data stored on Palantir’s Federated Data Platform (FDP), and some Palantir staff are granted

“unlimited access”

to identifiable patient data by NHS England. 


First secretary of state Louise Haigh used her conference speech to delegates on Sunday to say Burnham’s government will refuse to “be in hock to foreign giants”, in a comment

understood to be aimed at

 Palantir. 


The Cheltenham Constituency Labour Party (CLP)

tabled a conference motion

 on tech sovereignty on Monday, stating that overreliance on US tech “poses unacceptable risks to the independence and security of the UK, its institutions and its people”. 


Exeter CLP called on the government to allow the NHS’s Palantir contract to expire in 2027, look to Greater Manchester’s approach as a “blueprint” and build an NHS-controlled replacement system. 


However, the motion was not chosen for debate, despite more than

20k members

 voting for it. 


Greater Manchester, where Burnham served as mayor for nearly a decade, has repeatedly rejected Palantir’s FDP in its NHS services, using

 a UK-created alternative

instead. 


More protests against Palantir are set to take place across England as part of an international week of action uniting health workers and unions in the US, Brazil and Europe.

author: CNT Santander
title: ¿Cómo paramos la siniestralidad laboral?
content:
Al momento de escribir estas palabras, son

12 personas trabajadoras muertas

 en accidentes laborales en Cantabria en lo que llevamos de 2026.


Recientemente, en este mes de septiembre, han perdido la vida dos trabajadores de una subcontrata de la empresa de residuos y aguas

MARE

 y un trabajador de

Dafer Carretillas

 al que se le cayó una saca de 1.200 kilos de sepiolita encima. De este último, los medios de comunicación principales de la región ni siquiera se han hecho eco hasta días después. Como si unas noticias fueran más relevantes que otras, dependiendo de la empresa en la que se trabaje, tratándose de pérdida de vidas humanas.


Como sindicato,

llevamos tiempo advirtiendo

 en nuestras redes sociales que estamos ante

una situación muy preocupante

 y que no vemos que desde las instituciones se estén poniendo las herramientas necesarias para que las tasas de accidentes, mortales o no, dejen de subir. Porque la realidad nos muestra que siguen

in crescendo

.


No nos vale con que

Inspección de Trabajo

 haga lo que tiene que hacer y estudie las causas que provocaron el accidente e intente esclarecer los hechos, sino que hay que implementar estrategias para que los accidentes no sucedan, hacer estudios relevantes que den toda la información posible y tomar medidas, con

urgencia

. Desde los centros de trabajo.


Desde CNT Santander, como sindicato de clase, lamentamos esta terrible situación porque es algo que nos lástima profundamente y nos preocupa mucho, porque

un empleo no puede costar la vida

, porque la clase trabajadora ha de realizar su labor en condiciones dignas y regresar a su casa tras cada jornada.


La realidad es que como muestran los informes del

ICASST

, desde el día 1 del mes de enero al 31 del mes de agosto, constan

4.820 accidentes con baja

, de los cuales

9 resultaron accidentes mortales

 (más los tres que han sucedido en septiembre y que aún no aparecen en estas estadísticas), y

4.291 sin baja

.


Por este motivo, desde el

GT de Comunicación de CNT Santander

 comenzamos nuestra propia

CAMPAÑA DE PREVENCIÓN DE LA SINIESTRALIDAD LABORAL

, poniendo nuestro granito de arena en la protesta, en la reivindicación y sobre todo en la visibilización de la alta siniestralidad y la necesaria prevención de riesgos laborales.


Nuestro objetivo es que las personas trabajadoras afiliadas a nuestro sindicato puedan expresarse libremente y darnos a conocer su situación en el día a día en sus empresas, por lo que realizaremos una

encuesta

 de seguridad laboral y llevaremos a cabo un estudio posterior con informes para intentar esclarecer las causas.


Así mismo, pondremos a disposición de todas las personas que lleguen a nuestras RRSS:

contenido interesante

 para que conozcan sus derechos en materia de prevención y pongan el foco en la seguridad laboral, en aquello que se pierde por la rutina, las prisas y los ritmos elevados de producción.


Creemos que acercar la prevención de riesgos laborales a las personas trabajadoras es nuestra obligación como organización, para intentar minimizar en lo posible, en lo que está en nuestras manos, que las estadísticas de accidentes con baja, sin baja y mortales sigan ascendiendo de manera vertiginosa.


Pero ante todo, reivindicaremos que las instituciones y las empresas destinen más presupuesto a la seguridad laboral de la clase trabajadora, haciéndolo de manera preventiva, no tras sufrir un accidente grave o mortal. Son ellos, como marca la normativa de la

Ley 31/1995 de PRL

, quienes deben poner a disposición todos los medios necesarios para proteger la seguridad y la salud de las personas trabajadoras a su cargo.


Como personas que conocemos de cerca el trabajo de prevención nos consta que todavía hay muchas empresas en Cantabria que no dan el valor que se merece a la prevención, que no poseen una cultura preventiva real y efectiva instalada en sus empresas y, también, por desgracia, que muchas personas trabajadoras ven en la prevención solo algo tedioso que no les apetece aprender y/o burocracia inservible que les fastidia la jornada, en muchos casos.


En PRL

no basta con cumplir la normativa en el papel

, cada departamento tiene que poner de su parte para mantener la correcta seguridad, tiene que ser parte indivisible del ecosistema de las empresas y estar en el ADN de cada persona. author: Alex Salmon
title: The absent history of social upheaval after WWI
content:
Riots: Returned soldiers and public disorder in Australia at the end of World War I By Fiona Skyring Perth: UWA Press November, 2025 225pp RRP $39.99

Peace Day celebrations were held across Australia on November 14, 1918, following the end of World War I.

Even though the shooting had barely ended, the social tensions created by the war would be exposed in riots and brawls involving returned soldiers in Adelaide, Broken Hill and Townsville. These were predecessors to the riots that occurred from 1919–21.

Author and historian Fiona Skyring explores this history in her 2025 book, Riots: Returned soldiers and public disorder in Australia at the end of World War I.

In Townsville and Broken-Hill, riots and brawls occurred between self-styled “loyalist” soldiers and trade unionists, socialists and anti-conscriptionists. In Adelaide, soldiers showed their support to striking tram drivers, 300 of whom had served in the Australian Imperial Forces (AIF), by organising and attacking strikebreakers.

The Australia that WWI soldiers returned to was deeply divided by class, religion, social and political issues. The country had been rocked by the 1916–17 anti-conscription referenda, the 1917 New South Wales general strike, and international events such as 1916 Irish Easter Uprising, the 1917 Russian Revolution and the 1918–19 influenza pandemic.

In 1918–19 these divisions continued, as the country experienced a cost-of-living crisis, which was compounded by the mass bereavement due to the war.

Industrial upheaval continued in 1919 with 6.3 million days lost to industrial action, figures unmatched even in the 1970s. The largest strike was waged by the Seamen’s Union, which shut down wharves across the country between May and August.

In Riots, Skyring examines the way the ANZAC legend was being constructed by writers such as Charles Edwin Woodrow Bean, even as WWI continued.

In Bean’s ANZAC Book, published in 1916, the stories of soldiers who said they didn’t want to fight, thought their comrades’ deaths were futile and felt the class divisions between officers and ordinary soldiers in the AIF, were excluded.

Bean wrote in 1919: “Australia (has become) a new nation. Five years ago, the world barely knew her. Today, the men who went to fight for her have placed her high in the world’s regard.”

The celebrated legend of the ANZAC was dominated by the ideal of the overwhelmingly white, tough man from the bush; a classless citizen soldier whose sacrifice was made in the name of nation, empire and freedom. This narrative excluded the 1000 Aboriginal men who served in the AIF and who would experience more discrimination upon their return after the war’s end.

The message that civilian society should honour the soldiers’ sacrifice and any criticism of WWI being seen as “an attack on the soldiers” made it easy for right-wing politicians, industrialists and organisations such as the Returned Soldiers and Sailors Imperial League of Australia (RSSILA) to paint anti-war activists, trade unionists, socialists, Irish republicans and members of the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) as “disloyal”.

When 1000 socialists and members of Brisbane’s Russian exile community carried red flags on a march through the city in defiance of the 1914 War Precautions Act, on March 23 1919, the conservative press and other forces in collaboration with military intelligence whipped up xenophobic anti-communist sentiment.

This resulted in a crowd of 7-8000 returned soldiers marching to South Brisbane, attacking the headquarters of the Russian Workers’ Association and engaging in an anti-Russian pogrom. These events became known as the Red Flag Riots.

Further soldier’s riots would occur in Fremantle, Melbourne, Kalgoorlie-Boulder and Sydney between 1919 and 1921. The Sydney 1921 riots inspired D H Lawrence’s 1923 book, Kangaroo.

However, the soldiers’ riots were not all directed against socialists and trade unionists.

Skyring describes the events of November 1918, when returned soldiers acted in solidarity with striking tram drivers in Adelaide by attacking strikebreakers.

Soldiers returning home on a troop ship to Fremantle Port in Western Australia on May 5, 1919, also gave their support to striking lumpers – workers who loaded and unloaded shipping cargo. There are accounts of soldiers fighting with police on Fremantle’s streets, in the days following.

title: تکنولوژی و نیروی کار3
content:
REzgar Akrawi: Lo que tenemos hoy delante no es un destino técnico ineludible. Es el producto de decisiones políticas y económicas que sirven a los intereses del capital, y puede ser combatido. Ello exige una organización de izquierda, progresista y de derechos a escala mundial, trabajar por construir alternativas digitales de izquierda y progresistas, situar la infraestructura de datos bajo el interés público y la administración social, convertir los algoritmos de «cajas negras» en software de código abierto sometido a auditoría independiente, imponer la transparencia en el diseño de los modelos y en las fuentes de sus datos, apoyar alternativas digitales cooperativas propiedad de quienes las usan y de quienes trabajan en ellas, y orientar esta tecnología al servicio de las necesidades de la sociedad y de la justicia social.


Sin estos mecanismos, el llamamiento a las leyes y a la supervisión sigue siendo general e insuficiente, y la tecnología continúa rehén de un puñado de corporaciones monopolistas y de grandes potencias. En cambio, mediante la propiedad social, la rendición de cuentas social y las alternativas cooperativas, se vuelve posible arrancar la inteligencia artificial a la lógica del monopolio y del beneficio, y convertirla en propiedad colectiva y en un medio de liberación humana.


Author


Rezgar Akrawi


رزكار عقراوي


    Submitted by

rezgar2

 on September 27, 2026


Un arma de destrucción masiva sin explosión: la inteligencia artificial y el desmantelamiento de la mente humana


Los directivos advierten y la carrera continúa: una lectura de izquierda del dilema de la inteligencia artificial


El lado ruidoso y el lado silencioso


Lo que presenciamos hoy no es una toma del poder sobre la humanidad por parte de los robots, tal como la imaginó el cine. Es otro modelo de control digital, asentado en la automatización y en los algoritmos para gestionar ámbitos cada vez mayores de la vida cotidiana. Perder el control sobre estos sistemas es, sin embargo, solo el lado ruidoso del peligro, que se desarrolla con rapidez por efecto de la competencia entre las grandes potencias y las corporaciones monopolistas, hasta el punto de que las leyes no logran seguirle el paso, y su desarrollo ocurre dentro de relaciones de propiedad y de una competencia feroz que hacen más probable que se salgan de control y multiplican su coste para la gente. Su cara más grave es mucho más callada, ya que la inteligencia artificial, bajo la estructura capitalista que la desarrolla, contribuye a moldear la conciencia de miles de millones de personas en un sentido que sirve a

la lógica del modelo capitalista

, y esta competencia puede, a falta de leyes eficaces, infligir los daños más graves a la mente humana y convertir la inteligencia artificial en un arma de destrucción masiva.


Estas inquietudes ya no provienen únicamente de quienes critican. La revista

TIME

 reveló que un sistema de inteligencia artificial se salió de control y atacó a otros sistemas, y días después cerca de 1.400 ingenieras e ingenieros de las mayores empresas firmaron

una petición conjunta

 que reclama poner freno al ritmo del desarrollo, y entre quienes la suscribieron figuran altos responsables de esas mismas empresas. Decenas de miles de personas, entre ellas científicos destacados del campo, han firmado

una declaración internacional

 que exige prohibir el desarrollo de la «superinteligencia» mientras no exista un consenso científico sobre su seguridad, mientras pensadores y técnicos han reclamado que su desarrollo se regule por ley y quede bajo supervisión social.


El 12 de septiembre de 2026, bajo una presión mundial popular, de derechos humanos y también técnica, las corporaciones del capitalismo digital se vieron obligadas a romper su silencio. Dario Amodei, director ejecutivo de Anthropic, publicó un artículo titulado

«Debemos pautar el ritmo de la frontera»

 en el que llama a su propia industria a frenar la carrera del desarrollo y propone abrir los laboratorios a evaluadores independientes con plenas atribuciones, un organismo de normas comunes entre las empresas y un acuerdo internacional que incluya a China. En cuestión de horas

Sam Altman

 anunció su acuerdo y adoptó la misma medida, Elon Musk escribió «Dario tiene razón», y a ellos se sumó Demis Hassabis, de Google DeepMind, mientras

las tres empresas revelaron

 que llevaban semanas dialogando sobre el asunto.


Esta admisión de los propios propietarios es la confirmación …

author: Luis Feliz Leon
title: German Amazon Workers Organize To Get Paid for Every Minute
content:
Amazon workers at four delivery and sorting warehouses in Germany are organizing to make every minute count. They’re demanding that Amazon pay them for every minute of work, saying in a petition that the company is stealing their time.


Working even 10 unpaid minutes a day, the workers say, adds up to 4.5 workdays per year of free labor, or about $712 U.S. (618 euros) in stolen wages. And at the most extreme, stolen time can reach up to 45 minutes per day.


The petition identifies three ways Amazon is stealing workers’ time:


1) Threshold time, where if a worker clocks in up to 15 minutes early for a shift or clocks out up to 15 minutes late, the company rounds back down to the scheduled time


2) Changing times to put on safety gear and boots


3) Walking time to pick up and return equipment


Stella de Palma, a delivery worker at a warehouse near Berlin, said workers normally change before clocking in. “Some shifts are only allowed to clock in or out at certain time clocks, which means we have to walk all the way across the shop floor first,” de Palma said.


She doesn’t think it makes sense, especially during peak night shifts from 11:10 p.m. to 9:30 a.m. “We’re already working near the locker rooms, where there are also time clocks.” What ends up happening is that they have to walk a long distance across the shop floor to clock in and then back to the locker room to change.


She has found workarounds: “I started leaving work unfinished instead of completing it, simply because I didn’t feel it was right to work those extra minutes for free.”


Amazon workers are bringing their case to an arbitration board, overseen by a retired judge, to rule on whether these extra minutes when clocking in and out qualify as working time. The workers are demanding a return to the “secondwise” system, where once you clock in, the exact time is logged in.


But whatever the legal outcome, the fact that workers weren’t consulted when Amazon made the change in 2024 has motivated them to redouble their organizing, so that they can block the unilateral authority of management to impose these kinds of workplace changes.


FROM TIME OFF TASK TO THRESHOLD TIMES


Workers said Amazon tells them they need to be more flexible with their schedules to meet customers’ needs. But Nils Carrara, a sort center worker, said when they show up earlier than scheduled in a show of flexibility, they aren’t paid for that time. “Why does a corporation like Amazon need to steal a few euros from me every day?” Carrara asked.


Workers like Carrara earn between $20 and $26 an hour. Amazon’s 1.5 million workers and misclassified contractors worldwide generate the company’s enormous wealth, driving its market valuation to nearly $3 trillion. That value created by workers has been funnelled into a $200 billion investment in artificial intelligence, including software for monitoring workers.


In squeezing workers down to the minute, Amazon is engaging in a long employer tradition. More than a century ago, management consultant Frederick Winslow Taylor popularized “scientific management,” a method of increasing output by following workers around with a clipboard and stopwatch, looking to optimize workers’ movements through incentives and by eliminating any superfluous motion or moment of slack.


Amazon has long subjected workers to a regime of algorithmic surveillance, tracking their every move to wring out more productivity. That has been a key spur to organizing as workers are penalized for “time off task” or missing productivity targets, a form of

algorithmic management

.


That’s old-fashioned twentieth-century Taylorism. Amazon has updated it from the era of stopwatches and clipboards to today’s algorithms, supplying the simple scripts for workers to follow and tracking them.


COMPANY CONTROL


High-tech wage theft is the latest battleground. Christian Harenberg, a supervisor, member of Verdi union, and vice chairman of the works council at an Amazon delivery station in Berlin, is organizing to revert back to a timekeeping log that records exact times a worker punches in and out. The petition is the opening salvo to revitalize the institutional structures of his site’s works councils.


Works Councils, a creation of German law, are elected representative bodies of workers who meet with management to deal with shop floor issues. As a Verdi union member and vice chairperson, Harenberg is a spokesperson and worker advocate; he and fellow works council …
