title: Συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στους/τις διωκόμενους/ες από τη παρέμβαση για την απεργία πείνας του Γ. Μιχαηλίδη, Τρίτη 29/9, 09.00 στα Δικαστήρια Λαμίας
content:
Αφίσες/Καλέσματα:


Συλληφθέντα από την παρέμβαση στις 13/6/23 στα δικαστήρια Άμφισσας


Δίκη από παρέμβαση στην τελευταία απεργία πείνας του αναρχικού συντρόφου Γ. Μιχαηλίδη


Καλούμε σε συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στο εφετείο Λαμίας, την Τρίτη 29/9/26, στις 9πμ


Τα καλοκαίρια του 2022 και του 2023 σημαδεύτηκαν από δύο μεγάλες μάχες που έδωσε μέσα από τη φυλακή ο αναρχικός σύντροφος Γιάννης Μιχαηλίδης.

Με κύριο αίτημα την αποφυλάκισή του

, που το κράτος εκδικητικά του αρνούνταν παρά τα χρόνια που ο σύντροφος είχε ήδη εκτίσει,

ο Γ.Μ. προχώρησε στην αναβαθμισμένη επιλογή των απεργιών πείνας

, φτάνοντας και τις δύο φορές σε οριακή κατάσταση υγείας. Την 30η μέρα κατά τη δεύτερη απεργία πείνας πήρε την απόφαση να κλιμακώσει και με απεργία δίψας, που είχε τελικά ως αποτέλεσμα τη νίκη του αγώνα του και την απελευθέρωση του συντρόφου.


Στη μάχη αυτή, ο αναρχικός χώρος στήριξε τον αγώνα του απεργού, καλώντας κεντρικές συνελεύσεις που διεξάγονταν πολλές φορές ανά βδομάδα, παράγοντας λόγο και δράσεις σε πανελλαδικό επίπεδο. Στην Αθήνα, το κίνημα αλληλεγγύης, από διαφορετικά μετερίζια αγώνα, προσπάθησε με όλες του τις δυνάμεις να δείξει την αλληλεγγύη του πολύμορφα στον αγώνα που έδινε ο σύντροφος. Στο πλαίσιο αυτό έδρασε και

η “Συνέλευση αλληλεγγύης στον αναρχικό απεργό πείνας Γιάννη Μιχαηλίδη”

 η οποία επιχείρησε να κεντρικοποιήσει το ζήτημα, να το ανοίξει κοινωνικά και να αναδείξει την εκδικητικότητα του κράτους απέναντι στους πολιτικούς κρατούμενους καθώς και να ασκήσει πίεση στο κράτος ώστε

να αποτρέψει τη δολοφονία του συντρόφου

.


Μία από τις παρεμβάσεις της συνέλευσης, που έλαβε χώρα στις 13/6/2023, ήταν η ανάδειξη της ευθύνης των δικαστικών αρχών που κρατούσαν τη ζωή του απεργού στα χέρια τους

. Των δικαστών της Άμφισσας δηλαδή, οι οποίοι, σε ευθυγράμμιση με την κρατική στρατηγική, καθυστερούσαν επί μήνες τις διαδικασίες αποφυλάκισής του μη εξετάζοντας καν το αίτημά του. Με την υγεία του απεργού να βρίσκεται λοιπόν σε οριακή κατάσταση, έχοντας ήδη ξεκινήσει και την απεργία δίψας,

πέντε συντρόφισσες και σύντροφοι της συνέλευσης

 πήγαμε στην Άμφισσα, όπου και

πραγματοποιήσαμε παρέμβαση με σπρέυ και τρικάκια στα τοπικά δικαστήρια που αναδείκνυαν την κρατική και δικαστική δολοφονία του συντρόφου μας

.


Αφού πραγματοποιήθηκε η παρέμβαση,κατά την αποχώρηση μας, μπάτσοι της περιοχή μας συνέλαβαν. Μετά από λίγες ώρες, βρεθήκαμε στα δικαστήρια της Άμφισσας, όπου περάσαμε από εισαγγελέα,στην οποία δηλώσαμε τους λόγους της παρέμβασης μας, με εκείνη να ειρωνεύεται τον απεργό πείνας Γ. Μιχαηλίδη και “προετοιμάζοντας” μας για την επερχόμενη καταδίκη μας.

Στο δικαστήριο που ακολούθησε, τονίσαμε την οριακή κατάσταση της υγείας του συντρόφου μας, το ιστορικό βάρος της ενδεχόμενης δολοφονίας του και την ευθύνη που φέρει το κράτος και ειδικότερα οι δικαστές της Άμφισσας

. Υπερασπιστήκαμε τον απεργό πείνας και τον αγώνα που έδινε βάζοντας ανάχωμα το ίδιο του σώμα διεκδικώντας την απελευθέρωση του. Τέλος, αναδείξαμε τη σημαντικότητα της αλληλεγγύης προς τους πολιτικούς κρατούμενους και τη συνολική εναντίωσή μας στον θεσμό της φυλακής. Καταδικαστήκαμε για διακεκριμένη φθορά και απείθεια λόγω άρνησης δακτυλοσκόπισης χωρίς εκπροσώπηση δικηγόρου.


Οι ποινές που μας αποδόθηκαν ήταν 30 μήνες φυλάκισης με αναστολή και 3.600€ χρηματική ποινή στο καθένα μας

. Τόσο το ύψος των ποινών, όσο και το μεγάλο χρηματικό ποσό που μας επιβλήθηκε, αναδεικνύουν την εκδικητική μεταχείριση μας από το δικαστήριο.


Αντιλαμβανόμαστε την αλληλεγγύη στους αγώνες των φυλακισμένων ως αναπόσπαστο κομμάτι των αγώνων που δίνουμε ενάντια σε κράτος και εξουσία.

Τις ιδέες και τα προτάγματά μας θα τα υπερασπιστούμε και στο εφετείο, που θα πραγματοποιηθεί στις 29 Σεπτεμβρίου 2026 στην Λαμία

, στοχεύοντας παράλληλα να περιοριστεί όσο το δυνατόν περισσότερο η έκδηλη εκδικητικότητα των πρωτόδικων ποινών.

author: groundxero
title: Labour department warns JNU management over non-compliance of orders, demands immediate cessation of layoffs and abuse of contract employees
content:
After over 1200 workers at the Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) threatened to go on strike on 28 September 2026 over alleged exploitation and labour code violations, a hearing overseen by a labour department conciliator has led to the management being warned over “legal implications” of repeated violations of binding labour agreements, and issued orders for immediate provision of safety equipment to workers, halting layoffs, constituting a Grievance Redressal Committee, and more. The strike has been called off for the time being under the assurance of the management’s future compliance.


 


by

Mouli Sharma


 


New Delhi, 28 September 2026:

 In the matter of an industrial dispute between the contract workers of Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi, represented by the All India General Kamgar Union and the university as well as private middle-man firms through which over 1200 of the university’s employees are contracted, a hearing on 25 September 2026 overseen by labour department conciliator Vinay Rana has led to stern warnings for the university and private firm managements over non-compliance with several labour laws, as well as directions for immediate rectification.


 


As per the 25 September settlement, the AIGKU, on 11 September 2026, served a notice to the university Registrar and Vice Chancellor announcing a contract workers’ strike on 28 September 2026 in pursuance of eight demands. These demands sought the rectification of various alleged labour-code violations by employers that jeopardised workers’ safety, made their employment financially exploitative and precarious, and undermined their rights and working conditions. The eight violations enlisted were as follows:


 


Non-payment of minimum wages on account of alleged manipulation of attendance.


Non-grant of earned leave and casual leave and uncompensated work on gazetted holidays.


Non-payment of statutory bonus with arrears for three years.


Augmentation of manpower in view of increased workload.


Unfair labour practices against workers and union office bearers.


Termination of contract workers engaged in hostel housekeeping and mess work with effect from August and September 2026.


Non-issuance of wage slips, identity cards, protective equipment, second uniform to security guards and non-display of statutory notices.


Illegal deductions, unilateral punishment of security guards and non-constitution of the Grievance Redressal Committee.


 


Copies of the notice were, as per the settlement, endorsed to the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), New Delhi, the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), New Delhi, and the Secretary, Ministry of Labour and Employment. The notice was then forwarded to the second Assistant Labour Commissioner,

named


Devendra Kumar Ram on the Labour Department website, in the office of the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) in Dwarka Sector 10. It was received on 24 September 2026, and the conciliation meeting overseen by Rana was held there the following day.


 


JNU is the principal employer responsible for the welfare of the aggrieved employees, but like most disputes in the contracting era, not the sole one. Two private security firms, Rakshak Securitas Pvt. Ltd. and A.E. Securitas Security and Allied Services (the security contractors of the university), along with Q Group (contractors of housekeeping staff in the university hostels) and Max Maintenance Services Pvt. Ltd. (contractors of maintenance staff) were also named.


 


Such conciliation proceedings take place in industrial disputes under Section 53 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.


 


AIGKU was represented by its President, Sucheta De, along with State Secretary of the All India Central Council of Trade Unions (AICCTU, which is a major Indian trade union affiliated with the CPI(ML) Liberation), Surya Prakash (State Secretary, AICCTU), Vice President of AIGKU’s JNU unit, Surya Prakash, and a member of AIGKU’s Executive Council, Manikant Patel.


 


JNU was represented by its Deputy Registrar and Labour Welfare Officer Abhishek Kumar Singh; Section Officer (Legal) Vineet Kumar Bizenia; “Assitant Admin (sic)” Imran Kataria; Sanitation Inspector Saurabh Kumar and Data Entry Operator Sandeep Kumar. None of the private contracting firms showed up to the meeting, despite being called upon by the authorised conciliator to appear and present written submissions and relevant employment records.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: ICE Is Still Targeting the Haitian Community in Springfield
content:
Hundreds of Haitians in Springfield are being forced to wear ankle monitors while they await immigration hearings.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

For the past two months, hundreds of Haitians in Springfield have been targeted by immigration authorities and forced to wear ankle monitors, as the Trump administration metes out collective punishment to appeal to its far right base.

Since the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians at the end of June, immigration enforcement has ramped up its detentions and deportations of Haitians — with its surge most concentrated in Springfield, Ohio.

The overturn of TPS was followed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sending letters to Haitian immigrants in Springfield, requiring them to report in person so they could be fitted with ankle monitors to track their locations until it is decided whether they will be deported. Throughout August, ICE’s surveillance of Haitians in Springfield through ankle monitors continued to rise.

Michaelle Louis, a Haitian organizer in Springfield, spoke with Truthout about the effects of the ankle monitoring program on members of her community.

Community members have “described their fear, their feeling of isolation, shame, anxiety and uncertainty,” as a result of being forced to wear ankle monitors, she said. For many, the monitors affect their ability to work, travel, and be around others, as community members sometimes fear being around people who are being tracked.

On August 31, Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old Springfield resident, died in an apparent suicide after being forced to wear an ankle monitor.

“I take it very personally,” Louis said, “because as a mom of a 16-year-old, they shared the same high school, and they knew each other.” Louis spoke of witnessing the confusion and pain in Haitian youth since the administration ended TPS at the end of July — and being unable to answer her own teenage daughter’s questions about why this was happening. “I can feel the pain” Damas Bel’s family is going through, she added.

Around the same time as Damas Bel’s death, faith leaders and community members — including Louis — launched the “Unshackle Springfield” campaign. In their initial press conference, organizers compared the ankle monitors to shackles forced onto Black people during slavery in the U.S.

Since then, activists have held press conferences, marches, and rallies, demanding an end to the government’s targeting of Haitians and the release of detained community members, including two local pastors detained at the end of August. The campaign is also demanding a path to citizenship or residency — permanent protected status — rather than a return to temporary status.

One of the pastors, Pastor Joubert Adrien, was released on bond in mid-September. While this was considered a victory for the campaign, Unshackled Springfield is still agitating for the release of many others, Louis told Truthout, noting that 76 members of the community have been detained by ICE.

Some community members have reported over the past few weeks that, when summoned to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) offices, they have been given a monitoring app on their phone rather than an ankle monitor, said Louis. This is likely a slight dialing-back on the part of immigration enforcement, and Louis considers it a result of the advocacy of the Haitian community and their allies. But it is not an official change, and hundreds of Haitians are still being forced to wear ankle monitors in Springfield — “so we have to keep pushing the campaign forward,” Louis concluded.

The targeting of Haitians in Springfield did not begin this year. It began in September of 2024, when false rumors of Haitians in Springfield eating their pets spread rapidly through far right and neo-Nazi online sites.

Brian Concannon, director of the Institute for Justice & Democracy in Haiti, explained to Truthout that these false reports “blew up” because of “people who were racist and opposed to Haitians,” including Donald Trump and now-vice president JD Vance, who was the senator of Ohio at the time.

Even though the lies were discredited, the far right “kept amplifying those demonstrably untrue accusations against Haitians,” Concannon added, “because they got value out of inflaming their base.”

author: Redazione_web
title: Salario giusto per chi?
content:
Il 24 giugno è diventato legge il decreto sul salario giusto. Accanto ad altre misure, il provvedimento interviene direttamente sul livello delle retribuzioni e, indirettamente, sul reddito e sulle modalità in cui si svolge la contrattazione; mettendo nelle mani dei capitalisti ulteriori strumenti per regolare a proprio vantaggio il mercato del lavoro.


Ancora una volta, ci troviamo di fronte ad un provvedimento che, accentuando il ruolo del governo nel controllo autoritario della società, attirando su questo stesso governo il malcontento di vasti strati della popolazione. Al tempo il provvedimento stesso svela la funzione effettiva del governo quale strumento della sete di profitto della borghesia, dimostrando con i fatti la validità della critica anarchica all’attuale modello di società, basata sul dominio politico ed economico da parte di una ristretta minoranza privilegiata.


La classe operaia e le classi sfruttate non hanno nulla da attendersi dalle loro istituzioni e dai loro rappresentanti: solo la loro organizzazione autonoma e unitaria, sulla base dell’autorganizzazione e dell’azione diretta, può contrastare il continuo peggioramento delle condizioni di vita e di lavoro e al tempo stesso creare le premesse per una nuova organizzazione della società, che superi il regime della proprietà privata e abbatta ogni forma di governo.


Il governo, con il decreto prima e con la sua trasformazione in legge poi, stravolge peraltro la gerarchia delle fonti su cui si basa il diritto del lavoro. Questa gerarchia vede al primo posto la Costituzione, poi le leggi ordinarie e poi la contrattazione; da notare che quest’ultima non può stravolgere quanto ordinato dalla Costituzione e dalle leggi ordinarie. Il testo approvato dal parlamento prevede invece una sorta di primato della contrattazione fra le parti: scompare ogni riferimento alla vita libera e dignitosa che dovrebbe essere assicurata dalla retribuzione corrisposta a chi fornisce la propria capacità lavorativa, secondo quanto previsto espressamente dalla Costituzione. Questa disposizione viene invece sostituita dal

riferimento al

 trattamento economico complessivo definito dai CCNL stipulati dalle organizzazioni dei datori di lavoro e dei lavoratori comparativamente più rappresentative sul piano nazionale.


Il rapporto di subordinazione che lega chi svolge lavoro dipendente al datore di lavoro, elemento che giustificava l’intervento dello Stato nel rapporto di lavoro – intervento comunque sempre volto a mantenere questa subordinazione – viene mascherato nel rapporto contrattuale, che diviene la base del trattamento economico di chi vende la propria capacità lavorativa.


È un ritorno ad una prassi liberale, già superata a parole dal corporativismo fascista, superamento poi recepito dalla Costituzione repubblicana e divenuto prassi comune in seguito alle lotte dell’autunno caldo.


Il completo abbandono dei salari operai alla discrezione dei capitalisti è ribadito dalle scelte dei sindacati confederali. Con l’ultima proposta per un accordo quadro sulle relazioni interconfederali CGIL, CISL e UIL si sono completamente subordinati di fronte alle richieste padronali e del governo. L’accettazione dell’indice IPCA NEI come riferimento per l’aumento delle retribuzioni nominali si traduce nella rinuncia alla difesa del potere d’acquisto, e quindi delle condizioni di vita per milioni di lavoratori e per le loro famiglie. Ma figuriamoci se questi sindacati pensano ad una redistribuzione del reddito a favore dei ceti sociali più svantaggiati e a danno dei profitti!


Il l

egame tra burocrazia sindacale e apparato statale è inevitabile: la principale fonte di entrate non sono le contribuzioni degli iscritti inseriti in attività produttive, sono i contributi dei pensionati e i compensi per i servizi di patronato. I sindacati maggiormente rappresentativi, poi, sono eredi diretti dei sindacati fascisti, e da questi hanno ereditato la subordinazione alla politica, giustificata in forme diverse ma concomitanti dalle burocrazie sindacali di ispirazione socialcomunista, cattolica o repubblicana.


Il processo di costruzione di un regime fascista, in atto oggi in Italia, non può che beneficiare dell’acquiescenza di CGIL, CISL e UIL.


Il benessere delle classi sfruttate, il loro elevamento materiale e morale, la loro emancipazione sta nelle loro mani, nella loro capacità di unirsi e dar vita ad organizzazioni stabili sotto il loro diretto controllo, autonome dai partiti e dalle …

Many libertarians say the traditional Left/Right political spectrum has become meaningless and useless. But to the extent that this is true for them, this is only because they have allowed themselves to be befuddled by political fraud and, perhaps, by a weak background in political history. The spectrum is just as useful and meaningful as it always was, which is very. It is necessary only to clarify one’s thinking about the past century in American politics to see that this is so.

But let us begin at the beginning — with what the left/right spectrum meant when it was created during the French Revolution. Murray Rothbard has written that 18th Century “liberalism” was “the party of hope, of radicalism, of liberty, of the Industrial Revolution, of progress, of humanity; the other [party] was Conservatism, the party of reaction, the party that longed to restore the hierarchy, statism, theocracy, serfdom, and class exploitation of the old order.” And according to Will and Ariel Durant in their book The Age of Napoleon, it was in the French Legislative Assembly in the fall of 1791 that the terms Right and Left were first used in this political sense. As the Durants tell it, when the assembly convened, the “substantial minority dedicated to preserving the monarchy … occupied the right section of the hall, and thereby gave a name to conservatives everywhere.” The liberals, meanwhile, “sat at the left.” Some fifty-odd years later, after another French Revolution (the one that took place in 1848) had unseated the last French king, Louis Philippe, the same seating arrangement was revived for the newly elected legislative assembly of the Second Republic. As has often been noted, two of the newly elected legislators who sat together on the left side of that assembly in 1848 and 1849 were the free market economist and publicist for free trade Frederic Bastiat and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, the first man ever to publicly declare himself an anarchist.

This conception of the Left/Right political spectrum also guided the political understanding of the 20th Century libertarian activist and writer Karl Hess, who wrote forty years ago that on “the far right […] we find monarchy, absolute dictatorships, and other forms of absolutely authoritarian rule,” while the Left “opposes the concentration of power and wealth and, instead, advocates and works toward the distribution of power into the maximum number of hands.” Just as the farthest right you can go is absolute dictatorship, Hess argued, so “[t]he farthest left you can go, historically at any rate, is anarchism — the total opposition to any institutionalized power, a state of completely voluntary social organization.”

Now, if we take this model of the Left/Right political spectrum and apply it to the politics of today, what follows from that? First, that all dictatorships, whether they are called communist or fascist, are on the Right. This is, of course, contrary to the doctrine set forth a few years ago in a ridiculous and unfortunately somewhat influential …

title: La France ne doit pas extrader Gino et Zaid !
content:
Communiqué de l'union régionale parisienne des syndicats

CNT

 à propos des antifascistes Gino et Zaid, menacés d'extradition.


«

 

Non bis in idem.

 

» Derrière cette locution latine se cache un principe essentiel du droit : celui de ne pas être jugé deux fois pour les mêmes faits. Et pourtant la France et l'Allemagne s'apprêtent à piétiner ce principe en revenant sur la décision prise en 2025 de refuser l'extradition vers la Hongrie de Gino, militant antifasciste poursuivi dans le cadre de l'affaire de Budapest.


Chaque année, autour du 11 février, se tient à Budapest la plus grande mobilisation ouvertement néonazie d'Europe. Lors de ce «

 

Jour de l'honneur

 

», des militants en uniformes de différentes milices nazies locales et européennes se rassemblent pour célébrer la résistance de la Waffen-

SS

, de la Wehrmacht, et de l'armée hongroise lors du siège de Budapest par les armées roumaine et soviétique en 1945. Une défaite pour les nazis, qui met fin au massacre des milliers de juifs perpétrés dans la capitale hongroise.


Et chaque année, des mobilisations antifascistes tentent de dénoncer et d'empêcher cette grande rencontre, qui constitue un véritable moment fédérateur pour toute la mouvance néonazie internationale. En février 2023, des affrontements ont eu lieu entre antifascistes et néonazis, certains de ces derniers ayant reçu 5 à 8 jours d'incapacité temporaire de travail. Pour faire exemple, les autorités hongroises, alors menées par le Premier ministre d'extrême-droite Victor Orbán, décident de mettre en place une véritable «

 

chasse à l'homme

 

» contre les militant·es antifascistes. Celle-ci prend la forme d'une campagne médiatique féroce — qualifiant de terroristes les collectifs se revendiquant antifascistes — et de l'émission de mandats d'arrêts européens à l'encontre d'une quinzaine de militant·es, encourant des peines pouvant s'élever jusqu'à 24 années de prison.


Face à l'évidence d'un procès politique, les antifascistes incriminé·es se réfugient à travers toute l'Europe. C'est ainsi que Gino, militant antifasciste italien, se retrouve en France, où il finit par être arrêté en décembre 2024 par la sous direction anti-terroriste alors qu'il se rendait à un match de football. À l'issue d'un long procès, doublé d'une large campagne de soutien mise en place par le Comité Solidarité Budapest et à laquelle l'Union régionale parisienne de la

CNT

 a participé, la justice française a décidé, en avril 2025, de refuser l'extradition du militant vers la Hongrie, estimant que les conditions d'un procès équitable et de conditions de détention respectueuses des droits fondamentaux n'étaient pas assurées par les autorités hongroises.


Cependant, moins d'un mois après ce premier refus sensé enterrer la procédure, c'est au tour de l'Allemagne de demander l'extradition de Gino, sur la base de la même enquête menée par la police hongroise, au prétexte que deux des victimes présumées seraient de nationalité allemande. Et cette fois le 19 août, la même Cour d'appel de Paris décide de retourner sa veste et d'accepter d'extrader Gino, cette fois vers l'Allemagne où il risque jusqu'à 10 ans de prison. Or, on peut légitimement craindre qu'il soit ensuite remis à la Hongrie — qui l'a peut-être déjà condamné en son absence —, l'Allemagne ayant déjà décidé d'extrader illégalement, selon l'aveu même de sa Cour constitutionnelle, la·e militant·e non-binaire Maya vers la Hongrie. Condamné·e en première instance à huit ans de prison, iel y est placé·e à l'isolement, ne bénéficie que d'une heure de sortie et est filmé·e 24h sur 24h.


Le 30 septembre prochain, la Cour de cassation peut encore renoncer à cette complicité de la France dans cette chasse à l'homme. De même, le 7 octobre, la Cour d'appel de Paris peut refuser l'extradition directe vers la Hongrie de Zaïd, militant antifasciste syrien et résident allemand, lui aussi mis en cause dans cette affaire. L'Union régionale parisienne des syndicats

CNT

 réaffirme son soutien à tou·tes les militant·es antifascistes persécuté·es dans le cadre de cette affaire, énième précédent inquiétant de criminalisation politique de l'antifascisme. À travers Gino, Zaïd, Maja, les autres inculpé·es de Budapest mais aussi de Lyon, c'est nous toutes et tous qui sommes visé·es.


Solidarité antifasciste internationale

 

!

title: Jorge Macri disputa el voto a LLA actuando contra los sectores populares
content:
El Gobierno de la Ciudad envió un protocolo que obliga a las directoras a denunciar a estudiantes que “podrían estar cometiendo un delito”. Mientras presiona a juezas por televisión y militariza los barrios, ahora Macri quiere que las escuelas sean prisiones.


Jorge Macri, Javier Milei y Patricia Bullrich. Foto: GCBA


Por Mario Hernandez


En una clara persecución a los jóvenes y una medida casi fascista, el gobierno de la Ciudad envió un protocolo a las escuelas que obliga a las conducciones de las escuelas a denunciar a estudiantes que “podrían estar cometiendo un delito”.


La circular llegó a las escuelas de parte de la Ministra de Educación porteña, Mercedes Miguel para informar sobre cómo aplicar el nuevo Régimen Penal Juvenil en las escuelas de la Ciudad. Régimen por el cual se aprobó la imputabilidad a los 14 años.


En el comienzo del mensaje que llegó por correo electrónico, Miguel informa cómo va a actuar desde el Ministerio para “resguardar la vida escolar y el bienestar de nuestras escuelas”. En lugar de fortalecer los equipos de orientación escolar para contener los graves problemas sociales de los jóvenes Jorge Macri a través de su ministra en Educación les declara la guerra a las principales víctimas de sus políticas que nada tienen que envidiarle a las de Milei.


Desde la agrupación 9 de abril advierten que es “un paso más en la confirmación de un estado policíaco que Macri está imponiendo a la Ciudad”. Además, militarizando los barrios y reprimiendo como se vio en el operativo Tormenta Negra.


Operativo “Tormenta Negra II”

 


Vecinos y vecinas de los barrios denunciaron el secuestro de mercaderías y pertenencias como materiales de construcción, colchones y carros por parte de Espacio Público, también la detención ilegal y al boleo de vecinos y trabajadores. Desde las villas 1.11.14, 21-24 y la 31 (entre otras) llegaron las primeras denuncias y videos.


Alejandrina Barry, legisladora porteña con mandato cumplido por el PTS en el FITU y con una trayectoria de casi 20 años como operadora social en la 21-24, respondió duramente al cinismo de Jorge Macri y su “ley y orden”.


Desde la Coordinadora contra los Desalojos y por la Vivienda Digna que vienen enfrentando los desalojos ilegales de Jorge Macri y su ladero “el desalojador” Walter Gómez Diz tambien criticaron fuertemente el operativo. “Repudiamos enérgicamente a estos gobiernos hambreadores y enemigos de los laburantes y la gente humilde. El mismo gobierno que en las calles de la Ciudad arremete contra vendedores ambulantes, jubilados, docentes y toda aquella organización de los de abajo. Ya les demostramos con una enorme Marcha de la Bronca que fuimos miles los que salimos a la calle. Repudiamos y nos solidarizamos con lxs vecinos del @movdevillasybarriospopulares”, replicaron en su comunicado.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida por Docentes de la 9 de Abril – Corriente Nacional (@9deabril.docentes)


Docentes, trabajadores de la salud y vecinos cortaron la calle en repudio al operativo en la 21-24


Después de ver cómo sus alumnos llegaban al colegio espantados por el operativo policial de la noche anterior, organizaron junto a trabajadores del Cesac y vecinos cortar la calle Iriarte en las inmediaciones del barrio para repudiar la escalada represiva de Jorge Macri contra los sectores más abandonados por el Estado.


En la tarde noche del jueves, de forma intempestiva se dieron operativos en 15 barrios y villas porteñas, entre ellas la 21-24. Con un despliegue de saturación policial, Jorge Macri reeditó el operativo Tormenta Negra del pasado 15 de mayo. Con policías de la Ciudad, Infantería, helicópteros, motos, cuatriciclos y camiones jaula durante horas montaron su show represivo el mismo día en que el Indec publicaba que 1 de cada 3 habitantes es pobre en la Argentina de Milei. Esa fue la respuesta del Macri para los vecinos y vecinas de los barrios populares al hambre, endeudamiento, precariedad laboral y estructural que sufren.


Federico Puy, docente de una de las escuelas del barrio, integrante del Consejo Directivo de Ademys, estuvo a la cabeza de organizar esta acción de repudio que debe multiplicarse. Junto a otros docentes, trabajadores de la salud y vecinos del barrio realizaron un semaforazo sobre el cruce de la avenida General Iriarte e Iguazú en el barrio de Barracas, a metros del acceso a la 21-24.

title: Karasu: Rıza Altun’s struggle will always guide us
content:
Rıza Altun, one of the leading cadres of the Kurdistan Freedom Movement, and those who lost their lives in the Freedom Movement’s struggle were commemorated at an event held in Paris.


In a video message to the commemoration, KCK (Kurdistan Communities Union) Executive Council member Mustafa Karasu spoke about Rıza Altun’s activities from the early years of his involvement in the struggle until his death. Karasu said that Altun assumed responsibilities in various areas of the Freedom Movement, from organizing work in Ankara’s Tuzluçayır neighborhood to Antep, from resistance in prison to his activities in Kurdistan and diplomatic work, highlighting his qualities as an organizer and activist.


Karasu also saluted commemorations for the martyrs that have been held in many cities across Kurdistan over the past month after the announcement of their deaths. He said that the public’s participation in and support for these commemorations had given them great morale.


The message sent by KCK Executive Council member Mustafa Karasu to the commemoration in the French capital is as follows:


“I greet all our people who have gathered to commemorate Comrade Rıza. This is the seventh anniversary of Comrade Rıza’s death. Comrades Baz and Garzan, together with Comrade Rıza, lost their lives in an airstrike on September 25, 2019.


As we remember these comrades, commemorations for the martyrs have been taking place across Kurdistan for the past month. Once again, I remember all those martyrs with respect and gratitude. I also commend our people who have participated in these commemorations with great enthusiasm.


Comrade Rıza holds an important place in the history of our party. He was one of the first cadres of our struggle. Our movement was a group that emerged among university students in Ankara and initially organized within the university youth.


The Apoists were organized among university students in Ankara. They also organized in Tuzluçayır, a neighborhood in Ankara known as ‘Little Moscow.’ Comrade Rıza was the leading figure in organizing the Apoist group in Tuzluçayır.


Comrade Rıza organized dozens of young people and brought them into the struggle. It was him who secured Tuzluçayır’s support for our movement. Just as he brought many young people from Tuzluçayır into our struggle, he also involved his entire family in it from the very beginning. His family became part of the struggle as well. Indeed, one of his brothers and two of his nephews lost their lives in this struggle. In this respect, his family stands among the foremost examples in the history of our struggle and our movement of families who participated collectively.


This in itself demonstrated what kind of militant Comrade Rıza was and what kind of Apoist he was. Because he believed deeply in this struggle and devoted himself to it completely, his entire family also became involved and took part in the struggle, and young members of the family lost their lives.


Comrade Rıza and I went to Kurdistan toward the end of 1976, more precisely, at the end of the summer. We went to Kurdistan at almost the same time. A month earlier, I had gone to Antep with Doğan Kılıçkaya, a valued militant from Tuzluçayır who later lost his life and whose nom de guerre was Yasin. A month later, Comrade Rıza also came to Antep.


At that time, Antep was one of the first places where our struggle developed and became most influential. Comrade Rıza played a very important role in this. While our struggle in Antep developed into a major struggle against fascists, a party culture also emerged there under the leadership of Comrade Haki. Comrade Rıza also played a role in shaping this party culture.


Comrade Rıza was truly known as a militant within the struggle. He was an important and influential militant of the Apoist group. He was very composed and highly effective in the struggle against fascists. While he was in Ankara, in Tuzluçayır, he also waged a significant struggle against fascists. During his struggle there, Comrade Rıza’s code name was ‘Şirket’ (‘Company’). He was given this name because of his organizational abilities.


In Tuzluçayır, a truly effective struggle was waged against fascists under Şirket’s leadership. Comrade Rıza was not only an influential militant in our freedom movement’s struggle against fascists, but also served on the first military council of our movement. Together with Comrade Mehmet Karasungur, he was a member of the military council.

title: Donald Trump and the Age of Evil
content:
By any standard of morality, Trump is depraved. But adorned with the power of the state, he descends to another level — the level of evil.


 


CHRIS HEDGES


25 SEP, 2026


 


Donald Trump exhibits the classic traits of psychopaths — superficial charm, grandiosity and self-importance, need for constant stimulation, a penchant for lying, deception and manipulation and incapacity for remorse or guilt.


 


But is he evil?


 


If, as the philosopher Susan Nieman

writes

, evil is not simply the opposite of good but inimical to it, if the aim of evil is to destroy all moral distinctions, then Trump qualifies as evil. Morality, for Trump, is for losers. All life is transactional. Self-interest and self-enrichment usurp all other considerations. No one else matters.


 


In her new

book

, “Call It Evil: Understanding the Trump Era,” Neiman argues that evil “isn’t cruelty but something much worse: the ideas that allow cruelty to become ordinary.”


 


She continues:


 


There’s a difference between calling one action evil and calling another a crime. Crimes are things for which we have procedures—at least for punishing, if not for preventing. This means that a crime can be fit in some way into the rest of our experience. To call an action evil is to suggest it cannot—and that it thereby threatens the trust in the world that we need to navigate it. There’s no signpost on the border between evil and awful. Evil is what you say when your jaw begins to drop if you sense that a line has been crossed.


 


Trump crosses line after line. He

declares

 wars on a whim. He

enriches

 himself and his family in crypto schemes, from which he has made over a billion dollars. He orders

assassinations

 and the

kidnapping

 of heads of state. He uses billions of taxpayer dollars to sustain genocide in Palestine and since January 2025 has

provided

 over $20 billion in new arms sales to Israel. He

guts

 government departments designed to lift up the vulnerable and

bloats

 the war budget. He builds

rogue

 paramilitary forces to terrorize citizens and immigrants. He attacks and attempts to

censor

 the news industry.


 


In short, he does what all who commit evil do.


 


He fosters a world where nothing is sacred and where democracy and civic virtues do not exist.


 


Concepts of fairness, decorum, justice and empathy are imploded by the Trump administration. His

threat

 to annihilate Iran – i.e. carry out genocide – announced of all places at the United Nations, is greeted with indifference by a public rendered numb by his moral vacuity.


 


“Once the supremacy of self-interest is enshrined as commonsense realism rather than a philosophical idea, moral capacities like empathy and shame become not just naïve but suspect,” Neiman writes. “Sadists exist and cause no end of pain. But the most common forms of evil arise from the view that only fools believe in anything but their own advantage.”


 


The institutions designed to protect democracy, to safeguard civic virtues, to foster equality — including the courts, law firms, universities and the media, all of which have been captured by the billionaire class — swiftly fell to their knees to curry favor with the Trump White House. The titans in Silicon Valley

showered

 him and his campaign with millions of dollars. The supposed virtues these institutions and individuals claimed they championed were jettisoned. These virtues, they illustrated, were nothing more than branding, performance art, a sham.


 


To an enraged public Trump’s transparent greed and cruelty is preferable to the slick hypocrisy of the politicians, Republican and Democrat, who preceded him. He does not engage in their faux empathy. In fact, he seems incapable of empathy.


 


Once morality is for fools, virtue makes no sense. Once we believe we should grab what we can, even at the expense of those around us, we surrender to evil.


 


“Unlike the rest of us, he permanently exhibits the combination of motives we are told are the true forces driving human behavior,” Neiman writes of Trump:


 


Nor does he appear to understand any other. Though he recognizes that other people, aka losers, have norms, he has no idea of how norms work, moving people to override self-interest in order to honor them. In acting on the international stage like Richard Dawkins’s ruthless genes, he has attracted millions of followers who tell us they admire his authenticity. This doesn’t mean his followers …

We join women, girls, and human rights defenders across Africa and the globe on this 28th day of September to commemorate the 2026 International Safe Abortion Day, reaffirming a simple truth: safe abortion is essential healthcare.

We are reminded of the transformative power of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol), which is lauded as one of the most progressive and comprehensive legal instruments for the promotion and protection of women’s rights globally, particularly in the area of sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR). Adopted in 2003 by the African Union, the Protocol goes beyond existing international human rights standards by explicitly articulating a wide array of SRHR protections that are often left ambiguous or unstated in other international and regional human rights instruments.

Article 14 of the Maputo Protocol guarantees women’s rights to health and reproductive autonomy, including the right to control their fertility, decide on family size and spacing, and to choose their method of contraception. Most critically, Article 14 makes the Maputo Protocol the first and only binding international human rights treaty to explicitly guarantee access to safe medical abortion in specific circumstances—namely, where the continued pregnancy endangers the mental or physical health of the mother or the life of the mother or the fetus, or in cases of sexual assault, rape, or incest. This Article also mandates access to comprehensive reproductive health services, including antenatal care, safe delivery, family planning, and sexual and reproductive health education. In doing so, the Protocol moves abortion access from a matter left to state discretion to one of binding treaty obligation — a distinction that remains central to the advocacy for its full domestication across the continent.

Currently, 46 of the 55 African states have ratified the Maputo Protocol, while nine – Burundi, Chad, Egypt, Eritrea, Madagascar, Morocco, Niger, Somalia, and Sudan – are yet to ratify it. Bringing these final states on board is vital because over 150 million African women and girls currently live outside the protective legal framework of the Maputo Protocol.

Despite its progressiveness, 9 out of the 46 member states have placed reservations to various provisions of the Maputo Protocol, with Article 14 being the most reserved provision. A reservation lowers the minimum human rights standards contained in a particular treaty for the reserving states and enables the reserving states to escape accountability for human rights violations.

Currently, Africa accounts for 70% of global maternal deaths. These preventable deaths are compounded by persistent gaps in access to sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) services, which are essential to safeguarding the lives and dignity of women, children and adolescents. title: Women in Amed call for a united struggle against femicide
content:
Following the femicide of Ayfer Çakmak, women in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) called for a united struggle against patriarchal violence. At the initiative of the DEM Party Women’s Council, numerous women gathered at a busy intersection in the Bağlar district. Ayfer Çakmak, 32, was killed by her husband, O.Ç., on September 25 in the 5 Nisan neighborhood of Bağlar. While the 37-year-old perpetrator was arrested after the killing, the investigation into the femicide is ongoing.


Participants in the rally included DEM Party Women’s Council spokesperson, Halide Türkoğlu, representatives of political parties and women’s organizations, and Amed Co-Mayor Serra Bucak. Ruçem Vefa Elyakut, co-chair of the DBP’s Amed provincial organization, pointed out that women are often killed by men in their immediate surroundings. “Enough is enough. We will not remain silent in the face of these killings,” Elyakut said.


‘Violence against women is a structural problem’


Serra Bucak rejected treating femicides as isolated incidents unrelated to one another. Violence against women is a structural problem and must be addressed accordingly, she said. Bucak particularly criticized shortcomings in the justice system and in the implementation of Law No. 6284 on the protection of women from violence. She noted that municipalities had established various structures to protect women from violence, but could not solve the problem on their own. In this context, she also recalled Rojin Kabaiş and Gülistan Doku. Women and families, she said, must not be left alone in their struggle for truth and justice.


Women are often killed in their own homes


Halide Türkoğlu said that the rally was prompted in particular by the femicide of Ayfer Çakmak, while the protest was also directed against ongoing violence against women as a whole. “Women are being killed precisely in places where they should feel safe, often by the men closest to them. At the same time, women are fighting both male violence and state policies that enabled such violence,” Türkoğlu said.


Türkoğlu stressed that women have the right to live freely and as equals rather than having to fear for their lives. “Can there be a greater disgrace than the murder of a woman?” Türkoğlu asked, stressing that overcoming patriarchal violence cannot be left to women alone. Equality, she added, is a responsibility for society as a whole.


Call to society as a whole


Türkoğlu therefore also addressed men directly, calling on them to take responsibility in the struggle against patriarchal violence. She also appealed to the DEM Party, municipalities, civil society organizations, human rights defenders, shopkeepers, and taxi drivers to join the collective struggle. “Come, let us all take a stand against violence together. Come, let us strengthen this struggle together.”


The rally ended with the slogan “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” [Woman, Life, Freedom].

author: David Swanson
title: Parliamentary Dialogue on Peace in Cameroon on the Occasion of International Peace Day 2026
content:
Africa, International Day of Peace, Nonviolent Activism

By Guy Feugap, World BEYOND War’s Africa Organizer, September 27, 2026

On the occasion of the International Day of Peace, celebrated on September 21, 2026, a parliamentary dialogue focused on peace, social cohesion, and the protection of populations was held in Cameroon at the invitation of the United Nations in Cameroon. The meeting, held at the National Assembly headquarters, brought together representatives from Parliament and the Government, civil society organizations, and various stakeholders and partners committed to promoting peace and combating gender-based violence, femicide, and infanticide. Cameroon, already mired in armed conflicts, is now characterized by growing insecurity for people in their daily lives. Unfortunately, institutions have proven unable to prevent and respond to the various forms of violence threatening the population.

The first session of the parliamentary dialogue, dedicated to Parliament’s role in promoting peace, focused on how the National Assembly, the Senate, and members of Parliament can use their constitutional functions and public leadership to contribute to a peaceful environment. Discussions focused in particular on inclusive dialogue, nonviolent political participation, prevention and early warning, accountability in political communication and information, as well as the protection and inclusion of women, youth, people with disabilities, and other vulnerable groups. Peaceful dispute resolution and dialogue were also identified as important elements of peacebuilding.

The second session was devoted to strengthening prevention and response to gender-based violence, femicide, and infanticide. Introduced by the Vice President of the National Assembly and the United Nations Advisor on Peace and Development, among others, the dialogue addressed these forms of violence as issues involving human rights, protection, justice, public health, governance, and peace. The discussions shed light on a troubling situation. The rise in certain forms of crime and violence is an additional cause for concern. Femicide and infanticide—including in places where women and children should be protected, such as homes and schools—illustrate the scale of the challenges facing Cameroonian society. Civil society reaffirmed its role in educating and raising awareness among the public, as well as in advocating for a legal framework to better prevent and punish these crimes. In this regard, World BEYOND War and WILPF Cameroon launched a letter-writing campaign addressed to the Prime Minister, Head of Government, to draw the authorities’ attention to the urgent need for strengthened action against femicides.

On the government’s side, it was noted that the process of drafting the bill on gender-based violence is at an advanced stage and that the text is nearly finalized. Parliamentary representatives, for their part, indicated that they are ready to review and vote on the bill as soon as it is officially submitted to them. This prospect was one of the key takeaways from the dialogue: the need to translate the concerns expressed by civil society and other stakeholders into concrete institutional and legislative measures. Beyond the adoption of a law, the discussions also highlighted the importance of a coordinated response encompassing prevention, reporting, referral of victims and survivors, protection, investigation, prosecution, justice, psychosocial support, and institutional coordination.

The parliamentary dialogue held on International Day of Peace 2026 thus brought together two dimensions that are often addressed separately: peacebuilding and the struggle against gender-based violence. For civil society organizations working on these issues, preventing femicides, infanticides, and other forms of violence is not merely a matter of justice or the protection of human rights. It also contributes to building a peaceful society, in which every person can live free from violence and where institutions fully assume their responsibility to protect. The organizations that participated in this session will continue to ensure that the commitments and discussions arising from this meeting are translated into concrete actions.

title: Kocaeli'de kadın cinayeti: Fatma Çiğil eski eşi tarafından katledildi
content:
Kocaeli'nin Körfez ilçesinde 54 yaşındaki İbrahim Ç. eski eşi 37 yaşındaki Fatma Çiğil'i sokakta ateşli silahla vurdu. Derince Eğitim ve Araştırma Hastanesine kaldırılan yaralı Çiğil müdahalelere rağmen kurtarılamadı.

Yerel basın, Fatma Çiğil'i Vadi Sokak'ta vurduktan sonra olay yerinden kaçan İbrahim Ç.'nin kısa süre önce cezaevinden çıktığını aktardı. Ses Kocaeli'nin haberinde saldırganın daha önce de Körfez Belediyesinde silahlı intihar girişiminde bulunduğu belirtildi.

Polis, cinayeti işleyen İbrahim Ç.'nin bulunması için çalışma başlattı.

Kadın Cinayetlerini Durduracağız Platformu verilerine göre 2026 yılında en az 256 kadın, erkekler tarafından katledildi. Ağustos ayında 22 kadın erkekler tarafından öldürülürken, 33 kadın da şüpheli şekilde ölü bulundu. Ağustos ayında işlenen kadın cinayetlerinden yüzde 64’ünde ateşli silah kullanıldı.

author: Cameron Mitchell
title: ‘No Bystanders’ concert highlights violence against women, raises funds for charities
content:
Caitlin Davies with the support of Australian Femicide Watch, Socialist Alliance, Violent Butterfly Records and other activist groups organised a fundraising concert on September 5 to highlight and educate people about violence against women.

The mixed-bill hardcore concert, titled No Bystanders, heard from 14 local bands, which volunteered to allow ticket proceeds to go to relevant charities.

The all-ages concert included face painting for children and adults, provided by Rhee Brown, and merchandise stalls which lined the Royal Park Hall venue, between two stages.

Each band, hosting several mosh pits, drew an impressive crowd. The energy of the punk/metal music matched the anger felt towards the injustice women face.

The stories of women who have become victim to femicide were highlighted. The wall was filled with faces of women who had been killed by men from 2024 to 2026. The memorial allowed participants to write letters to be read by speakers affected by domestic violence.

Two women, in particular, were the focus of photo collages: Ebony Lee and Ali Lauren. Lee, a close friend of Davies, had her life taken earlier this year. Lauren, a local, was murdered last year by a conspiracy theory podcaster.

Davies said a fundraiser after Lee’s death had raised $46,000 for victims of male violence, and was one of the main inspirations behind No Bystanders.

Violence against women is reaching catastrophic levels. Australian Femicide Watch reports that 49 women and 19 children have been killed by male violence this year, and more than 1300 women and children have been killed since 2000.

Femicide has been exacerbated by the rise of reactionary “manosphere” influencers, such as Andrew Tate, whose profile big tech algorithms push to young men.

Attendees reflected on all the issues at a candlelit vigil towards the end of the night.

Erinn, another volunteer, read Davies’ speech: “We’re standing here surrounded by the faces of women whose lives were taken by violence. They weren't statistics. They were people. They were loved. They had families, friends, futures, whole lives that should never have been cut short. They should still be here.

“A while ago, we lost my two friends, Ebony and Tam, within six months of each other. Their life ended because of a lot of complicated reasons, and so much of that traces back to male violence and the fall-out of it. That kind of harm doesn’t stop in one moment. It keeps moving through people. It affects their mental health, their safety, their relationships, the way they cope, and the weight they have to carry.”

Davies said it is important to stand up against this violence. “What you walk past, you accept. That’s part of why I called this event No Bystanders. Because silence is not neutral. Looking away is not neutral. Grief on its own is not enough. If we actually want things to change, then we have to be willing to look at this clearly, call it what it is, and do something with that.”

The event raised $10,000, of which $8000 was donated to Australian Femicide Watch, and a further $2000 to ERICA Women’s Centre.

Davies told Green Left afterwards that she wanted the event to focus on encouraging young people to recognise the signs of sexual or domestic violence “so that kids can see what toxic relationships can turn into”.

author: Jian Sanz
title: CLSU Student Regent red-tagged in latest attack on student leaders
content:
Image of packaged sent to Balllesteros (photo from CLSU USSC)

Central Luzon State University Student Regent (CLSU SR) Rashela Ballesteros received a package containing red-tagging messages around 12:30 pm on September 17 at the University Supreme Student Council (USSC) office.

The package, sent by a certain Jared Mariano from Guimba, Nueva Ecija, contained a red-tagging message formatted as a love letter, an altered photo showing Ballesteros’s face pasted onto a soldier’s body, and a list of requirements to become an officer in the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP). The letter in the package read, “Hope I’ll see your smile in campus.(sic)”

In a statement, Anakbayan CLSU condemned yet another harassment and red-tagging of Ballesteros, reiterating that incidents like these result in serious violations of students’ rights to security and freedom of expression.

“This is a threat not only to SR Ballesteros, but also to the democratic rights of the entire CLSU community. It is crucial to protect the freedom of students to voice their demands and participate in social issues, both inside and outside the university,” the youth organization added.

The organization also compared the tactic to the documented methods used by the AFP and National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC) against several student leaders in CLSU. They noted that this incident is a form of surveillance and harassment against Ballesteros, especially since this is reportedly not the first suspicious attempt to contact her.

Related story: Youth groups sound alarm over red-tagging, forced interrogation of student leader

Ballesteros also serves as the national convener of Network Opposed to Pax Silica (NO to Pax Silica), and convener of the Movement Against Destructive Solar Farms (MADSOLAR) and Save the Rice Granary (STRG).

The CLSU University Supreme Student Council (USSC) called the harassment an attack on the broader student masses of CLSU as well. They also noted that the package came months after Ballesteros stood against the continuous cases of surveillance, harassment, red-tagging, and intimidation suffered during the first week of classes in the university.

Since 2024, Ballesteros, fellow student activists and leaders Eyu Bartolome, Cairo Sandoval, and Loi Matias, have faced repeated red-tagging and harassment by military forces and the NTF-ELCAC. Notably, on June 12, 2026, two unidentified men approached CLSU employees to inquire about Ballesteros’s whereabouts.

CLSU USSC also emphasized that despite the university’s formation of a committee addressing red-tagging and attacks on CLSUans, attacks on student activists persist in the university. (RVO)

title: Día de Acción Global por el acceso al Aborto Legal y Seguro
content:
Ante el Congreso de la Nación, colectivas y activistas feministas se manifestaron “para defender el derecho a decidir, el acceso a la salud sexual y reproductiva, la Educación Sexual Integral y todos los derechos conquistados gracias a nuestra lucha”.

Bajo la consigna “Educación sexual para decidir, anticonceptivos para no abortar y aborto legal para no morir”, la Campaña Nacional por el Derecho al Aborto Legal, Seguro y Gratuito junto a otras organizaciones y activistas realizó un pañuelazo en la Plaza del Congreso, denunciando el “vaciamiento sistemático de las políticas de salud sexual y (no) reproductiva” por parte del gobierno nacional de ultraderecha de Javier Milei.


Desde hace más de tres décadas, el 28 de septiembre se conmemora el Día de Acción Global por el Aborto Legal, una fecha que nació en América Latina y que cada año reactualiza la consigna por el derecho a decidir. Su origen se encuentra en 1990, cuando durante el V Encuentro Feminista Latinoamericano y del Caribe realizado en San Bernardo,  activistas de toda la región declararon el 28 de septiembre como Día por la Despenalización y Legalización del Aborto, a partir de una propuesta de la delegación brasileña que recuperó un antecedente histórico: ese mismo día de 1871, Brasil promulgó la Ley de Libertad de Vientres, que liberaba a los hijos de mujeres esclavizadas.


La sanción de la Ley 27.610 en 2020 convirtió a Argentina en referencia regional: la norma garantiza la Interrupción Voluntaria del Embarazo hasta la semana 14 y la Interrupción Legal del Embarazo en casos de violación o riesgo para la salud. Sin embargo, las organizaciones que convocan a la movilización advierten que, si bien la ley continúa vigente, el acceso efectivo al aborto enfrenta problemas de financiamiento, provisión de medicamentos y desigualdades territoriales. Entre las dificultades señaladas figuran recortes en políticas de salud sexual, dificultades en la provisión de anticonceptivos y medicamentos como misoprostol y mifepristona, y retrocesos en programas como el Plan ENIA.


En ese marco político, el presidente Milei volvió a atacar al feminismo y al aborto legal: frente a su público favorito, empresarios, responsabilizó a los sectores que impulsaron la legalización por la caída en la tasa de natalidad.


Desde las organizaciones feministas y sectores académicos se responde que la baja de la natalidad no se explica por la interrupción del embarazo, sino por causas económicas y sociales como la precarización laboral, la falta de vivienda y la sobrecarga de cuidados.

title: Rencontre avec Sandeep Bakshi sur Frontières queer
content:
Jeudi 15 octobre à 19h30, rencontre avec Sandeep Bakshi pour la sortie de son livre Frontières queer, sexualité, colonialité, décolonialité. La rencontre sera animée par Zaid du collectif sud-asiatique/Brown antiraciste.


Le queer est-il seulement occidental

 

? Conçu au cœur même des Empires, son lexique est-il utile loin des métropoles et logiques coloniales

 

? Dans cet ouvrage, Sandeep Bakshi remet en question les généalogies admises du queer pour échapper aux instrumentalisations et aux normalisations dont il est l'objet.


Partant de pratiques et d'analyses des Suds, ce livre montre que, si les études et le militantisme queer ont produit des formes de pensée radicales, elles ne sont pas immunisées contre les a priori culturels, sociaux et raciaux. Le queer, lui aussi, a sa colonialité. Dès lors, c'est en adoptant une perspective décoloniale que le queer retrouvera toute la vigueur de son insurrection initiale, pour semer à nouveau le trouble.

author: TGEU
title: TGEU contributes expertise to new guidance on SOGIE rights in detention
content:
TGEU served on the Expert Advisory Group for the publication Advancing SOGIE Rights in Detention: Promising Practices, a new guidance note published by the

Association for the Prevention of Torture


(APT). This included providing initial input on the project, reviewing a first draft during a consultation meeting in Geneva in March 2026, and providing expert feedback on an advanced draft.


The publication documents promising practices by governments, prison administrations, staff and oversight bodies to improve conditions for LGBTI people in detention. It pays particular attention to trans communities and highlights approaches that address the structural challenges faced by LGBTI people deprived of liberty.


The publication was presented during a dedicated session at the TGEU Trans Council in Ljubljana on 11 September 2026.


read the publication


Advancing SOGIE Rights in Detention: Promising Practices is available in English, Spanish, French and Portuguese.

author: Bram Sable-Smith
title: Missouri’s Abortion Rights Face a Second Vote in Two Years
content:
Abortion returns to ballots in Missouri and other states as voters and lawmakers reshape post-Roe policies.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

After Missouri voters added abortion protections to the state constitution in 2024, Kelly McCoomb decided to keep her yard sign supporting the measure in the basement of her suburban St. Louis home.

Abortion access is important to McCoomb. She wants her daughter to grow up in a state where the option is available if needed, and the sign was a keepsake from the day Missourians voted to reverse the state’s near-total ban. McCoomb also couldn’t shake the feeling that she’d need to display the sign in her yard again soon.

“I have little faith in our Missouri government,” McCoomb said, sitting on her front porch.

Sure enough, just two years later, the state’s Republican-dominated legislature is asking Missouri voters to overturn the abortion protections they recently supported. The conflicting measures even have the same title: Amendment 3. But while a “yes” vote in 2024 supported adding protections to the state constitution, a “no” vote in 2026 would keep them. McCoomb covered the “YES” on her yard sign with a “NO” made from black duct tape before placing the sign back in her yard.

Voters will weigh in on abortion in Missouri, and three other states, in the November general election. Missouri is also one of two states voting on it for the second time since 2024. Nevada will vote again, too.

The spate of referendums comes after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned federal abortion protections with its 2022 decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, leaving each state to make its own abortion policy. The result has been a patchwork of state rules with varying degrees of bans or limitations, and even a series of “shield laws” in states where abortion remains legal that aim to protect providers from prosecution in states where it’s not.

“I just think there’s a constitutional crisis that’s coming,” said Kristi Hamrick, vice president of media and policy for the anti-abortion organization Students for Life Action.

“Can you have 50 state standards on whether or not a human being is a human being? Can you have 50 state standards on whether human beings have legal protection?” Hamrick said.

That patchwork of abortion protections is the reason Nevadans for Reproductive Freedom introduced the 2024 ballot measure to enshrine the state’s law allowing abortions up to 24 weeks after conception into the state constitution, said Denise Lopez, president of the coalition.

The measure received strong support two years ago, with 64% of voters in favor. Nevada law requires two majority votes to enshrine constitutional amendments, so voters will need to support the expanded protection again in November for it to be enacted.

The Nevada ballot measure wouldn’t change the state’s existing law allowing abortions up to 24 weeks after conception. But the proposal would make it more difficult to overturn abortion access, requiring voter approval of any new ban in two elections.

Lopez said Nevadans for Reproductive Freedom has been campaigning to ensure voters are still mobilized.

“Folks care about it,” she said. “They’re seeing what’s happening at the national level, and they want to make sure that whatever’s happening in our neighboring states, like Idaho and Utah, doesn’t happen here in Nevada.”

Idaho, where a ballot measure establishing abortion rights recently qualified to go before voters in November, has one of the strictest abortion bans in the country. Voters will decide whether state statute should allow abortion through fetal viability, the point when a fetus can survive after birth, which is generally considered to be around 24 weeks.

In Utah, abortion is allowed up to 18 weeks while legal challenges to the state’s ban continue.

In Virginia, where abortion is already allowed through two trimesters of pregnancy, until 28 weeks, voters will decide whether to amend their state constitution to codify those rights.

Missouri is the only state voting this year on removing abortion protections already on the books. The measure would repeal the 2024 amendment that guaranteed abortion access through fetal viability in the state and replace it with a ban on abortions with exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies, and pregnancies resulting from rape or incest. Abortions for rape and incest …

author: Isaac Nellist, Chiara Reeves
title: USyd students vote to cut ties with Israel
content:
Students at the University of Sydney (USyd) have overwhelmingly voted for an academic boycott of Israel in a referendum held alongside elections for the Student Representative Council (SRC) over September 22–24.

Honi Soit reported that more than 3500 students, 86% of the 4065 students who voted, were in favour of calling on USyd to adopt an “academic boycott policy against Israeli institutions complicit in apartheid and genocide”.

The referendum motion called on the university to cut ties with Israeli universities, including Tel Aviv University, Technion and the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

It also called on management to “end all research partnerships with weapons companies supplying Israel” and for the SRC to “support the struggle for Palestinian freedom”.

All four candidates for SRC President supported the referendum, including incumbent president Grace Street from Grassroots, Emma Searle from Socialist Alternative (SAlt), Ava Cavalerie from National Labor Students (NLS) and Vieve Carnsew from Solidarity.

The referendum was activated by Carnsew and Students Against War/Solidarity after they collected at least 500 signatures.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese gave Carnsew and Solidarity’s “Globalise the Intifada” ticket more coverage by describing it as a “hateful slogan”.

Albanese, NSW Premier Chris Minns and federal Education Minister Jason Clare reportedly contacted university management about the campaign. USyd Vice-Chancellor Mark Scott described the ticket a “psycho social hazard” and banned the ticket from using its signage on parts of the campus.

The Globalise the Intifada ticket said “the smears against our slogan are racist attempts to cover for these crimes that our government and university are complicit in”. “Intifada is the Arabic word for uprising … we are proud to campaign under the slogan. It is a call to end the genocide in Gaza and to free Palestine.”

The referendum result indicates that students support the university taking stronger action to support Palestine and oppose Israel’s genocide.

“Management is attacking the ticket whose members initiated the referendum … this is another blatant attack on the Palestine movement on campus, and an attack on free speech,” Students Against War said on social media.

Honi Soit’s exit polls say Street is likely to win an unprecedented second term as SRC President, collecting 41% of the primary vote. This was followed by Cavalerie (30.5%), Searle (20%) and Carnsew (2.88%).

SAlt won the highest percentage of SRC council votes, with 25%. This was followed by Grassroots (22%), NLS (13%) and PENTA (13%).

Street told Honi Soit that: “Students have said ‘Enough is enough’, that they stand against these oppressive systems and institutions, and that they are fed up with our university’s complicity in apartheid and genocide. We need collective action and a strong student movement, and that’s exactly what students have voted for.”

[Isaac Nellist and Chiara Reeves are students at the University of Sydney. Reeves stood on the Grassroots for Queer Liberation ticket.]

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Expert on white nationalism in Canada disturbed, not surprised by demonstration at Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc
content:
A public demonstration by the white nationalist group Second Sons of Canada on land near the Kamloops residential school site over the weekend sent shockwaves across the country. For people who study the group and others like it, it was not surprising.


“White Nationalism 3.0 has emerged as a unifying organizational model within Canada’s white supremacist ecosystem,” wrote Steven Rai in

 Tribe and Train

,

 a March 2026 article which examined “Canada’s new model of white supremacist mobilization.”


Photos circulating Sunday showed men in black clothing, white face coverings and matching caps on the

Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc

 reserve, some with flags. A later image appears to show the same group on the Pacific Way overpass in Kamloops holding a banner that read “Got Bones?”


“Despite frequent rebranding and occasional infighting, groups that have adopted this model (including

Second Sons

 of Canada and the so-called Active Clubs) share a common strategy, unifying a previously fractured movement. This has allowed them to foster sustained growth since their emergence in Canada in 2021,” Rai, a senior research manager at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue Canada (ISD), wrote. ISD provides ” threat detection, analysis and real-world strategies to combat terrorism, extremism and authoritarianism – in all their ideological forms,” according to its website.


Active Clubs are decentralized networks of white supremacist and neo-Nazi cells that masquerade as fitness and mixed martial arts clubs. 


Since late 2024, these groups have increasingly engaged in public demonstrations for propaganda and recruitment purposes as well as to mainstream extremist narratives and expand influence,” Rai said in the report. 


In an interview with

APTN News

 Tuesday, Rai said Sunday’s display served a specific purpose.


“It was incredibly disturbing to see, but, unfortunately, having tracked this network for a number of years now, it did not surprise me that this happened,” he said. “And it’s not a coincidence that this demonstration happened just a few days before the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. 


“This group is very much capitalizing on the increased attention right now in the public on the residential schools and the atrocities against the Indigenous peoples and they realized that by conducting this rally at this time they are going to maximize their impact and their visibility amongst the Canadian public.


“So as vile and shocking as it was to see them engage in this activity, it’s unfortunately quite par for the course that they would pick an opportunity like this to kind of ruffle feathers and get attention from people,” Rai added. 


The demonstration happened on Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc land where 215 anomalies were announced on May 27, 2021 following a ground penetrating radar survey.


Political leaders from across the country, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous, condemned the group Monday for its action. Notably absent from the voices speaking out was Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, who was photographed shaking hands with Jeremy MacKenzie, the founder of the far-right, anti-government Diagolon movement, which is associated with Second Sons, according to a report from

Canada’s National Observer.


The photo was taken in August 2022 during a Nova Scotia campaign stop in Dartmouth during Poilievre’s leadership campaign. Poilievre’s campaign team later disavowed racism and stated the leader was unfamiliar with MacKenzie at the time of the impromptu handshake. Later in 2022, after MacKenzie made threatening and misogynistic comments regarding Poilievre’s wife, Anaida Poilievre, Poilievre denounced MacKenzie and referred the comments to the RCMP for investigation.


“They’re hoping that by engaging in demonstrations like this and getting their name out there and their cause out there that they will reach some Canadian individuals who may be like-minded in their views so that they could hopefully recruit them to their cause and further indoctrinate them,” Rai said. 


“So, I think it’s incredibly important, given that longer-term strategy about trying to normalize those political views, that people in positions of power speak forcefully and powerfully against this kind of mobilization and to really contextualize some of the very sensitive issues that are taking place right now and some of the sensitive topics of conversation to really tease out the nuances with which we need to understand these issues.” …
