title: Trump, yapay zeka yerine "süper zeka" teriminin kullanılmasına ilişkin kararnameyi imzaladı
content:
ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, "yapay zeka" (AI) yerine "süper zeka" (SI) teriminin kullanılmasını öngören başkanlık kararnamesini imzaladı.

Beyaz Saray tarafından yayımlanan bilgi notuna göre, kararname, tüm bakanlık ve kurumların resmi yazışmalar, kamuoyu duyuruları, politika belgeleri ve yasal nitelikte olmayan tüm evraklarda "süper zeka" ve "SI" terimlerini kullanmasını zorunlu kılıyor.

Kararname ayrıca Başkanın Bilim ve Teknoloji Danışmanına bu teknolojinin mevcut durumunu yansıtan bir "süper zeka" tanımı hazırlaması talimatı veriyor.

Öte yandan Trump, önde gelen teknoloji şirketlerinin yöneticileriyle imzaladıkları belgeyi sosyal medya hesabından paylaştı.

Trump ile "Beyaz Saray Süper Zeka Mutabakatı" başlıklı belgeyi imzalayan Alphabet Üst Yöneticisi (CEO) Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO'su Dario Amodei, Meta CEO'su Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI Başkanı Greg Brockman, xAI CEO'su Elon Musk ve Nvidia CEO'su Jensen Huang, sorumlu teknoloji geliştirmeye yönelik taahhütlerde bulundu.

Paylaşılan belgede, "ABD halkı ve dünya için olumlu bir gelecek inşa etmek amacıyla, her şirketin kendi teknolojisini güvenli bir şekilde ve müşteriler ile kamuoyunda güven inşa edecek bir yolla geliştirmekten sorumlu olduğuna inanıyoruz" ifadesine yer verildi.

Bu durumun öncü modelleri eğiten ve dağıtan her şirketin, teknolojilerinin amaçlandığı gibi davranmasını ve herhangi bir sorunun derhal tespit edilip çözülmesini sağlamak için sağlam iç süreçlere ve kontrollere sahip olmasıyla başlayacağı vurgulanan belgede, şirketlerin uygulaması gereken kontrol ve denetimler sıralandı.

Belgede, söz konusu adımların her şirkete, müşterilerine ve kamuoyuna teknolojinin amaçlandığı gibi çalıştığına dair güven vereceği ibaresi yer aldı.

Şirketlerin sistemlerinin güvenliğini artırmak amacıyla standartları ve en iyi uygulamaları belirlemek için düzenli olarak toplanacağı aktarılan belgede, "Zamanla, bu adımları yasalara veya yönetmeliklere dönüştürmek mantıklı olabilir. Bunun şirketlerden talep edilip edilmediğine bakılmaksızın, bu kontrolleri ve denetimleri uygulamanın herkes için güvenli bir gelecek sağlamada kritik olduğuna inanıyoruz ve her bir şirketimiz bunu yapmaya kararlıdır" ifadeleri kullanıldı.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Kebaowek Nation pulls out of nuclear consultations, saying other parties failed
content:
Kebaowek First Nation announced Tuesday that it is suspending consultations on the proposed nuclear waste dump near its territory after it says the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) and Canadian Nuclear Laboratories (CNL) “failed to meet critical commitments.”


According to a press release from Kebaowek First Nation, CNSC and CNL informed Kebaowek leadership that they would “no longer fund the Nation’s participation costs as previously understood,” and also that they would “end their participation in the co-development of a consent-based agreement to support the process.”


In

a decision in February 2025

, Federal Court Justice Julie Blackhawk found that the CNSC failed to consider the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in developing plans for nuclear waste dump in Kebaowek’s ancestral territory. Blackhawk ordered CNSC and CNL to consult with Kebaowek through an Indigenous-led Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) process. That FPIC process has also been suspended as a result of Kebaowek’s ending consultations.


In a statement emailed to APTN News, CNL representatives said they have engaged with Kebaowek and its representatives for 19 months in accordance with Federal Court instructions.


“Following this the parties will participate in a further regulatory proceeding to enable the CNSC to reconsider whether the duty to consult was satisfied, in view of UNDRIP, as directed by the Court,” the statement said. “It is CNL’s understanding that the CNSC’s reconsideration process will be public, as will CNL’s submissions regarding the efforts it has made and the resources it has provided to KFN [Kebaowek First Nation] to facilitate meaningful and robust consultation aimed at satisfying the instructions of the Federal Court.”


CNL representatives did not address questions about whether they had ended funding or had ended their participation in the FPIC process.


CNSC also sent comment to APTN by email. They wrote that the renewed consultation with Kebaowek has been fruitful, and that the CNSC “has been listening, adapting and working with KFN  to collaboratively incorporate Kebaowek law, knowledge, and practices into the process.”


“While the CNSC has provided feedback on the proposed process agreement and remains open to discussing with KFN,” representatives write, “the immediate priority has been to continue the substantive consultation. CNSC staff remain committed to continued dialogue and collaboration with KFN throughout the renewed consultation process on near surface disposal facility and beyond.”


They added that they are continuing to make funding available to Kebaowek for both the renewed consultation process and commission hearing, though they did not address questions about Kebaowek’s allegation they had ended the funding necessary for the FPIC process.


Kebaowek Councillor Justin Roy said he was shocked to receive a letter on Aug. 21 informing him, he said, “that they’re not going to be giving any more funds that we need to not only finish the work, but to cover expenses we have already incurred. With that announcement in funding, that has led to Kebaowek being indebted significant sums of money while also not being able to finish all the work that we’ve been working towards the last 10 months.”


Since August, he said, he has been in discussions with CNL and CNSC to find a way through the situation.


“They wanted more facts on the funds that we incurred,” he said. “I gave them all those facts. The last three weeks has been a lot of back and forth and hoping to try and find a solution, a way forward. But unfortunately, no one wants to budge and no solution is being found.”


The FPIC process and the R&R law


Following Blackhawk’s decision last year, Roy said the community worked to develop its FPIC process, which led to Kebaowek creating its own Rights and Responsibilities Assessment law (known as the “R&R law”). Roy said the community plans to use the R&R law for all future consultations involving unceded Algonquin territory, and the Near Surface Disposal Facility (NSDF) for nuclear waste, related to the nearby Chalk River Laboratories facility, is the first project to be subject to the new legislation.


“A key part of the law is the creation of an assessment committee that’s made up of Kebaowek members that help drive the law and work with a member of council, and one of our technical staff and the whole team. We put that committee in place in the beginning of …

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: Indian hospital survivors shape future of $385M foundation as northern claimants navigate compensation process
content:
For decades, Indigenous patients were sent to federally operated hospitals where they could be segregated from other patients and subjected to psychological, verbal, physical and sexual abuse; now, survivors are being asked what should happen next.


The Federal Court approved a settlement June 24, 2025, involving 33 Indian hospitals operated by the federal government at various times between 1936 and 1981.


The

settlement

 provides individual compensation to eligible primary class members and establishes a $385.5 million foundation intended to support healing, research, education and commemoration.


The claims process and work to establish the foundation are happening at the same time, but they serve different purposes.


For northern claimants, accessing compensation can come with additional barriers.


Public awareness


Dr. Mike DeGagné, who is leading engagement sessions with the Indian Hospital Engagement Foundation for the future foundation, said Survivors have an opportunity to help shape what it should look like.


“If I go somewhere in Canada and I mention Indian residential schools, everybody sort of knows what I’m talking about, but if I say Indian hospitals, often they have no idea,” DeGagné said.


That lack of public awareness was a focus of a Yellowknife engagement session Sept. 22, one of a series being held across Canada.


DeGagné told APTN News participants discussed the need to share the history of Indian hospitals with a wider audience, along with ideas such as scholarships, curriculum development, and opportunities for Survivors to document their own experiences as they see fit.


The $385.5 million foundation will manage two funds. A $150-million healing fund and a $235.5 million research and commemoration fund.


DeGagné, who has spent decades working on Indigenous healing initiatives including the Aboriginal Healing Foundation, is helping lead the cross-country engagement process.


The settlement agreement requires the foundation’s structure, activities, design and establishment to be informed by engagement with Indigenous stakeholders, including class members and Indigenous communities.


“From what I understand, that’s the first time a settlement has said, before you set things up, you have to ask people what they want,” DeGagné said when comparing the settlement to prior agreements such as residential schools and day homes.


X-ray being taken by a technician from Ottawa in the Hudson’s Bay Company Store in Lutselk’e, 1955. Many people from the NWT who suffered from tuberculosis were sent to Edmonton for years to recover, usually at the Charles Camsell Hospital. NWT Archives/©Bart Hawkins/N-1992-254-0116.


Commemorating the hospitals


“It’s great to have a giant statue on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, but it’s just as good to have one in front of the hospital here in town so that it reminds patients of the current hospital about the Indian hospital system,” DeGagné said.


Commemoration rooted in specific places came up repeatedly during the engagement process, he said.


“Survivors have discussed monuments at former hospital sites, travelling exhibits in existing hospitals and museums where students and young people could learn the history,” DeGagné said. “Some have also suggested recognizing the experiences of hospital staff.”


Participants at the Yellowknife session also discussed healing and the need to avoid creating another set of programs separate from existing Indigenous mental health and healing services.


“I think what it is is to take a look at what is happening now in mental health and healing, and then piggyback on that a little bit,” DeGagné said. “We may not create new programming around mental health, but we can maybe extend it to a whole wider group of people, so provide access.”


Access to medical records


Access to medical records has emerged as a major issue during the engagement process.


“I went to an Indian hospital, I came home with a scar. I couldn’t tell you why it was there,” DeGagné said, describing what he had heard from Survivors.


The records can be difficult to locate as they may be held by health authorities, hospitals, universities or archives.


“When we talk about research, we really talk about what records exist and where to find them,” DeGagné said.


According to information available from the settlement administrator, claimants do not require medical records or hospital documents to submit a claim.

author: The Canadian Press
title: Manitoba to purchase private campground near site of former residential school
content:
The Manitoba government is partnering with the province’s second-largest city to purchase a private campground where historical records show a cemetery for children who died at a residential school is located.


Premier Wab Kinew announced his government is working with the city of Brandon to acquire the Turtle Crossing Campground site, located south of the former Brandon Indian Residential School in western Manitoba.


A news release says the cemetery was used from 1985 to 1912 after the area was converted into a suburban park.


First Nations groups have long advocated for a search of the area to determine how many children were buried in the area and their identities.


Kinew says any future decisions regarding the site will be be done in consultation with residential school survivors, impacted First Nations and advocacy groups.


Chief Jennifer Bone of Sioux Valley Dakota Nation says any searches will be Indigenous-led and technical expertise and community knowledge will help guide the work.


“This is important work for our nation and for Indigenous Peoples across Canada,” she said in a joint statement with the province.


The First Nation previously worked with researchers to investigate unmarked graves at the former Brandon Indian Residential School.


It has said more than 50 are on the campground.


Church records and provincial vital statistics files have documented the cemetery for generations, a Tuesday news release said.


“These graves have been known about since long before the invention of ground-penetrating radar,” said Kinew.


In 2001, the land was sold and developed as Turtle Crossing Campground.

author: Chris Walker
title: Johnson Pitch to Voters: GOP Will Keep Doing “What We Have Been Doing”
content:
Polling data indicates that likely voters want change, not more of the same, as the speaker of the House is promising.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

During an interview on CNBC on Tuesday, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) attempted to persuade viewers to vote for Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections, suggesting that Americans want a repeat of the last two years, despite polling indicating otherwise.

“What we would do in the next two years is exactly what we have been doing already,” Johnson said, attempting to make the case for his party retaining control of Congress.

Johnson also claimed that the GOP is “putting the conditions in place for a strong America,” citing a supposed “vibrant economy” — disregarding a number of worrying trends, including rising grocery costs, gas prices exceeding $5 per gallon on average across the country, and other indicators demonstrating that the “Trump economy” isn’t delivering what was promised.

“We have so much more to do, and we can make things so much better,” Johnson added in his televised appeal to voters.

Mike Johnson on what Republicans will do if they hold the House: "What we would do in the next two years is exactly what we have been doing already" pic.twitter.com/WSUZ2x9cBG

Many critics have lambasted congressional Republicans for acting as a “rubber stamp” for President Donald Trump’s executive actions. In response to Johnson’s interview, one Democratic lawmaker condemned Republicans for defending Trump’s agenda at every turn.

“Protecting child predators, facilitating extra-judicial murders, jacking up everyone’s prices through tariffs and military misadventures, all so that Donald Trump can get rich and he doesn’t yell at you, is a hell of a closing message,” wrote Rep. Sean Casten (D-Illinois) on Bluesky. “But totally on brand for Mr. Johnson.”

Johnson’s remarks come as the Republican Party is polling poorly among voters. According to an Economist/YouGov poll published on Tuesday, the Republican Party’s net favorability rating is presently -25 points among likely voters. While both parties have negative marks from voters, that number is significantly worse than the Democrats’ -15 point approval rating.

Voters are split when it comes to whether the Democratic Party is extreme. But a majority of likely voters, 56 percent, view the GOP as extreme, while only 39 percent disagree.

Asked who they plan to vote for in the 2026 elections, 53 percent of likely voters said they were backing the Democratic option in their House district, while only 38 percent said they were going to vote for the Republican — a 15-point difference in favor of a change in leadership.

Political observers have noted that Republicans’ continued fealty to Trump is likely dragging them down further in the polls. Indeed, Trump’s approval rating average is dipping into the low 30s and sinking even into the 20s range in some surveys, potentially spelling disaster for the GOP come November.

An NPR/PBS NewsHour/Marist poll from earlier this month asked voters whether their preference in congressional races was based on being “a vote for President Trump,” with only 24 percent saying that it was. Meanwhile, a plurality of respondents, 45 percent, said their pending choice was meant to signal “a vote against President Trump.”

In spite of mounting evidence of voter dissatisfaction with Republicans, Johnson has indicated that he believes the GOP will retain control of Congress.

“We’re gonna win the midterms. I’m very bullish about the outcome. … This is a God thing,” Johnson said in July.

title: Conference in London discusses international experiences of peace and political settlement
content:
The Centre for Kurdish Affairs (CKA) convenes the Peace and Democratic Integration Conference in London on 29–30 September 2026, bringing together Kurdish political and civic figures, parliamentarians, policymakers, academics, peace-process practitioners, journalists, researchers and representatives of civil society.


The conference provides a structured and non-partisan forum for examining the prospects for peace, democratic participation and political settlement in relation to the Kurdish question, with particular attention to the evolving process in Turkey and its wider regional and international implications.


The conference is taking place at a significant stage in the current political process. In August 2026, the Turkish Parliament adopted the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Cohesion, establishing a legal framework for certain procedures connected with the disarmament, dissolution and reintegration process, subject to the conditions set out in the legislation. The law was approved by Parliament on 10 August and published in the Official Gazette on 18 August 2026.


This development represents an important institutional stage in a process that now raises questions extending beyond the cessation of armed conflict. These include the future of democratic politics, political participation, local governance, legal guarantees, institutional reform, social reconciliation, rights and the reintegration of individuals and communities affected by decades of conflict.


The conference therefore seeks to examine how a political opening can develop into a sustainable, peaceful and democratic settlement, drawing both on international experience and on Kurdish perspectives from Turkey, the wider region and the diaspora.


Peace processes rarely conclude with a single agreement or legislative act. International experience demonstrates that the transition from armed conflict to sustainable peace involves a longer process of political, legal, institutional and social transformation.


The conference will therefore consider questions including:


● How can a political opening be transformed into a durable peace?


● What legal and institutional guarantees are required for confidence between political actors?


● How can former participants in armed conflict be reintegrated into political and civilian life?


● What forms of democratic participation can support a transition from conflict politics to democratic politics?


● How can constitutional and institutional arrangements accommodate political, territorial, linguistic and cultural diversity?


● What role can local and regional governments play in a sustainable settlement?


● How can women, minorities, civil society and the media participate meaningfully in peacebuilding?


● What can be learned from international peace processes, including experiences in Northern Ireland, Colombia, South Africa, the Basque Country and elsewhere?


● How might the Kurdish question evolve within the changing political and strategic environment of Turkey, Syria, Iraq, Iran and the wider region?


● What role can international actors, including the United Kingdom and European institutions, play in supporting peaceful and democratic political processes?


The conference is intended not simply as a discussion of the past, but as an opportunity to consider the political and institutional choices that will shape the next stage of the process.


Panel I - Why Peace Processes Succeed or Fail


The first panel examined the conditions that allow peace processes to move beyond an initial political opening and develop the resilience necessary for a durable settlement.


Drawing on comparative experience from cases including Colombia, South Africa, Cyprus and other international processes, the discussion considered the importance of political commitment, sequencing, implementation, institutional guarantees and public legitimacy.


It also examined why peace processes can become vulnerable to delay, reversal or renewed confrontation, and what lessons may be relevant to the Kurdish peace process.


The contributors of the first panel included Mahmoud Patel (Online); Radha D'Souza; Dr Andrei Gomez-Suarez; Mariela Kohon; Prof. Vasileios Fouskas; Victoria Sandino (Video Intervention). The panel was moderated by Mustafa Gündoğdu, a Kurdish author, editor and human rights practitioner with over two decades of experience in conflict resolution, peace processes and international legal …

title: Conference in London addresses issues of power-sharing and constitutional arrangements
content:
The Centre for Kurdish Affairs (CKA) has organized a Peace and Democratic Integration Conference in London on 29 and 30 September 2026, bringing together Kurdish political and civic figures, parliamentarians, policymakers, academics, peace-process practitioners, journalists, researchers and representatives of civil society.


Today, the conference’s second panel was titled “Peace, Power-Sharing, and Constitutional Arrangements: Lessons from the United Kingdom.” The panel explored the role of constitutionalism in conflict resolution, drawing on the UK’s experience of power-sharing, devolution and differentiated forms of governance. It will examine how constitutional arrangements can provide credible guarantees, distribute political authority and accommodate distinct political and territorial claims within a stable democratic framework. The discussion will consider what these experiences can offer to the Kurdish question, particularly how constitutional reform can provide durable channels for recognition, political participation and meaningful local authority while strengthening confidence in the wider political settlement. 


Speakers were Prof. Michael Gunter, Dr. Matthew Whiting, Prof. Michael Keating, Geraint Thomas, while Matt Broomfield was the moderator.


Prof. Michael Gunter said: “In Turkey, the so-called peace process that formally began in October 2024 between the government and the PKK is looking more like a PKK surrender. Turkey frames the process as little more than PKK disarmament and dissolution, while the PKK claims that it seeks constitutional rights as Kurds and the release of its incarcerated leader Abdullah (Apo) Öcalan. The two sides appear to be inhabiting two different universes, while the entire process seems interminably slow. The long-anticipated legislation amounted to little more than a humiliating PKK capitulation.”


Prof. Gunter added: “The so-called peace process was concluded on grounds that it amounted to little more than a virtual PKK surrender. Even those minor PKK members eligible for parole were given no guarantees once they had surrendered their arms and returned to civilian life. It would be relatively easy for the government to rearrest them on any manufactured excuse. The once formidable PKK now seemed to be in decline and on very shaky ground. The fate of Rojava or the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria is arguably the most prominent example of the Kurdish decline.”


Prof. Gunter continued: “Once held as a brilliant example of Kurdish self-government, its sudden collapse in 2026 after 14 years of existence was striking, but predictable. Although the ultimate outcome remains to be completely decided and the Syrian Kurds appear headed for a more positive position than the misery they suffered from under the Assad regime, Rojava’s sudden collapse resembled a Shakespearean tragedy. Although I have shared with you my serious doubts, we must all give the new current Turkish framework law a chance, even though it is at its best, only a modest beginning. Hopefully, this law offers us an opening for Öcalan’s call for democratization to benefit all Turkish citizens, Turks and Kurds  both. Despite his pessimistic evaluation, even Cemil Bayik did vouch, the [framework] law can act as a foundation.”


 


Dr. Matthew Whiting said: “They realised at some point in the 1980s, so 15 years before they took part in the peace process, that they could achieve their aims just as well through political means as they could through violence. If not, in fact, they were more likely to achieve them. So suddenly, in this sort of long reappraisal over a 15-year period, the movement went from violence being an asset and a sine qua non to violence actually being what's holding us back from being able to advance our political demands. And so we see this gradual shift in this way. We see a rebalance from the military element to the political element and embrace of exclusively political politics.“


Dr. Whiting added: “They said, okay, well, this shift to being political is a change in our tactics but not a change in our goal. We are still pushing our ultimate aim, which is the unity of Ireland, but what we're doing now is seeing how we can pursue short-term reforms to policies and not always say Brits out and that fix everything and then move on.


We can pursue fair employment law, we can pursue educational opportunities, we can pursue housing reforms, etc. As an example of that …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Opposition to AI Data Centers Is Actually a “Chinese Psyop,” Mike Johnson Says
content:
“This is not a conspiracy theory,” the House speaker added.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) has dismissed popular concerns among the American public over Big Tech’s hastened buildout of data centers across the U.S. as nothing more than propaganda pushed by the Chinese government.

In an interview on AI with Fox Business on Monday, Johnson was asked how he plans to fight back against Democrats seizing on opposition to data centers to attack Republicans in the midterm elections.

“I’ve had several tech executives and lawmakers, to be clear, say that the information against data centers, that push back against data centers, that is coming from China,” said Fox host Cheryl Casone.

“Yes,” replied Johnson. “Don’t buy it. It is a Chinese psyop.”

“I really believe that. It’s not a conspiracy theory,” he went on. He then contradicted himself, claiming that “the community concerns are important” and that companies seeking to build a data center must “ensure the local community they’ll be good corporate partners.”

Johnson’s comments ignore the massive, nonpartisan anti-data center movement that’s erupted in the past months.

A mountain of polls and grassroots campaigns across the country this year have revealed a groundswell of opposition to tech companies’ massive buildout of data centers amid the explosion of AI adoption. Proposals by tech companies to build data centers in communities across the country have been met with protests and organizing campaigns.

Polls repeatedly find that the vast majority of Americans say in surveys that they oppose the construction of a data center in their community, and the very concept of them is extremely unpopular, even among Republican voters.

A New York Times/Siena University poll conducted earlier this month, for instance, found that 61 percent of voters oppose the construction of AI-supporting data centers in the U.S. entirely, including 40 percent who said they “strongly oppose” the idea. Opposing voters cited water and environmental impacts, local resource usage, and distrust of AI as their top concerns.

Still, Republican officials and tech executives have tried to spread the conspiracy theory — which cybersecurity and media experts have cast doubt on — that it is China that is behind the opposition. President Donald Trump told Fox earlier this month that it’s a “China PR thing” that people don’t want data centers in their communities, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has blamed the opposition on a “propaganda war.”

Officials have cited reports from tech firms that claim to have rooted out and banned bot-run Chinese accounts that spread anti-data center sentiment. But these reports have not found evidence of a widespread campaign. Last month, X said that it found 200 Chinese anti-data center accounts — on a platform with more than 500 million monthly active users, according to owner Elon Musk. Meanwhile, OpenAI said in June that it banned a set of Chinese accounts that were highlighting harms of data centers to local communities, but admitted that the campaign didn’t gain much traction.

“This was not a case of an influence operation creating a debate. The debate existed already. This was an influence operation from China trying to interfere in it. We didn’t see any signs that they succeeded,” said Ben Nimmo, OpenAI’s principal investigator for threats, per NPR.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) criticized Johnson’s claim for sweeping aside public opinion.

“No, Mr. Johnson. The 75 percent of Americans who oppose data centers, including a majority of Republicans, have not fallen victim to a ‘Chinese psyop,’” said Sanders on social media on Tuesday. “They are rightly concerned about AI billionaires raising their electricity bills, destroying the environment and threatening humanity.”

author: Chris Walker
title: AI School Praised by McMahon Reportedly Does “More Harm Than Good” for Students
content:
“Accuracy of the content provided by the [AI] is a concern,” read an internal assessment of Alpha School’s lessons.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

During a Fox Business interview on Tuesday morning, Education Secretary Linda McMahon promoted the use of artificial intelligence in schools, citing a controversial online charter school that has been criticized for utilizing inaccurate and confusing AI-generated lessons.

When asked whether she viewed AI as a “tool” or a “threat,” the former World Wrestling Entertainment CEO chose the former.

“I certainly believe AI is definitely a tool used correctly, and I’ve seen it in action,” McMahon said in the interview. “I have visited the Alpha School in Austin, Texas, where they use AI for the first two hours every single morning.”

AI is an “additional tutor” that can provide “one-on-one instruction” to students, McMahon said. “It is incredibly effective.”

Alpha School is used by online-only K-12 students as an alternative for in-person learning across the country, and McMahon frequently touts the Austin-Texas-based company as a success story. Yet some families have reported concerns about its effectiveness, with parents warning that its lessons can lead to high stress levels among students.

Evidence of the online school’s problems was obtained and published by 404 Media earlier this year. The outlet reported that internal documents from the company suggested that AI lessons generated at the school were doing “more harm than good.”

For example, lessons and tests with questions often featured multiple-choice answers that didn’t make sense.

“These questions not only fail to meet SAT standards but also fall short of the quality we promise to deliver,” one employee’s assessment of the AI-modeled lessons read. “From a student’s perspective, when answer options don’t logically fit the question, it feels like a betrayal of their effort to learn and succeed. How can we expect students to trust our assessments when the very questions meant to test their knowledge are flawed?”

“Accuracy of the content provided by the [AI] tutor is a concern,” another internal assessment stated. “There are instances where it not only delivers incorrect answers but also provides convincing yet flawed justifications. Despite raising multiple queries about a particular answer, the chatbot erroneously confirmed an incorrect option as correct.”

Former employees of the company also expressed their concerns.

“Students are being treated like guinea pigs,” one former Alpha School employee said.

“Students incoming into AP Biology the previous year were seriously lacking in their foundational skills,” another employee noted.

Disturbingly, Alpha School also collects data on the students themselves, including video recordings, and publishes it to a Google Drive online. That folder, 404 Media reported in February, was made accessible to anyone who had the link.

“We are not computers or algorithms. We are simply people who need breaks. We are people that don’t like being watched through their computers,” one student said in a company feedback form.

The company also lacks transparency, making it difficult to conduct a real analysis of its successes or failures, said Victor Lee, an associate professor at Stanford University’s Graduate School of Education.

Alpha Schools “refus[es] to allow for any independent research to evaluate the claims or to really scrutinize what’s going on from disinterested parties,” said Lee, speaking to CNN about the school in January. “That sort of behavior sort of implies there’s something to hide.”

title: Israeli Settlers Violently Block Displaced Palestinian Family’s Return Home
content:
The family had been forced out after their home was besieged for weeks by state-backed settlers.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

More than 100 Israeli settlers in the illegally occupied West Bank rioted in the early hours of Tuesday morning to prevent the return of a Palestinian family that was driven from its home in the village of Jalud.

The Israeli military, which was forced by a court ruling to facilitate the Tubasi family’s return, said in a statement that rioting settlers “blocked roads,” “set fires” to structures and vehicles, and hurled rocks at security forces as they tried to escort the Tubasis. Haaretz reported that after the Israeli military failed to prevent rampaging Israeli settlers from storming the family’s homes, “they put the family members into an armored military vehicle and evacuated them from the scene.”

One family member told Haaretz that “half an hour later, smoke began to rise from the homes.” The Israeli military said that three Israelis were detained for taking part in the riots.

Hordes of settlers rioted overnight into Tuesday in the West Bank village of Jalud as Israeli forces failed to secure the return of a Palestinian family to its home, the IDF said this morning, despite a court ruling ordering that the family be allowed to return to their home… pic.twitter.com/U1Q26usZZY

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose government has been accused of “actively enabling” mass violence against Palestinians in the West Bank, issued a statement early Tuesday condemning the attacks while downplaying them as the work of a “handful of rioters.”

The Jerusalem Post reported that the Tubasi family’s return “had been coordinated after they were previously forced to evacuate following attacks by extremist settlers.”

“The attempted return followed a September 6 High Court of Justice order requiring Israeli authorities to arrange within 14 days for three Palestinian petitioners and their families to return to their homes in Jalud,” the outlet added. “The court ordered the IDF and police to protect the families during the return and allow them to bring in supplies needed to repair the homes and restore water and electricity.”

Tuesday’s riots were just the latest eruption of violence in the West Bank, where Israeli settlers are committing attacks on Palestinians at an unprecedented rate, according to data from the United Nations.

“Israeli officials are now condemning settler terror, but the state itself is backing this violence,” said Breaking the Silence, an Israeli advocacy organization. “The Tubasi family had been expelled because the IDF backed terrorists who besieged their house for weeks. They allowed terrorists to roam free while barring journalists and solidarity activists from accessing them.”

“Even after committing a pogrom, the vast majority of them, if not all, will never be held accountable and will continue to terrorize Palestinians,” the group added. “Why? Because the state backs it.”

The settler attack came days after the leading Israeli human rights organization B’Tselem published a report characterizing the Israeli government’s actions in the West Bank, including large-scale land seizures, as “an elimination project,” noting that Israel has “sharply escalated longstanding policies of control, violence, and dispossession, implementing them more openly, more violently, and at a faster pace.”

“What Palestinians are living through in the West Bank is not a series of separate incidents,” said Yuli Novak, B’Tselem’s executive director. “It is a single political project that reaches into every part of life. Communities are being expelled, the economy is being pushed toward collapse, and millions are living in constant fear of Israeli military or settler violence.”

“These mechanisms work together to dismantle Palestinian collective life while entrenching a permanent system of Jewish supremacy across the West Bank,” Novak added. “The world is watching and still failing to respond with anything close to the urgency this demands.”

title: NFL Threatened to Ban Player From Game for Honoring Slain Palestinian Girl
content:
Texans linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair wrote Wafaa Akila, the name of an 8-year-old girl killed by Israel, on his face tape.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

An NFL official reportedly threatened to remove Houston Texans linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair from his game earlier this month unless he removed his memorial for an 8-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israel in Gaza.

During the Texans’s week two game against the Cincinnati Bengals on September 20, Al-Shaair wrote the name of Wafaa Akila on his eye black, which refers to the strip or paint streaks that many football players wear on their cheeks.

Wafaa was an 8-year-old girl who was killed, along with her father, in an Israeli airstrike on a vehicle in Gaza City on September 6. She and her father were on their way home from her first day of school, according to Al Jazeera.

Al-Shaair, who is rated as one of the top linebackers in the league, was reportedly told by an NFL official that he would have to remove his eye black or else be barred from playing in the game, an anonymous NFL source told The Athletic. Al-Shaair complied, the reports said. Fox News’s sports vertical also confirmed the league’s threat.

The linebacker’s latest tribute came just days after the NFL gave him an $11,941 fine for writing Hind Rajab’s name on his eye black during the Texans game against the Buffalo Bills on September 13. In a show of solidarity, Dallas Mavericks player Kyrie Irving said in a post on social media that he would “take care of his fine.”

“It’s bigger to me. What’s a life worth? Is a life worth $11,000? I think it’s priceless,” said Al-Shaair when asked about the penalty.

“You can’t get so lost in your own problems that you can’t have compassion for other people in the world,” he went on. “We don’t have to have all the answers to everything to know that an innocent man, an innocent woman, an innocent child losing her life is not right … whether they’re here in America or somewhere halfway across the world.”

Ahead of the Texans game against the Indianapolis Colts this past Sunday, Al-Shaair once again wore the names of children killed by Israel — Lana and Bana Ahmed, two sisters who Israel killed along with their family in an airstrike earlier this month. The sisters were 12 and 8 years old.

The NFL gave Al-Shaair a similar fine in January when he wrote “stop the genocide” on his eye black during the pregame, but took it off for the actual game. At the time, he said that he was similarly told that he would be banned from playing in the game if he kept the message on.

“At the end of the day, it’s bigger than me. When things that are going on makes people uncomfortable — imagine how those people feel. I think that’s the biggest thing. I have no affiliation, no connection to these people other than the fact that I’m a human being,” Al-Shaair told reporters after that fine. “Even when I’m walking off this field, that’s the type of stuff that goes through my head, that I have to check myself — when I’m sitting here crying about football, when there’s people dying every single day.”

He was told that he violated league rules about displaying non-approved personal messages — but he pointed out that other players have written messages on their eye black without a fine.

“They always fine you, but I was told if I wore that in the game, I would be pulled out of the game,” he said. “I understood it was a fine, but I ain’t never seen Stef get pulled out of the game for having eye tape with writing on it.” Al-Shaair was referring to New England Patriots receiver Stefon Diggs, who frequently writes messages honoring his Christian faith on his face tape.

author: Solange Guimarães
title: Pesquisa: Vídeo de Porchat sobre Master “fura bolha” mas campanha de Lula falha nas redes
content:
O vídeo “Grandes Igrejas, Master Negócios, publicado pelo ator e comediante Fábio Porchat, na semana passada conseguiu dois feitos almejados pela campanha eleitoral do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, candidato à reeleição. O primeiro foi “furar a bolha” dos grupos já alinhados com as pautas de esquerda, e o segundo foi

explicitar o elo entre o maior escândalo financeiro do país,

o caso Master

, e o grupo político ligado ao principal adversário de Lula na corrida presidencial, senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ).

 A conclusão é do cientista político e diretor executivo da

Ipse Global,

 Leonardo Magalhães. 


“O Flávio Bolsonaro aparece como o segundo nome mais citado em um caso que nem é diretamente sobre ele, mas o envolve como um potencial beneficiário ou agente envolvido. Depois vêm o André Valadão com 11,6%, e o Nicolas Ferreira com 2,9%.”


O vídeo de Porchat foi alvo de um relatório da Ipse Global que realiza monitoramentos dos temas que movimentam a esfera pública digital para o desenvolvimento de estratégias de marketing político e eleitoral. Em entrevista à Agência Pública, Magalhães não aponta apenas pontos positivos sobre a campanha do presidente candidato à reeleição. 


Magalhães explica que o acesso ao vídeo do Porchat para fora da “bolha” de Lula não significa conversão em voto. “O material circulou mais fora do campo que o produziu do que dentro dele, o que é um caso raro. Mas o alcance não é [necessariamente] adesão. Nós medimos a exposição”, explica. 


Além disso, o cientista político afirma que o marketing eleitoral dos dois principais candidatos à Presidência da República estão perdendo oportunidades de obter resultados melhores nas redes sociais. O motivo seria a adoção de estratégias rígidas, ou como Magalhães nomeou: “receitas de bolo”. Para o diretor, o sucesso do filho do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro tem ocorrido nas frentes digitais da corrida eleitoral “mais por lacunas deixadas pela campanha do Lula do que por outra coisa.”  


O diretor executivo também faz um alerta, vindo das pesquisas qualitativas realizadas pela Ipse Global. A falta de confiança do eleitor nas instituições e no futuro segue crescendo, o que mantém um forte sentimento anti-sistema. 


“Quem vem com uma proposta de resetar o sistema, uma coisa muito forte em 2018, fabricada pelo [Jair] Bolsonaro, acaba mantendo um eleitorado cativo.

 E quem sugere uma mudança no sistema, segura esse eleitorado”, argumenta.


Segundo Magalhães, isso é um desafio para o presidente que está no poder e, para o eleitor, mantém e representa esse mesmo sistema. “A campanha do Lula não entendeu que precisa dar esperança, que as pessoas precisam de caminho. [Falta dizer] ‘olha, nós também estamos insatisfeitos, se nós pudéssemos, teríamos feito mais, não tivemos oportunidade, mas, a gente quer fazer mais’”, conclui. 


Leia os principais trechos da entrevista de Leonardo Magalhães à

Pública

: 


Cientista político e diretor executivo da Ipse Global, Leonardo Magalhães


No relatório sobre as reações ao vídeo do ator Fábio Porchat, os dados mostram que o engajamento diário saltou de 1,15% para 5,78% em uma semana. Esse vídeo conseguiu furar a bolha e chegar aos eleitores indecisos?


Chegou a quem não tem lado fixo, mas não há evidência matemática de que tenha convertido alguém.

Na análise de mídias sociais, você não consegue cravar a conversão de voto a menos que tenha uma massa histórica de dados muito explícita.

 O que o dado preciso nos mostra é que o engajamento quintuplicou em uma semana, e o pico não aconteceu no dia do lançamento do vídeo, mas no dia da remoção do perfil do ator pelas plataformas.


Foram duas pautas que se somaram: a denúncia original e a pauta da censura. Essa segunda acabou se sobrepondo, o que atraiu muito o público que consome teorias de conspiração e polêmicas. Entre os perfis sem posicionamento definido, uma em cada quatro publicações nomeava o vídeo ou o Porchat. Na bolha de esquerda, era apenas uma em cada oito. O material circulou mais fora do campo que o produziu do que dentro dele, o que é um caso raro. Mas o alcance não é [necessariamente] adesão. Nós medimos a exposição. 


Entre os nomes citados no caso, Daniel Vorcaro concentra o maior desgaste, seguido por Flávio Bolsonaro; instituições como a Igreja Batista da Lagoinha lideram o engajamento. É possível concluir que o episódio conseguiu ‘colar’ o escândalo do Banco Master ao campo bolsonarista?

author: Joe Sandler Clarke
title: UN’s Israeli Settlements Blacklist Names Firms With UK Public Contracts
content:
Several companies with major British government contracts have once again been named in a

UN database of firms

 involved in the expansion of illegal Israeli settlements.


The database names 214 companies – 61 more than the previous year – that the UN human rights office has “reasonable grounds to believe” are involved in activities linked to Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.


Earlier this month, the UK government announced new sanctions targeting the settlements, including a ban on the import of goods. 


Foreign secretary Ed Miliband

said the move

 – which will also involve action against companies that support settlement expansion – was the “beginning of a new approach”.


The firms named in the UN list include French infrastructure giant Egis, which operates the M40 motorway for National Highways; Motorola Solutions, which owns Airwave, the radio network used by British emergency services; and Heidelberg Materials, with which the UK government agreed a major carbon capture deal in 2025. 


Egis was listed for its role in planning the construction of a new light rail network in Jerusalem, which

rights groups say

 will connect Israeli settlements in occupied East Jerusalem with each other. An Egis spokesperson said the firm “has formally expressed its disagreement with this inclusion” in the UN database. 


Norwegian pension fund KLP

divested from Motorola

 in 2021 over the firm’s involvement in providing services for use in surveillance in the West Bank. 


Heidelberg directed us to

a statement it issued last year

 where it said its Israeli subsidiary had ceased all operations at the Nahal Raba quarry – located in the  West Bank – in 2023, and that neither it nor its Israeli subsidiary operates “any facilities in the occupied Palestinian territories, including East Jerusalem”. 


Spanish trainmaker CAF, which is involved in the Jerusalem light rail project, was also named in the UN list. The firm is in the running to build new trains for a suburban rail service in Scotland.

Trade unions have urged

 the Scottish government to exclude CAF over its links to the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank, while ScotRail drivers have said they will

refuse to drive

 CAF trains if the deal goes ahead. 


ScotRail, which has the final say on the new train deal, told Novara Media it is “committed to a thorough evaluation” to ensure the final decision on the deal is fair. 


CAF has said

 its “operations cannot be interpreted as contributing to, facilitating, or benefiting from settlement related practices”. 


On the publication of the most recent database, Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, said: “This report is another reminder to companies that they have human rights responsibilities and are expected to conduct due diligence to ensure that they do not become involved in human rights violations or abuses.” 


A spokesperson for the Scottish government’s transport department said its guidance holds that “firms who are exploiting assets in illegal settlements can be excluded from tender exercises for grave professional misconduct. The Scottish Government is clear that all Public Bodies should take any such evidence into account when deciding where to award public contracts.”

author: Alessandra Bergamin
title: Lebanon’s Environmental Defenders Say Israel Is Deliberately Targeting Them
content:
Israel has decimated Lebanon’s land — and is also slaughtering the people who protect it.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

In late April 2025, after 41-year-old farmer Oussama Farhat was discharged from the hospital, two pieces of shrapnel still lodged in his body, he hurried to check on an injured red fox. In his southern Lebanon village of Meiss el-Jabal, Farhat, a volunteer with the environmental organization Green Southerners, had helped rescue the cub from beneath the rubble of ongoing Israeli air strikes — the same kind that has decimated southern Lebanon and its people for the past three years. Now, the young fox was curled atop a starry blanket, its outstretched leg wrapped in a blue bandage.

In a message to Hisham Younes, the founder and president of Green Southerners, Farhat wrote that the fox cub would soon be ready for release.

Concerned, Younes replied: “Oussama, where are you?”

A member of the Lebanese Civil Defense, Farhat had been injured on April 25, 2025, after he and a fellow volunteer went to check for casualties unknowingly halfway through an Israeli double-tap strike — a tactic where an attack is followed by a second in the same location. In the days following October 7, 2023, Hezbollah, an armed group and political party formed in response to Israel’s 1982 invasion of Lebanon, launched rockets and artillery into occupied Shebaa Farms as an act of solidarity with the Palestinian people. Since then, Israel has continued to attack southern Lebanon near-daily, making Farhat’s village — just 700 yards from the UN-demarcated “Blue Line” that separates the two states — a hotspot.

After Farhat was discharged from the hospital, Younes implored him to go to Nabatieh, about an hour north, and rest with his family, including his elderly mother. But, says Younes, steadfast in his commitment to the south, Farhat explained that he needed to stay in Meiss el-Jabal.

“Please Oussama, you need to leave,” Younes replied.

The next day, Farhat was killed.

For the past three years and over two ceasefire agreements, Israel has systematically and violently erased life from southern Lebanon, committing what many, including Lebanon’s environment minister, have deemed an ecocide. An agricultural borderland in the heart of the historic fertile crescent, Israel has transformed southern Lebanon from small-scale and subsistence farms of tobacco, olives, and goats to a landscape set ablaze by white phosphorus munitions, littered with unexploded ordnance, and poisoned by the pesticide glyphosate. In a region where around 70 percent of families rely on farming, explained Ghassan Makarem, an organizer with the Lebanese food sovereignty organization AgriMovement, Israel has used airstrikes, shelling, and the steady roar of bulldozers to destroy around a quarter of the country’s cultivated land, burning olive groves to ash, slaughtering flocks of livestock, and flattening entire villages.

“Nothing that lives has been spared … It’s all part of the genocide that’s occurring.”

“Nothing that lives has been spared,” said Makarem. “It’s all part of the genocide that’s occurring.”

Since 2023, that genocidal violence, as described by multiple outlets, has displaced more than 1 million people, killing nearly 9,000 and injuring more than 30,500, mostly in the south. Included within that figure, alongside a high number of emergency services workers, are southern Lebanon’s land and environmental defenders — displaced, disappeared, injured, and killed, because of their commitment to steward and protect the land.

As Julia Choucair Vizoso, a senior fellow at the Arab Reform Initiative and researcher for The Public Source who has written about environmental struggle and food sovereignty in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), explained, Israel has long had a policy, stretching from occupied Palestine to southern Lebanon, of attacking those who resist occupation by refusing to leave. Because of that, farmers, shepherds, fishers, and beekeepers have not only suffered as Israel destroys their livelihoods and land, but have been marked as a threat because of their very connection to it in the first place.

Among those environmental defenders is Farhat.

Six years ago, explained Younes, the farmer reached out to Green Southerners asking how best he could help local animals, especially those that were injured or sick. Farhat soon became part of the all-volunteer team …

author: Chris Walker
title: Alito Reverses Course, Announces Recusal From Major Corporate Fossil Fuels Case
content:
The Supreme Court associate justice had previously refused to step away from a case involving fossil fuel companies.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito is recusing himself from a climate crisis-related case before the court this year, reversing his previous announcement that he would remain on the case despite his personal financial interests in its outcome.

Clerk of Court Scott Harris sent the announcement to attorneys on both sides of the pending matter on Monday.

“I am writing to inform the parties that Justice Alito has determined that he will not continue to participate in this case,” Harris wrote.

The letter gave no explanation as to why Alito came to the decision to recuse himself.

The case features ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy, which are seeking to have a Colorado-based lawsuit against them dropped, citing federal law they claim supersedes state statutes. State municipalities are suing the companies, seeking to hold them financially liable for the impacts of the climate crisis.

Alito does not have any financial stakes in either company. However, the associate justice does hold stocks in other fossil fuel-based companies, which means the outcome of the case could still directly benefit him.

Earlier this year, Alito said he would not recuse himself from the case, claiming that, because he doesn’t have any stocks in those companies specifically, he doesn’t have a vested interest in the case’s outcome.

“Justice Alito does not have a financial interest in any party,” a statement from the court read in May.

A coalition of progressive watchdog groups pushed back against that assertion, submitting evidence to Congress that Alito could be influenced by the pending ruling and urging lawmakers to investigate.

Alexandra Nagy, organizing director for Consumer Watchdog, one of the organizations involved in that request, reacted positively to Alito’s decision to recuse.

“Justice Alito’s recusal from Suncor v. Boulder is the right decision, and one he should have made from the start,” Nagy said, noting that “the Supreme Court’s Code of Conduct says a justice should step aside when the justice has a financial interest in the subject matter of a case or another interest that could be substantially affected by its outcome.”

“The public should not have to wonder whether a justice’s personal investments could benefit from a ruling that shields the fossil-fuel industry from liability,” Nagy added.

Others reacted to the decision by calling for limits on the stocks justices are allowed to invest in — if they’re allowed to have stocks at all.

“The real question is: Why does any justice hold stock in an individual company that is part of an industry that is going to appear before the court?” asked Louis Virelli, a law professor at Stetson University and an expert on judicial recusals.

Alito’s refusal to recuse in other key cases has been highlighted in the past, including in 2024, when he refused to step aside in cases involving January 6 defendants and in other high profile cases relating to President Donald Trump.

That year, it was revealed that Alito had flown a U.S. flag upside down — a symbol adopted by Trump loyalists and the “Stop the Steal” movement — outside of his Virginia home in 2021, shortly after Trump was impeached for instigating the January 6 attack. Alito also flew an “Appeal to Heaven” flag outside his home, a symbol commonly used by Christian nationalists.

This past Supreme Court term has been viewed negatively by most Americans. According to an Economist/YouGov poll conducted in July, only 36 percent of respondents gave the high court approving marks, while 50 percent said they disapproved of the court’s job over the past year. Alito also received a negative review, garnering a -7 point net approval rating from voters.

author: CMI Argentina
title: “Se crean más condiciones para el ingreso al sistema de encierro juvenil y menos oportunidades de salir”
content:
La Comisión Provincial por la Memoria (CPM) presentó la sección de niñez de su Informe Anual 2026, un diagnóstico sobre los lugares de encierro y el sistema de promoción y protección de derechos que realiza en su calidad de Mecanismo Local de Prevención de la Tortura. Con la presencia de funcionarios judiciales e integrantes de organizaciones por los derechos de la niñez, sindicales y políticas, se generó un espacio de diálogo y debate para pensar los desafíos en torno a las políticas destinadas a niños, niñas y jóvenes, en particular a partir de la puesta en vigencia de la nueva y regresiva ley penal juvenil. Los ejes de un debate de larga data que no parece avanzar en más oportunidades para las nuevas generaciones sino en más encierro y violencia.


Las políticas de niñez están en crisis y no pueden responder a los problemas actuales de les jóvenes. Las graves regresiones en derechos de la nueva ley penal juvenil son el último eslabón de una sistema que desde hace muchos años viene reforzando el sistema penal y punitivo en detrimento del sistema de promoción y protección de derechos. Un sistema que responde con más encierro y violencia a las y los jóvenes más vulnerables.


El diagnóstico parte de lo relevado por la Comisión Provincial por la Memoria en su calidad de Mecanismo Local de Prevención de la Tortura y se pública en la sección de niñez del Informe Anual 2026, El sistema de la crueldad XX, que el organismo presentó días atrás en su edificio.


Los datos aportan claridad a la discusión: la cantidad de niños, niñas y adolescentes abordados por el sistema de promoción y protección de derechos pasó de 41.511 en 2018 a 85.907 en 2025, sin que el sistema haya sido dotado de los recursos necesarios para ese abordaje. En el otro extremo se encuentra el fuero de responsabilidad penal juvenil extendido ahora por la nueva ley, aunque las estadísticas indiquen otro cosa: en los últimos 10 años la cantidad de jóvenes imputados descendió un 55% mientras que la de detenidos se mantuvo constante.


“Se recargan las capacidades de actuaciones punitivitas por parte de los mismos operadores judiciales que antes actuaban de otra manera. No logro entender esta extensión de la mirada punitivista sin nada que lo justifique porque el delito no creció”, describió brevemente el defensor del fuero penal juvenil de La Plata Ricardo Berenguer sobre las primeras reacciones de los funcionarios judiciales ante la puesta en vigencia de la reforma de la ley penal juvenil que bajó la edad de punibilidad a los 14 años y extendió, además, la persecución a delitos leves que antes no eran abordados por la justicia penal. El funcionario, no obstante, advirtió que la ley cristalizó acciones de la justicia que ya venían ocurriendo: “A la extensión de la prisión preventiva como regla se suma la retención de los jóvenes en el sistema. No hay revisión de las penas ni medidas morigeratorias, que sí se le conceden a los adultos”.


En esa línea coincidió la jueza de garantías del joven del departamento de Moreno-General Rodríguez Mirta Guarino: “Las llaves de cualquier medida, ya sea una internación en un hogar o una de seguridad, la tenemos los jueces, pero estamos en un momento muy crítico y hay magistrados que ni siquiera responden un teléfono”. La jueza también llamó a revisar el funcionamiento del sistema de promoción y protección de derechos que funciona en una fragmentación absoluta y aún más con el penal.


Los funcionarios judiciales fueron algunos de quienes tomaron la palabra durante la presentación de la sección de niñez del Informe Anual de la CPM junto a las organizaciones y el propio organismo. “Es el triunfo de las políticas neoliberales, que pensaron con estrategias muy precisas, como endurecer el sistema penal. En la provincia de Buenos Aires desde el gobernador Ruckauf hasta acá, se profundizaron las políticas punitivistas de mano dura y no podemos seguir sosteniendo que son los resabios del patronato: el sistema de promoción y protección ha creado sus propios monstruos”, señaló Roberto Cipriano García.


De hecho uno de los datos más sobresalientes del informe es cómo la baja en la edad de punibilidad que entró en vigencia recientemente a partir de la reforma de la ley penal juvenil ya se implementaba en los hechos: el 20% de los menores de edad encerrados en la Provincia durante 2025 tenían menos de 16 años y estaban detenidos con la aplicación de una medida de seguridad determinada por la justicia.

title: Besê Hozat: The process cannot succeed without democratization
content:
Besê Hozat, co-chair of the KCK Executive Council, said in an interview with Medya Haber that the Peace and Democratic Society Process cannot succeed in Turkey without democratization.


This is the first part of the interview.


The discussions regarding the Peace and Democratic Society Process are ongoing. As movement, you have already taken a number of significant steps in this regard. Also, before Parliament adjourned, the framework law – which you referred to as a law that creates a foundation on which to build on – was passed. What has been done afterward, and what hasn’t? Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş stated that the process is running smoothly. Do you assess it similarly?


Before addressing your question, September 25 marked the anniversary of the martyrdom of our comrade Rıza Altun. He was commemorated extensively both in Kurdistan and abroad, and many commemorations were held. I commemorate all the martyrs of the revolution and freedom – represented by our comrade Rıza – with respect, love, and gratitude. Our comrade Rıza holds a very significant place and value within our struggle. With his theoretical, ideological, political, and practical experiences, as well as his consciousness and expertise, he has contributed greatly to this struggle. He has contributed immense value to this struggle. On the path illuminated by comrade Rıza and all our martyred comrades, we will carry out this struggle successfully – with determination, conviction, and resolve – and we will achieve success based on the principle of living up to their memory. This struggle will lead to victory. I wish to reaffirm this pledge once again on the occasion of this anniversary.


Coming to your question; we have made several statements regarding the framework law. From the very beginning, both Rêber Apo [Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan] and our movement have clearly laid out our standing on this matter. We have made many assessments and statements based on the premise that this law should be a comprehensive one, that it should truly play the role of a foundational law, and that it should pave the way for a democratic solution to the Kurdish issue. This law did not fully meet these criteria, and accordingly, we have criticized it. It is an extremely flawed, internally contradictory, and paradoxical law. Implementing it as it stands – in a straightforward manner – is hardly possible anyway. This is quite clear. When we speak of the law’s comprehensiveness, it should have encompassed Rêber Apo’s physical freedom, his conditions for a free life and work, the leadership of the movement as a whole, and the entire organizational structure – from the top leadership down to every level – including Rêber Apo, who is excluded from the scope of this law.


The law should have demonstrated an approach and a commitment to taking democratic, political, and legal steps. It is known that both the emergence of the PKK and the armed struggle came about because of the lack of this. The existence of the Kurdish issue gave rise to the PKK and to the armed struggle. There is a very serious need for democratic, political, and legal steps that lay the groundwork for and pave the way toward resolving this issue. This law did not fully address this; that much is clear. It is also very, very difficult to describe it as a truly fundamental law in this regard. It is a legal text, and in that sense, it may have some significance. It is a step – a step on the legal level – that has emerged and developed within this process. However, it would not be realistic to ascribe much more meaning to it beyond that. Since the process began, we have taken very important steps as a movement. In particular, many steps were taken following the Call for Peace and Democratic Society on February 27, 2025 by Rêber Apo.


The PKK’s dissolution congress was a historic development. At this congress, the decision was made to cease armed struggle against Turkey. However, for this process to proceed, it was established as a fundamental requirement that Rêber Apo’s physical freedom be secured, allowing him to freely lead this process. This remains valid today. Numan Kurtulmuş made a statement the other day saying the process is running “like clockwork.” In reality, there is no such process running “like clockwork.” That is the truth of the matter. There is a process that is moving extremely slowly, a process driven by unilateral steps. At present, the state has not taken any …
